achad-anatomy-of-the-body-of-god-1925:
Geometry crowns Achad's trilogy in The Anatomy of the Body of God, printed in 1925. Charles Stansfeld Jones here throws the Tree of Life into three dimensions. Will Ransom drew the plates that give the scheme its solid form.

The spheres and paths of the Tree become a body that can be turned, cut, and viewed from each side. Achad holds that the flat Tree hides truths the solid one shows plainly. The book is bold, strange, and wrought with great care throughout. It ends his bold reworking of the Kabbalah he learned from Crowley. Few occult books of its decade reach so far.
adventures-of-huckleberry-finn-chapters-: The Duke and the King, those peerless frauds, take over the raft in these chapters, and Twain's satire bites deep. The circus, the camp meeting, and the Wilks swindle show human gullibility at full flood. Comedy with a moral sting.
almadel-sloane-3825:
The Ars Almadel survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825, a seventeenth-century English manuscript. The Almadel forms Part Four of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. Among the grimoires it counts as the gentlest high magic, concerned with good spirits rather than demons.

The art uses a wax tablet, the almadel, pierced and inscribed for the rite. Through it the magician addresses the angels of the four chorae, the quarters of the heavens. Colors, perfumes, and seals vary by quarter. The manuscript's own words guide the working step by step. Faithful transcription keeps a working magician's handbook readable in its original form.
anderson-dark-laughter-1925:
Sherwood Anderson published Dark Laughter in 1925, and it became the only bestseller of his career. Anderson had worked in Chicago newspaper rooms and Ohio factories, and both worlds meet here. The novel is also famous sideways: Hemingway's Torrents of Spring parodied its manner to break with Anderson's influence.

Bruce Dudley, a Chicago journalist, walks out on his wife and his job and drifts downriver under a new name. He takes factory work in Indiana and watches his employer's unhappy wife, drawn to the unforced laughter of Black workers around the plant. Anderson sets instinct against a tired, talkative civilization. The writing is loose and incantatory. Dark Laughter is his strangest popular success.
arcana-divina-paul-and-mary-mellon-colle: Arcana Divina, Paul and Mary Mellon Collection, 1725. The divine secrets. This book preserves that manuscript. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
ars-paulina-sloane-3825:
The Ars Paulina, the Pauline Art, survives here in a transcription of Sloane MS 3825. It forms Part Three of the Lemegeton, the Lesser Key of Solomon. The seventeenth-century English manuscript teaches the art of the spirits who govern the hours of the day and night.

Angels of the hours, and of the signs of the zodiac, fill its tables. The magician calls them with seals, prayers, and a table of practice. Compared with the Goetia's demons, these are orderly celestial clerks. The transcription keeps the manuscript's working detail intact. Students of the Lemegeton need the Paulina to see the whole system: hell in Part One, heaven's timetable here.
arxiv-2511-20425:
Gingrich repairs a modified gravity theory so its equations stay consistent. His 2025 paper applies the generalized uncertainty principle to gravity. That principle tweaks the basic rules of position and momentum. Implemented through deformed Poisson brackets, the theory breaks canonical form. Its constraint equations then likely fail to produce a proper metric.

Gingrich constructs a new Hamiltonian for the same physics. Under the usual canonical rules it yields the original metric. The constraint algebra closes, restoring mathematical consistency. The repaired theory is both canonical and covariant. Scalar matter and dust are then coupled in covariant fashion. That coupling allows real dynamical questions to be studied. Within black holes and near the Big Bang, such models may resolve singularities. The work comes from the University of Alberta and TRIUMF. Phenomenological models like this hint at what quantum gravity might do. Canonical consistency is a minimum requirement for trusting them.
arxiv-2511-20725:
Deng Fucheng and four colleagues survey in 2025 five algorithms that train deep learning models by gradient descent, the process of nudging a model's settings downhill on its error. Their five are stochastic gradient descent, its mini-batch variant, Momentum, Adam, and Lion. The survey is written for practitioners choosing and tuning an algorithm, not for theorists.

For each, they give the core idea, strengths, weaknesses, and advice. Stochastic gradient descent traces back to the Robbins-Monro framework of 1951 and remains the baseline. Its behaviour anchors the comparison. On convex problems its error gap shrinks like one over the square root of the step count. On strongly convex ones it shrinks like one over the step count. Mini-batches trade noise for better hardware use, Momentum smooths the path, and Adam and Lion adapt step sizes per parameter. The survey ends as a tuning reference across model scales and training scenarios.
arxiv-2511-20825:
Mingcheng Sheng proves in 2025 that two flows can be spectrally invisible to each other, generically. The systems are special flows built over irrational rotations, also called von Neumann flows: a point circles at constant speed while a roof function stretches its vertical timing. Two flows are spectrally orthogonal when their spectral measures share no component, a strong form of independence between the systems.

Sheng treats two roof types. When the roof is real analytic and the starting flow is weak mixing, a dense G-delta set of parameters works. Those flows are weak mixing and spectrally orthogonal to the original. When the roof is piecewise smooth with one discontinuity, the conclusion strengthens: for a full-measure set of parameters, the two flows are spectrally orthogonal. The results extend Kolmogorov's work and Shklover's 1967 weak-mixing examples, paralleling recent theorems for interval exchange transformations.
arxiv-2511-21025:
Shijia Yang and colleagues ask in 2025 a blunt question about image captions: could a downstream system work from the caption alone, without the picture? Their benchmark, CaptionQA, judges captions by utility. It spans four domains, natural images, documents, e-commerce, and embodied AI, with taxonomies of 25 top-level and 69 subcategories marking what information tasks need. Annotators wrote 33,027 multiple-choice questions, about 50.3 per image, all requiring visual facts.

A language model answers using only a model's caption, and the score gap against image-based answers exposes lost utility. Strong proprietary models dropped 9.2 to 16.4 percent when fed captions instead of images. Open-source models lost 11 to 32.4 percent, and the embodied AI gap exceeded 40 percent on the hardest split. Two models nearly tied on standard image-QA diverged by up to 32 percent here. Caption quality, the authors argue, should be measured by usefulness, not resemblance.
arxiv-2511-21325:
Ido Nitzan Hidekel, Gal Lifshitz, Khen Cohen, and Dan Raviv hunt fake voices in the part of the sound most detectors ignore, in 2025. Neural networks learn low frequencies first, a quirk called spectral bias. Audio generators therefore leave their sloppiest artifacts in faint high-frequency details. Their system, SONAR, splits each clip into two views. One path encodes the dominant low-frequency content. A second path, with learnable high-pass filters, distills the fragile high-frequency residuals.

Hidekel and his coauthors reunite the views with frequency cross-attention. A contrastive loss pulls real recordings' patterns together while pushing fakes apart. On the ASVspoof 2021 and in-the-wild benchmarks, SONAR reached state-of-the-art detection scores and converged four times faster than strong baselines. It stayed robust under audio codecs and bandwidth shifts, the distortions that usually break detectors in the wild.
arxiv-2511-21425:
Muhammad Bilal and Ashwin Renganathan build faster stand-in models for supersonic airflow in 2025. Engineers use reduced-order models, compact surrogates trained on expensive simulations, to explore designs quickly. The standard POD approach excels on smooth flows but mangles shock waves: when shock position shifts with flight conditions, the surrogate smears the shock, stair-steps it, or invents oscillations.

Bilal and Renganathan's CRLS framework smooths each simulation snapshot with a Gaussian blur before extracting POD modes, choosing the blur settings by Bayesian optimization. Coefficients are interpolated across conditions, then a regularized least squares deconvolution, centered on the nearest known snapshot, sharpens the shocks back. Tested on transonic flow over the RAE2822 airfoil, CRLS located shocks more accurately with lower pressure errors than standard baselines. It also needed 42 percent fewer modes to capture the same share of flow energy.
arxiv-2511-21725:
Yizhou Xu and Janet Davis introduce PromptTailor, a system that rewrites rough user instructions into strong prompts for small language models, in 2025. Lightweight models suit on-device and privacy-sensitive use, but their output quality swings wildly with prompt wording. Non-expert users rarely craft good prompts consistently, and optimizer tools often drift away from what the user actually wanted.

PromptTailor expands minimal instructions into rich, domain-aware prompts while preserving stated preferences. The engine is a quantized Llama3-8B model with a small LoRA adapter, fine-tuned on 12,300 prompt-refinement dialogues spanning 41 everyday domains. Those dialogues were distilled from three stronger teacher models. In human and automated judging, PromptTailor beat chain-of-thought prompting on preference rates. It matched or surpassed leading prompt optimizers while needing fewer model calls, three versus nine in one comparison.
arxiv-2512-00025:
Federated learning trains shared models on many devices without gathering their raw data in one place. Yun Ji and co-authors study a version with several edge servers whose coverage areas overlap, in a 2025 study. Clients in the overlap zones can reach models from more than one server, which complicates training.

The authors propose a relay framework that stays aware of delay when it moves information between clients and servers. Their goal is to cut the communication bottleneck that slows single-server federated learning. The work matters for networks where many devices train together at the edge and speed decides whether the system is practical.
arxiv-2512-00225:
Deconvolution sharpens microscope images by undoing the blur of the optics. Jerome Mertz presents a method for three-dimensional deconvolution when the blur varies across space, in a 2025 study. Most techniques wrongly assume the aberration is the same at every point.

Methods that track spatially varying aberrations usually need heavy calibration or computation, or they rely on symmetry in the aberration patterns. Mertz uses computed point spread functions to handle the variation directly. Biologists could get cleaner three-dimensional images of thick samples, where focus and distortion change from one region to another. Point spread functions describe exactly how a microscope blurs a single point of light. Computing them per location is what makes the correction space-variant.
arxiv-2512-00325:
Bug reports are often long, unstructured, and hard for developers to absorb quickly. Shaira Sadia Karim and co-authors present progressive code integration for summarizing bug reports in 2025. Their focus is abstractive summaries, written in fresh words rather than copied lines.

Existing approaches lean on surface-level textual cues and often produce incomplete or redundant summaries. They also tend to ignore the code snippets attached to reports, which are essential for accurate diagnosis. Weaving code into the summary pipeline should help developers grasp defects faster and route fixes to the right place. Abstractive summaries can be graded against the report itself, keeping evaluation honest. Progressive integration adds code context step by step rather than all at once.
arxiv-2512-00425:
Video generators produce gorgeous clips that quietly break physics: objects float and collisions misbehave. Minh-Quan Le and co-authors tackle gravity in video generation in 2025, post-training models on Newton's laws with verifiable rewards. Their framework is called NewtonRewards.

The authors describe NewtonRewards as the first physics-grounded post-training framework for video generation based on verifiable rewards. Rewards that can be checked mechanically give the model a clear signal when acceleration or falling motion looks wrong. Physically believable video matters for simulation, education, and any world model meant to predict rather than merely depict. Verifiable rewards can be computed automatically, so training signal stays honest. Objects that float or fall wrongly are exactly the failures the rewards target.
arxiv-2512-00725:
Xinyue Wang, Yuheng Jia, Hui Liu, and Junhui Hou wrote a 2025 paper on clustering, the task of grouping data points that belong together. Most deep clustering methods give just one grouping for a dataset. They assume the data follows one fixed pattern, which may not match what a user needs.

Wang and her team present ESMC, which uses a large multimodal model to select embeddings for explainable multiple clustering. Embeddings are numeric summaries that capture what each item is like. Producing several good groupings, each with an explanation, lets users pick the view that fits their question. That matters in fields where one dataset holds many stories.
arxiv-2512-01025:
Mohit Kumar and five coauthors build an operator-theoretic framework for federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains models across many clients without gathering their data. In practice it must handle client heterogeneity, strict communication and computation limits, and data privacy, all while keeping performance high.

Their framework uses operator theory, the study of transformations on function spaces, to treat these demands together. The goals include statistical heterogeneity, performance guarantees, and privacy under realistic constraints. A gradient-free version matters because some clients cannot share gradients safely or cheaply. The theory aims to give federated systems firmer guarantees.
arxiv-2512-01225:
Jun Wu, Yue Liu, and Zhong Wang study lone waves that hold their shape. The waves solve a family of equations with a free index. Some members of the family are well known and fully solvable. Others are not, and their waves act in new ways.

The team looks at a type of still wave that fades fast away from its peak. They prove those waves are stable in the long run for a set range of the index. Small bumps to the wave die out rather than grow. That proof helps show which of these wave models can be trusted for real water and plasma work.
arxiv-2512-01525:
A compact platform images polarization in near-infrared light with flat optics. Polarization tells how light waves are aligned. It can reveal stress, form, and traits that plain images miss. Past tools for it were bulky and narrow in range.

The system uses second-harmonic generation in flat gratings. Each pixel's full polarization state is read from one shot. The parts are made from a dielectric that boosts the effect. A small, broad tool could serve in clinics, labs, and field sensors where size matters. Pixel-wise readout avoids scanning parts, so moving scenes can be imaged at video rates once the flat optics are scaled up.
arxiv-2512-01625:
William Barford computes how temperature shapes charge and exciton transport in one-dimensional systems. Such systems face static and dynamic disorder at once. Key traits are the long-time diffusion rate and the sub-diffusive exponent. Both shift with heat in ways that matter for devices.

Barford uses three complementary methods to pin those traits. One integrates the velocity autocorrelation over time. Cross-checks between methods firm up the results. Organic wires and light tools rely on such transport, so clear temperature laws guide their design. Agreement across three methods is stressed, since transport exponents are easy to misread from any single curve fit on finite time data.
arxiv-2512-01725:
Jiannan Guan and co-authors warn of reasoning overconfidence in multi-solution tasks. Language models shine when one answer is right. Tasks that need many diverse answers expose a flaw. Models state high certainty for partial answer sets. That certainty hides missing cases from users.

The team names that flaw reasoning overconfidence. They trace where it enters the thought process. Fixes must teach models to doubt coverage, not just steps. Better coverage checks matter for law, medicine, and planning tasks where a missed option can be costly. Coverage doubt is distinct from step doubt, and naming it apart lets trainers target the exact stage where answer sets go thin.
arxiv-2512-01825:
Andrew Rae MacKellar, Stuart Adams, and Kevin Weatherill image at two terahertz bands at once with an atomic sensor. Terahertz imaging sees through many materials. Doing two bands plus an optical overlay in one shot is new. Their cell holds laser-pumped rubidium and caesium atoms together.

Each species converts one narrow terahertz band to optical light. Standard CMOS sensors then read both images. Dual-band views reveal material traits one band hides. Uses span security screening, quality checks, and non-destructive testing of parts. Atomic sensors need no cryogenics, which keeps the dual-band camera portable enough for field trials outside a dedicated optics lab.
arxiv-2512-02125:
Europium in a star's spectrum is a fingerprint of violent events like neutron star mergers, where rapid neutron capture builds heavy elements. Sarah Kane and five co-authors deliver in 2025 a value-added catalogue of europium abundances for nearly a million stars in the GALAH survey's fourth data release.

GALAH's wavelength range happens to include europium's key absorption feature for almost every star it observed. The authors use a neural network to extract abundances at that scale, far beyond hand analysis. A catalogue this size lets astronomers trace where and when the universe forged its heaviest elements, written across the Milky Way's stars.
arxiv-2512-03225:
Minimizing a noisy function is a common hard problem. Christophe Andrieu, Nicolas Chopin, Ettore Fincato, and Mathieu Gerber study such methods in this 2025 work. The function may be non-smooth, hard to write down, or known only through a black box.

The authors study when a class of gradient-free schemes converges. Gradient-free means the method does not use slope information. Proof of convergence tells users when they can trust the result. Such schemes are used in engineering, statistics, and machine learning, where slopes are often missing or noisy. Black-box objectives arise in tuning and design, where gradients rarely exist in practice.
arxiv-2512-03725:
Cosmic-ray experiments sometimes record striking patterns in which the most energetic particles land in a line on the detector. Aleksei Nikolskii, Igor Lokhtin, and Alexander Snigirev ask how much of that alignment is real physics and how much comes from how events are chosen. Their 2025 preprint works within the HYDJET++ model of heavy-ion collisions.

The authors show the strong alignment seen earlier for single energetic particles also appears when particles are grouped into clusters. In busy events with many particles, the clustering step matters greatly, because it separates overlapping groups on the detection plane. Cleaner clusters give a sharper picture of the alignment patterns. Their results point to two ordinary influences behind the effect: the formation of clusters and the conservation of momentum. Together these shape the correlations around the beam direction that experiments observe.
arxiv-2512-03825:
Markov chain Monte Carlo methods explore the likely states of physical and chemical systems, from folding proteins to magnetic models. Aingeru Ramos and colleagues explain in a 2025 distributed computing preprint why plain sampling struggles in complicated landscapes. Parallel tempering improves accuracy by running several replicas at once and letting them swap states, but the trick multiplies the computing bill.

The team implemented the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with parallel tempering in parallel code for modern processors and graphics cards. The processor version, built on OpenMP, ran about fifty times faster across forty-eight cores. The graphics version, built on CUDA, ran nearly a thousand times faster than the serial baseline. Beyond the speed itself, the authors offer the numbers as a reference point. A quantum version built later will be judged against these classical benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-04025:
Attention lets foundation models weigh what matters in an input, but its cost grows quadratically, choking long video work. Xiaolong Li and colleagues present Pyramid Sparse Attention in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Standard sparse methods keep or drop whole blocks, and at high sparsity that binary choice throws away too much information.

Their module instead keeps several pooled versions of each block at different resolutions. Critical blocks are read at fine granularity, unimportant ones at coarse granularity, and nothing vanishes entirely. The design echoes fixed-point arithmetic and classic feature pyramids in vision. A hardware-friendly kernel built on a decoupled block-tile layout keeps execution efficient. Across video benchmarks, the method preserved context and fidelity while matching or beating existing sparse baselines. The team releases code and weights publicly.
arxiv-2512-04225:
Genome-wide association studies hunt genetic variants tied to disease, but publishing their summary statistics can leak who took part and what conditions they have. Anupama Nandi, Seth Neel, and Hyunghoon Cho build a safer release mechanism in a 2025 preprint on quantitative biology. Differential privacy offers protection, yet existing techniques add too much noise or release a slice of the results.

Their GOPHER mechanism releases the complete set of association statistics with privacy guarantees. One ingredient is an optimisation-based randomisation that minimises the expected error in the released results. The second is personalised priors: predictive models trained privately on a data subset let noise be tailored sample by sample. Tests on UK Biobank data, real and simulated traits alike, show the released statistics stay accurate. The authors offer the tools as a route to sharing genome-wide results without exposing participants.
arxiv-2512-04525:
Biao Xu, Gen-Sheng Ye, Yue Chang, and co-authors show how to tune the faint nonlinear response of light at the level of single photons, over a wide range. Nonlinear optics usually needs bright beams, since one photon barely nudges matter. Strong single-photon effects would speed photonic entanglement and logic gates. Their 2025 arXiv paper reaches that regime with Rydberg atoms, whose huge electron orbits interact strongly.

Microwave-assisted shaping of the Rydberg wave function lets the team dial the interaction strength across two orders of magnitude. They store light in the atoms and fetch it back, then check the quantum statistics of the returning photons. As a first use, the scheme sped up the making of single photons in low Rydberg states by a large factor. Fine control at this level could quicken quantum operations built on light, from repeaters to small photonic processors.
arxiv-2512-05025:
Nicolas Houdré and six co-authors introduce RAMEN, a single encoder for Earth observation data of every kind. Satellites deliver a jumble of products — sharp optical photos, coarse multispectral scans, radar time series — each at its own resolution. Existing foundation models usually demand fixed inputs or a separate encoder per sensor. That rigidity keeps them from generalizing across the full mix of data that orbit provides.

RAMEN treats the sensor type and the spatial and time resolutions as inputs in their own right. It also lets the user choose the resolution of the output, trading detail against computing cost directly. One transformer is trained by hiding and reconstructing pieces of mixed satellite data from many sources. Once trained, it transfers to sensor setups it has never seen and beats larger rival models on a standard community benchmark spanning many downstream tasks.
arxiv-2512-05325:
Ömer Faruk Akgül and four co-authors present LYNX, a method that teaches reasoning models to stop thinking once they know enough. Large reasoning models often overthink, rambling on after the answer is settled, which wastes computing and can even hurt accuracy. Earlier fixes relied on decoding tricks, verifier models, or after-the-fact analysis with no guarantees. LYNX instead listens to the model's own internal state.

It attaches exit decisions to natural reasoning cues, the verbal tics where a model pauses. It trains a lightweight probe on the hidden states at those moments, supervised by forced exits. Conformal prediction then wraps the probe's scores in distribution-free control over stopping too early. One probe, trained once on mathematics, transfers unchanged across benchmarks and non-mathematical tasks, matching or improving accuracy while cutting token use by large fractions. Users get an explicit confidence knob rather than a heuristic.
arxiv-2512-05925:
Federico Bianchi, Yongchan Kwon, Zachary Izzo, Linjun Zhang, and James Zou ask an uncomfortable question: how many plain mistakes sit inside published AI papers? Errors in formulas, derivations, or tables can mislead everyone who builds on them. The team built a Paper Correctness Checker on a frontier language model and ran it on papers from top venues. Only objective errors counted.

The harvest is sobering. Published papers carry a non-negligible number of objective mistakes, and the average per paper has climbed. At one leading conference it rose from under four mistakes per paper to nearly six within four years. Human experts reviewed a sample of the machine's accusations and confirmed about five in six, a strong precision for such a tool. The checker could also propose correct fixes for about three quarters of the mistakes found. The proposal: let machine readers audit the literature.
arxiv-2512-06025: Thierry Coquand, Jonas Höfer, and Christian Sattler write a short note for synthetic algebraic geometry, which rebuilds geometry inside type theory. The approach needs models: concrete settings where its axioms hold. The authors build such models over rings with a key property. For finitely presented algebras over it, equality is decidable. The work is done in a constructive, deliberately weak metatheory, no stronger than dependent type theory with universes. Weakness is a feature: such results transfer widely. Model building is the plumbing of a new foundation.
arxiv-2512-06225:
Nicolas Abgrall and seven co authors describe a Chicago sensor network built to catch radiation in a busy city, and the data sets it shares. The network, called PANDAWN, mixes radiation sensors with cameras and other feeds that show the scene around each alert. That mix matters because city life is full of harmless radiation sources that can look like threats at first glance.

The study lays out what each node records and how staff turn raw feeds into clean, labeled data sets with machine help. Labels mark both the radiation signal and the scene around it, so new detection and tracking tools can learn from real city cases. The authors also sum up past studies that used these data. Shared, well kept data like this lets labs across the country test safety tools on the same ground.
arxiv-2512-06425:
Nilson Bernardes, Antonio Bonilla, and Joao Pinto sort out when a class of operators is expansive, meaning it steadily pushes apart points that start close. The operators join two actions: they move the input of a function around, then weigh the result. They act on spaces of continuous functions, a broad family that covers many classic settings, from functions that fade at infinity to functions on general spaces with a natural topology.

The authors give complete tests, with no gaps, for several flavors of expansivity in these spaces. They do the same for the Lp spaces used across analysis, widening results once known only for the unweighted case. For energy losing systems they show the weighted operator can be recast as an unweighted one, and use that bridge to study more traits. The work gives a unified map for a tool used across modern analysis.
arxiv-2512-06525:
Jiaming Wei and Dihan Zou ask how a government should rein in a monopolist when it cannot hand the firm a subsidy. The firm alone knows its true cost of production and sets the price for a single product. The regulator cares about a weighted mix of consumer gain and firm profit, and its only tool is a per unit tax.

The authors find a clean test for when doing nothing, laissez faire, is already the best policy. When action is called for, the best policy can be a progressive price cap in tax form: prices below a benchmark go untaxed, while higher prices face rising, even prohibitive, tax rates. That design leaves the firm free at low prices and squeezes only the high ones, balancing access, affordability, and profit. The work clarifies when taxes can stand in for subsidies, and when they are only a rough substitute.
arxiv-2512-06625:
Jaime Munoz Rivera, Elena Ochoa Ochoa, and Ramon Quintanilla study how a heated elastic plate settles over time. Their model couples the plate's bending to heat flow of the simplest type, with the material described by a second gradient theory that accounts for finer scale effects. The core question is qualitative: do solutions calm down, and how smoothly do they behave?

The team proves the solutions decay exponentially fast, a strong form of stability. Their main result concerns smoothness: when the heat equation carries a certain double Laplacian term, the solution flow cannot be differentiated in time in the strong sense, a sharp limit on regularity. They also treat a case with a negative elastic parameter, where they prove solutions are unique but unstable. In a one dimensional, near static case they show solutions exist and decay exponentially under stated conditions.
arxiv-2512-07025:
Stefan Höche, Matt LeBlanc, Jennifer Roloff, and Grant Whitman compute splitting functions for quantum chromodynamics, the rules that say how a heavy particle showers into three lighter ones. Such splittings drive the simulations used to predict what particle colliders will see. Existing formulas lean on limiting cases, valid only when the emitted particles are soft or nearly parallel. The authors instead present a compact form that holds beyond those kinematical limits.

Their result is organized into pieces: lower-order expressions already known, scalar antenna functions that capture pairs of emitters, and a genuinely new remainder. Two-gluon radiator functions appear here for the first time, generalizing what the double-soft approximation had suggested. Because nothing in the derivation assumes a limiting regime, the formulas can be used across the full range of collision geometries.
arxiv-2512-07325:
J Ramya Parkavi, R Muthuganesan, and V K Chandrasekar tune the knobs of a quantum battery, a device that stores energy in a two-qubit system governed by quantum rules. Their battery is a dipolar spin pair with an extra twist, the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, which couples the spins antisymmetrically. Following the system through repeated charging cycles, they score it on the measures that matter for any battery: usable work, charging power, capacity, and the quantum coherence that fuels them.

Temperature, magnetic field, and the strength of the twist all reshape the performance. Coherence and the twist interaction together raise both the storage efficiency and the power output substantially, marking them as design levers rather than nuisances. The authors also place the battery in a shared dephasing environment, the kind of noise real devices cannot escape, and show how it caps long-term work extraction.
arxiv-2512-07825:
Hamid Bakhtiarizadeh wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on spinning black holes in anti-de Sitter space. Anti-de Sitter space curves inward, giving black holes a tidy thermodynamic playground. He proposes a new inequality linking a rotating hole's spin, mass, and volume.

The bound is built to keep naked singularities from ever forming. A singularity without a horizon would break cosmic censorship, a core hope of relativity. The derivation studies the roots of an identity among thermodynamic variables. Kerr-AdS black holes supply the first test of the new bound. Rotating black strings, uncharged, supply a second and different test. Both families respect the inequality. A broad class of further solutions adds more supporting evidence. The author also checks a famous neighbor result, the reverse isoperimetric inequality. Rotation leaves that inequality unchanged, he demonstrates in the paper.
arxiv-2512-08025:
Varun Shiri, Maggie Xiong, Jin L C Guo, and Jinghui Cheng, researchers in human computer interaction, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is online privacy, and how ordinary users help each other handle it. Instead of studying rules or platform design, they look at bottom up discussion on the question and answer site Quora.

The authors map the privacy topics users raise there, from risks and dangers to protection strategies, company practices, and laws. Their results show how personal, technical, organizational, and social factors shape privacy attitudes together. They close with ideas for community based tools that make privacy help easier to find and share. Such tools, they argue, should connect designers and developers more directly with the user community.
arxiv-2512-08125:
Tharindu Wickremasinghe, Chenyang Qi, Harshana Weligampola, and colleagues, computer vision researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their method, FlowSteer, adapts flow based image generators to image restoration. These models are strong at making pictures from text, but when asked to restore a damaged photo they tend to drift away from the real measured image.

Earlier fixes leaned on flows built for one dataset, or adapters built for one task, and they do not scale. FlowSteer instead conditions the frozen flow model along its sampling path, mixing the model own guidance with direct constraints from the measurement. The authors explain how the noise sensitivity of flow models shapes that design. Across super resolution, deblurring, denoising, and colorization, it improved faithfulness and identity preservation in a strict zero shot setting, with no retrained models or adapters.
arxiv-2512-08525:
Krzysztof Szczygielski, a mathematical physicist in Poland, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. His topic is the mathematics of open quantum systems, where a system evolves while leaking into its surroundings. The evolution is described by families of maps, and a key question is which of those maps can be split into simpler, well behaved pieces.

He analyzes semigroups of such decomposable maps on C star algebras, the abstract setting for quantum observables, through the structure of their generators. The treatment also covers von Neumann algebras, including the algebra of all operators on a Hilbert space. He then develops a divisibility notion for dynamical maps acting on trace class operators. The results extend earlier work that handled only finite matrix algebras. They also partly generalize a landmark theorem of Lindblad on completely positive semigroups.
arxiv-2512-08725:
Giulio Attenni, Youssef Moawad, Novella Bartolini, and Lauritz Thamsen study whether moving cloud work in place or time can cut its environmental footprint. Cloud computing uses carbon emitting power, water for cooling, and land for facilities. Shifting work to cleaner regions or cleaner times could reduce all three, if the gains hold in realistic settings.

Their simulation uses public data from two major cloud providers, real workload traces for big data and serverless tasks, and grid mix data. Spatial shifting gives large cuts in carbon, water, and land use, especially for serverless work. Time shifting helps as well, but less, and the two together give the best result. Tests show the gains are robust to forecast errors in grid data and to changes across seasons. The study offers practical guidance for greener cloud scheduling.
arxiv-2512-09125:
B Z Djordjevic and coauthors use Bayesian optimization to tune laser wakefield acceleration. In such accelerators, a laser drives a plasma wave that can accelerate an electron bunch trailing behind it. The study uses channel guided acceleration.

Spectral shaping changes the time profile of the laser while keeping its total energy fixed, which affects both acceleration and injection. The parameter space is broad and complex, so particle in cell simulations are guided by Bayesian optimization to find high performers. Profiles with extra spectral content, paired with optimal channel settings, give an electron bunch with charge an order of magnitude above the standard Gaussian baseline. Mean bunch energy also rises. The work shows systematic optimization can unlock shaping gains that manual scans would likely miss.
arxiv-2512-09325:
Cheongho Han leads a very large collaboration reporting four new planets found by gravitational microlensing in the 2024 KMTNet survey season. Microlensing reveals planets when a foreground star briefly magnifies a background star, and a planet near the lens leaves a short extra blip in the brightening. Each of the four events showed a different kind of anomaly.

One event had a positive bump near its peak, one an asymmetric peak, one a brief central dip, and one a caustic-crossing feature. Careful modeling of the light curves confirmed that all four blips came from planetary companions. Despite the varied signals, every planet turned out to be a giant, with a mass comparable to or larger than Jupiter's. Each orbits a star less massive than the Sun. The authors note the haul shows microlensing's strength at uncovering planetary systems around low-mass stars that other methods miss.
arxiv-2512-09425:
Xuan Cai leads a team improving quantitative susceptibility mapping, an MRI technique that turns phase data into maps of tissue magnetic susceptibility. Such maps help image brain microstructure, measure iron deposits, and study brain disease. The catch is that reconstructing them from a single head orientation is ill-posed: part of the signal's frequency space is missing, causing streaking artifacts and lost structure.

Their framework, QSMnet-INR, joins a 3D U-Net backbone with an implicit neural representation working in frequency space. The added module models the dipole response continuously across directions and fills in the missing cone region explicitly, while a frequency-domain dipole loss keeps results consistent. The two parts train together by alternating optimization. On challenge data, multi-orientation data, and clinical scans, the method beat recent deep learning approaches, recovering structure in the missing regions and suppressing artifacts without needing multiple scan orientations.
arxiv-2512-09925:
Patrick Noras and colleagues present GAINS, a method for recovering the materials of a scene from only a few photographs. Inverse rendering works backward from images to geometry, surface reflectance, and lighting. With sparse views, the problem becomes ambiguous and accuracy collapses. GAINS counters the ambiguity with priors borrowed from foundation models, large pretrained networks that already understand images. The framework runs in two stages inside one optimization scheme.

First, geometry is refined using monocular depth, surface normal, and diffusion based priors. Then material recovery is steadied by segmentation, intrinsic image decomposition, and further diffusion priors. Tests on synthetic and real scenes show clear gains in material accuracy, relighting quality, and new view synthesis over leading Gaussian based methods. The advantage is largest exactly where cameras are fewest, with captures ranging from a handful to a few dozen views. In that regime, learned priors supply the missing information.
arxiv-2512-10025:
Nikolaos Chalmoukis, Georgios Tsikalas, and Dmitry Yakubovich study matrices that nearly satisfy the Kreiss condition. That condition bounds a matrix's resolvent outside the unit disk and controls how its powers can grow. The authors push the Kreiss constant down toward one, the smallest possible. They prove lower bounds on the power growth of such matrices, refining estimates by Nikolski and by Spijker, Tracogna, and Welfert. The bounds show that even near perfect resolvent control still permits a certain amount of transient growth.

They also study a variant where the constant is allowed a small excess that vanishes as the spectrum approaches the unit circle. Under conditions on where the spectrum touches the circle and how the resolvent grows there, this weaker assumption still guarantees the operator is similar to a contraction, a much simpler object. The proof's core is a positivity argument using the double layer potential operator.
arxiv-2512-10225:
Ananga Mohan Datta, William J. Munro, Nicolo Lo Piparo, and Kae Nemoto design a chip scale source of entangled light for teleporting delicate quantum states. Entangled coherent states are a powerful non Gaussian resource for continuous variable quantum links, but making them in scalable hardware is hard. Their scheme carves the states from squeezed vacuum by photon subtraction in a waveguide device. Single photon catalysis then purifies the state after lossy transmission.

With those purified resources, the authors analyze a teleportation protocol based on photon counts. Both ordinary coherent states and Schrödinger cat states transfer with high fidelity. For cat states, the fidelity beats the classical threshold across a broad range of realistic channel and squeezing settings, exactly where resources built only from Gaussian steps fail. The payoff is practical: generation and purification live in one integrated architecture, suited to photonic chips.
arxiv-2512-10325:
Francesco Alemanno presents a derivative free solver for nonlinear inverse problems, the task of recovering hidden parameters from observed effects. Such problems fill engineering and science, and scoring their residuals is often noisy, non differentiable, or expensive, defeating solvers that need Jacobian matrices. Current derivative free methods demand smoothness, huge populations for covariance guesses, or stall where gradients fade. His method, residual subspace evolution strategies, probes around the current guess with Gaussian samples. It records how the residuals change along those probe directions, then solves a small least squares problem to merge the probes into an optimal step.

Each iteration costs only a handful of residual scorings plus small linear algebra, since the probe count stays far below the parameter dimension. No Jacobians and no sampled covariances are ever formed. Benchmarks show it matching or beating leading rivals at equal budgets.
arxiv-2512-11025:
Hao Geng and co-authors bring new evidence to a deep claim of quantum gravity: that exact global symmetries cannot exist in a complete theory. In holographic setups, a gravitational universe is paired with a non gravitational bath on its boundary, and information can seem to leak into that bath. Special regions called entanglement islands change how that information is counted.

The authors construct concrete examples, from simple models and from string theory, where global symmetries appear in such island setups. They argue the symmetries are allowed precisely because islands preserve the missing information. The symmetries also mix with broken gauge symmetries, which makes black hole hair detectable in the bath, a feature they call wet hair. The work also resolves a puzzle raised by earlier researchers.
arxiv-2512-11125:
Benedictus Cinun and colleagues give a robot safety controller a direct formula instead of a calculation that must be solved fresh at every step. Their testbed is a Stewart platform, a parallel robot whose top plate moves on six legs. Safety rules on position and speed must hold at all times, and the usual barrier function approach enforces them through repeated optimisation.

Their closed form law handles several position and velocity constraints at once. They derive exact conditions for when the formula stays well defined, guaranteeing the method is sound for the multi constraint case. Tests in simulation and on a custom built hardware platform matched the safety performance of the optimisation based version. Computation time fell by more than tenfold, making the approach attractive for real time safe control of parallel robots.
arxiv-2512-11225:
Gabrijel Boduljak, Yushi Lan, Christian Rupprecht, and Andrea Vedaldi forecast the future of a scene not as pixels but as features from a vision foundation model. Video generation predicts realistic images, yet it is costly and its output must still be translated into signals a robot or planner can use. Feature based forecasts decode directly into depth, segmentation, and surface orientation, but plain regression blurs together several plausible futures.

Their generative forecaster instead extends flow matching, working step by step inside a compact latent space built from the foundation model's features. That latent space keeps more information than earlier compression choices, helping both forecasting and image generation. Predictions decoded into segmentation, depth, normals, and even colour images were sharper and more accurate than regression with the same architecture and compute. The authors propose stochastic feature generation as a scalable base for world models.
arxiv-2512-11525:
Hao Wu and fellow authors present NeuralOGCM, an ocean model that weds a physics solver to a neural network inside one trainable system. Ocean model run has long traded speed against physical fidelity: numeric models are faithful but slow, pure AI models fast but prone to drift and implausible behaviour. Their setup makes the dynamical core itself differentiable.

Key physical parameters, such as diffusion coefficients, become learnable, so end to end training tunes the physics core automatically. Alongside it, a neural network corrects for small scale processes and discretisation errors the physics misses. A single differential equation solver integrates both outputs jointly. Tests show long term stability and physical consistency, beating traditional numeric models on speed and pure AI baselines on exactness score. The authors present the design as a template for fast, trustworthy model run across scientific computing.
arxiv-2601-06725:
Mahsa Mitcheff and Adam Czajka study how humans judge iris images in 2026. Iris recognition is a mature biometric with remarkable precision and speed. Large-scale deployments exceed a billion enrolled users, as in India's AADHAAR.

In forensic applications, a human expert may need to review matches. The expert confirms identifications before results become court evidence, they explain. Processed samples may be degraded, as in post-mortem cases they note. Pupil size normalization is tested as an aid for human judges. Synthetic irises are tested as a challenge to human judgment too. Their findings matter where algorithms alone cannot testify in court. Biometrics researchers get evidence on the human side of the pipeline.
arxiv-2601-06825:
Research by Shuai Xu and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with quarkonium light-cone distribution amplitudes. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The authors present a systematic study of the leading- and next-to-leading-twist light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) of ground-state pseudoscalar and vector quarkonium within. The light-front quark model (LFQM).

By implementing the replacement M → M 0 M. The authors analyze the longitudinal and transverse structures of the LCDAs, together with their Gegenbauer moments, ξ -moments, and transverse momentum moments. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07425:
Long Wang and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers free-fall-based switching criterion for p 3 \text{P}{{}^{3}} t hybrid n n -body methods. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The P 3 P3 T scheme is a hybrid method for simulating gravitational N N -body systems.

It combines a fast particle-tree (PT) algorithm for long-range forces with a high-accuracy particle-particle (PP, direct N N -body) solver for short-range interactions. Preserving both PT efficiency and PP accuracy requires a robust PT-PP switching criterion. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07625:
Konstantin Moser, Christos Likos, and Vittoria Sposini study a mixture that gets stuck between separating and freezing. Their 2026 preprint covers a hard colloid and star polymer mixture in its arrested phase separation range. An early demixing process interferes with a nearby line where the material turns glassy. The authors focus on the protein limit, where the hard component is the smaller one.

They examine both structure and dynamics in this arrested state. When separation halts midway, the material keeps a patchy structure that changes very slowly. Knowing how single-particle motion separates from collective motion explains that slowness. Soft matter physicists use such mixtures to model protein solutions and industrial formulations. The work helps connect microscopic motion with the visible behavior of dense mixtures.
arxiv-2601-07725:
Jessica Bariffi and colleagues connect lattice theory with error-correcting codes that use the Lee metric. Lattices and partially ordered sets now play a growing role in coding theory. They give combinatorial frameworks for studying structural and algebraic traits of codes. Recent work links lattices, anticodes, and coding invariants. Their 2026 preprint studies ring-linear codes under the Lee metric.

The authors introduce weak composition lattices and ring-linear anticodes. The Lee metric suits channels where errors shift symbols by small amounts, common in phase modulation. Algebraic structure can reveal code properties that brute force cannot reach. Anticodes bound how good a code can be. The paper serves coding theorists who like algebraic tools. It extends the lattice viewpoint into a less explored metric.
arxiv-2601-07825:
Yu Yang and colleagues propose mechanical resonators as hardware for quantum computing. Hybrid quantum systems combine platforms to gain more than any offers alone. Bulk acoustic wave resonators hold many highly coherent harmonic modes in a compact footprint. Superconducting circuits bring strong nonlinearity and fast operations. Their 2026 preprint develops resonator-based quantum computing on that pairing.

Many modes in one device could store and process quantum information densely. Coherence means the modes keep their quantum behavior long enough to be useful. Coupling them to superconducting circuits supplies the control and readout. The paper lays out the concept and its requirements. Quantum hardware scholars are the readers. The work adds mechanical systems to the list of serious computing platforms, beyond their sensing roles.
arxiv-2601-07925:
Emma T. Chickles and a large team report a binary star system with an orbit of only 8.56 minutes. The system, ATLAS J1013 minus 4516, transfers mass between its two stars. It belongs to the AM Canum Venaticorum class, ultra-compact binaries of white dwarfs. Its mean brightness in Gaia data is magnitude 19.51, quite faint. The system eclipses, so each star periodically blocks the other. Their 2026 preprint announces the discovery.

An orbit under nine minutes makes this one of the tightest known binaries. Such systems radiate gravitational waves strongly and evolve quickly. Eclipses let astronomers measure sizes and masses with unusual precision. Mass transfer at this period tests models of white dwarf pairs. The paper serves astronomers studying compact binaries. The coming merger of such a pair may end as a supernova or a merged white dwarf.
arxiv-2601-08225: Jungho Cho, Minbyul Jeong, and Sungrae Park wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on training chats for AI agents that use tools. Large reasoning models now act as agents that work on their own, which raises the call for rich chats across many turns. Data sets in use rest on fixed tool sets set in advance. Such sets can not scale to open-ended work with a user. The authors build chats with the user at the core, to meet that need at scale.
arxiv-2601-08425: Mark de Berg and Sandor Kisfaludi-Bak prove lower bounds for dominating set problems on ball graphs. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on results that many classic graph problems run in subexponential time on unit-ball graphs. Those runtimes are tight under the exponential time hypothesis. The result generalizes to intersection graphs of similarly sized fat objects. The authors now pin lower bounds for dominating set in ball graphs and weighted dominating set in unit-ball graphs. Sharp bounds tell algorithm designers where faster methods cannot exist.
arxiv-2601-08725:
Juhani Merilehto wrote a study that tries to repeat an older study on how to spot bad software. The older work was by a team led by Fellicious. It counts how often a program calls on the system, and it does not care about the order of those calls. A random forest model then sorts programs into safe or bad.

Merilehto uses the same public data set as the first team. The set holds a large group of training samples and a large group of test samples. He builds four forms of the model. They use single calls, pairs of calls, triples of calls, and all three mixed. A reader learns how well a known result holds up when a new person runs it again.
arxiv-2601-09125:
Ryota Inagaki, Tanya Khovanova, and Austin Luo play a chip game on a grid of whole count points. Chips sit on points of a grid. When a point fires, it sends one chip to each next point up the grid. They start with a vast pile of chips at the start point. The count is a power of two, set by a size pick in the game.

They track where chips land as fires spread, and when the spread stops. Grid chip games can show neat forms from plain rules. This grid is the Hasse form of count pairs, a shape with rich links. A reader in play math gets a new game case, with forms that may tie to known count laws.
arxiv-2601-09225:
Lihwai Lin and eight co-authors ask why some galaxies in a mid zone stop forming stars. The mid zone, called the green valley, sits between blue star rich and red dead galaxies. On mean, such galaxies hold less gas and form stars with less yield. But a mean can hide more than one path in lone cases.

The team reads gas and stop time scales galaxy by galaxy. Some may stop for lack of gas. Some may hold gas, yet form stars at a poor rate. That split shows more than one quench path at work. A reader in galaxy work gets a case by case view of how galaxies die, not just a mean tale.
arxiv-2601-09325:
F. Ciavattini, M. Farotti, and C. Lucamarini set a new mark for how order can grow in a moving system. Their mark is called the Emergent Order Spectrum. It is built from chains of small steps from one state to a next. Each step must fit a set order, and the steps shrink as the chain is made fine. The type of the end order is what the mark holds.

The mark does not change when the system is recast in a like form. That makes it a trait of the system, not of our view of it. It is set for homeomorphisms, moves that can be run back with no tear. A reader in dynamics gets a new trait to sort systems by how their order grows.
arxiv-2601-09625:
Ben Nassi, Bruce Schneier, and Oleg Brodt argue that attacks on AI systems have grown into full malware campaigns. Their 2026 arXiv paper lays out a promptware kill chain. Systems built on large language models now run from chatbots to agents that execute code and move money.

The authors say the catch-all label prompt injection hides this shift. Real attacks now unfold in steps, much like classic malware intrusions. Naming the stages gives defenders a map of where to intervene. The paper urges security teams to treat model abuse with the same rigor as other intrusions.
arxiv-2601-09725:
Kaustubh Shivshankar Shejole and Sourabh Deoghare poke at a weak point of machine translation: punctuation. Their 2026 arXiv paper tests punctuation robustness in English-Marathi translation. Punctuation resolves meaning and structure in written text, yet real input is often sloppy.

Marathi is a low- to middle-resource language, so its translation systems have less data to learn from. The authors assess how missing or shifted punctuation degrades translations. They also work on improving that robustness in working systems. Findings like these matter wherever translated text is messy in daily use, from chats to scanned forms.
arxiv-2601-09825:
Alireza Bakhtiari and four co-authors refine a yardstick used to bound learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper localizes the eluder dimension. They first prove a lower bound for generalized linear model classes, showing the standard measure cannot yield first-order regret bounds.

The authors then introduce a localization method for the eluder dimension. It recovers and improves classic results for Bernoulli bandits. It also gives the first genuine first-order bounds for finite-horizon reinforcement learning with bounded total returns. Sharper yardsticks mean sharper guarantees for bandit algorithms and for learning algorithms in wide use.
arxiv-2601-10125:
Yalin Sun, Cheng Xing, and Ruiwei Xu work on a class of curved sheets in affine space. The sheets are named Calabi affine maximal sheets. They are best in a sense tied to area in that space. Such sheets link to a hard old task named the centroaffine Bernstein task.

That task asks when a whole such sheet must be a plain quadric form. The team brings the two themes into one frame. Their work uses the sheet class to shed new terms on the old task. Shape tasks of this kind test how far a local rule can fix a whole form.
arxiv-2601-10425:
M. G. Donato and co authors report light driven lift near a rare surface. The surface is of epsilon near zero type. On such a surface, light acts in odd ways. A small grain near it can be pushed by light with a strong force. That push can lift the grain.

The team show this lift in a lab test. Light alone holds the grain up near the surface. Such lift needs no trap beam from a lens. It rests on the surface's own field. The work may aid ways to move tiny grains with light, for chips and sensors at small scale.
arxiv-2601-10725:
Hieu Do Quang, Chien Truong-Quoc, and Quoc Tran Van plan paths for robot teams that move in formation. Their setting is leader-follower control in cluttered space. Two leaders set the shape, and the rest of the team holds its pattern around them. The planner they built is based on diffusion models, the same family used to generate images.

The diffusion policy draws the path of the midpoint between the two leaders, treated as a rigid bar in the plane. That bar's motion fixes the desired paths for the whole formation. Sampling paths this way can dodge obstacles smoothly. The work targets drone and ground robot teams that must stay in shape while threading through mess.
arxiv-2601-10925:
Michael Ginn and co-authors work on joint segmentation and glossing across many languages. A gloss labels each word part in a documented language with its grammar. Automated glossing with neural networks could speed up language documentation. The best models score well on gloss benchmarks, yet user studies with linguists found real barriers to their use in the field.

The authors tackle segmentation and glossing together, at a massively multilingual scale. Splitting words into parts and labeling them are linked jobs; doing both jointly can help each. Documentation of endangered languages is a race against time. Tools that linguists will actually use could help record languages before their last speakers are gone.
arxiv-2601-11125:
Qianqiao Zhou and co-authors report a gas-enshrouded broad-line active galactic nucleus at redshift near seven. The Lyman-alpha absorption profile in star-forming galaxies traces dense neutral hydrogen around them. That gas is a key player in the Epoch of Reionization. The team found a unique galaxy, A2744-z7DLA, at redshift about 6.87.

Its absorption shows a galaxy wrapped in dense neutral gas while hosting a broad-line black hole. Such a pairing was not expected so early. The case bears on how the first black holes grew inside gas-rich cradles. JWST spectroscopy made the find possible, and it gives reionization studies a vivid new data point.
arxiv-2601-11225:
Parseval frames and the tools they build are the topic of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. A Parseval frame is a set of vectors that acts like a basis. It sits in a Hilbert space, the home of quantum states.

From one such frame and a set of real numbers, two things grow. One is an operator, a map that acts on states. The other is a POVM, a kind of quantum measure. POVMs give the odds for outcomes of a measurement. The study maps in detail how those two builds relate. That link helps link frame design to measurement design in quantum work.
arxiv-2601-11325:
Dheeraj Poolavaram, Carsten Markgraf, and Sebastian Dorn pack boxes with a genetic search. Their 2026 preprint is named GENPACK, for 3D bin packing. Bin packing asks how to fit items into the fewest bins. The 3D form is a long-standing hard task in logistics.

Classic fast methods build packings in a quick, greedy way. They often miss what real industry needs from a packing. Loads must be stable, balanced, and easy to handle. GENPACK uses a genetic algorithm guided by key metrics. Those metrics, called KPIs, score each trial packing. More than one goal is chased at the same time. The search breeds packings that plants can truly use.
arxiv-2601-11525:
Yi Zhao and six coauthors benchmark vision-language models on plot-to-code tasks. Their 2026 preprint introduces PlotGen-Bench for that test. Vision-language models now write code from images with skill. Turning a plot back into code is a sharp test of that skill.

The bench covers realistic and complex visualization cases. Hard cases include 3D plots and animated plots. Plot-to-plot transformations stretch the models further. Multi-library scenarios ask for code in more than one toolkit. Generated code must run and match the source plot. Such tests show where multimodal coding still falls short. They also guide training for data-science AI helpers.
arxiv-2601-11625:
Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar tracks when a model's reasoning settles in training. The 2026 preprint defines the Reasoning Stabilization Point, or RSP. Fine-tuning a pretrained model can lift task scores quietly. It can also shift the evidence the model relies on.

The view here is a training-time interpretability lens. Token-level attributions are tracked across fine-tuning epochs. Explanation drift is the epoch-to-epoch change in those attributions. It is measured on a fixed probe set of inputs. RSP is the earliest epoch after which drift stays low. It needs no tuning on out-of-distribution data at all. A stable point can flag shortcut reliance early. Trainers gain a signal for when to stop or intervene.
arxiv-2601-11725: Timothy A. Elmslie, Luca Basso, Adam Dodson, Jacob Henshaw, and Andrew M. Mounce tackle a tool problem in high pressure science. Tiny flaws in diamond, called NV centres, can sense fields and stress. They work well under high pressure, but the cells that press the sample are small and hard to reach. The team seeks a way to send wave fields to the diamond in an even way. Even fields matter, since weak or patchy fields spoil the sense work.
arxiv-2601-11825: Arya Rahgozar and Pouria Mortezaagha test an AI co-scientist for medical work. Medical study waste grows from repeat work, poor reports, and slow sums of past proof. Hand sums of proof take long and do not scale well. Their tool aims for scaled, clear sums of what is known. It states each study in PICOS form. That form lists who was studied and what was done. It also lists the match, the checks, and the study build. A proof of concept test checks if this form helps.
arxiv-2601-12225:
Oliver C. Gorton, Konstantinos Kravvaris, Jutta E. Escher, and Calvin W. Johnson define radiative strength functions from a localized form of the Brink-Axel hypothesis. These functions model how excited nuclei emit light in bulk. They are key inputs to statistical reaction codes.

Their form fits Hauser-Feshbach codes and can be computed with the shell model by the Lanczos strength method. Good strength functions improve rates for neutron capture and other reactions. Those rates feed models of star element making. The work puts the link on a clean base.  Firm rates feed star models that make the elements.
arxiv-2601-12325:
Eli Passov, Nathan S. Netanyahu, and Yosi Keller match data from many sensors with hypernetworks. A hypernetwork makes or modulates the weights of a second network. That gives a flexible way to add context and task state to a model.

Such conditioning has worked in many fields with little growth in model size. For sensor matching, context may be the sensor type or the scene state. A conditioned matcher could adapt to new sensors with less retraining. The work sets out that design.  Context in this case may be sensor type or scene.
arxiv-2601-12425:
Peterson Mambondimumwe, Sphiwe B. Skhosana, and Najmeh Nakhaei Rad, based at the University of Pretoria, work on mixture regression models. In these models, data come from several groups, each with its own regression line. Some parts of the model can be left as free functions of the inputs. That freedom makes the class flexible and useful.

The flaw is that most such models assume Gaussian errors in each group. That choice makes fits bend toward outliers and heavy tailed noise. The team propose a robust fix based on the contaminated Gaussian distribution. A contaminated law mixes a main Gaussian with a wider one. That mix can soak up stray points while the main fit stays on track.
arxiv-2601-12525:
Nikolaj Tatti studies decision trees that learn from a stream of data. Decision trees are among the most popular classifiers in machine learning. Stream versions must update the tree as new data flows in, with no full batch to revisit. A standard move is to turn a leaf node into a split when the data support it.

Picking a good split fast is the core cost of that update. Tatti focuses on sparse data streams, where each record holds few active features. Sparsity changes which split tests are cheap and which are dear. Fast split search keeps a stream tree fresh without falling behind the flow. The work was supported by Academy of Finland projects on machine learning.
arxiv-2601-12625:
Parisa Ansari Bonab, Elisabeth Andarge Gedefaw, and Mohammad Khajenejad work on safety for platoons of connected cars. Cooperative adaptive cruise control lets cars follow closely by sharing data. That connectivity opens a door to cyber threats, though. False data injection attacks can feed a car fake sensor values and break its control.

The team propose a control framework built to resist such attacks. It pairs a nonlinear controller with an interval observer. The observer gives robust state estimates even under measurement noise. Interval bounds tell the controller what range the true state must lie in. Control that stays safe inside those bounds can ride out an attack. The work serves the security of future autonomous traffic.
arxiv-2601-13125:
Denan Li, Chris Ahart, and Shi Liu chase a long gap in how heat marks a key change in a lead based crystal. The crystal is PbTiO3, a model case for matter that holds a built in electric lean. Its Curie point is the heat level where that lean fades.

Sums from first rules tend to land far below the lab value for that point. The team asks why. They run long atom path sims at fixed push, all from first rules. They also test fast sims that use machine learnt force fields drawn from the same first rules data. By set side by side, the two runs show which part of the gap is real and which is a flaw of the fast route.
arxiv-2601-13325:
Raz Lotan, Neta Elad, Oded Padon, and Sharon Shoham verify time traits of systems with no bound on state count. Their frame is deductive, built on well founded ranks. A rank map that must fall at each step can prove that a run ends or holds a trait. Check tasks are passed to SMT solvers, tools that test if a logic claim can hold.

Their new step is a cut from trait checks to end checks. A fresh tool of timers joins the ranks to make that cut work. With it any first order time trait can be recast as an end task. For proof tool teams, one strong end engine can then serve all traits.
arxiv-2601-13425:
Gian Sebastian Mier Bello and co-authors guard the truth of science data with a blockchain log. Big compute projects draw data from many sources. Some sets are so huge that a full copy is not real to make or keep. That scale makes a plain check of truth hard. A moved or marred file may pass unseen.

Their system logs a firm mark of each set on a chain. Any later copy can be checked next to the mark with no need to move the full set. If the marks part, the file is known to have changed. For big sim teams, the log gives trust in shared data at low cost.
arxiv-2601-13525:
Chunsheng Zuo and Daniel Khashabi show that to squeeze embeddings can help dense search fit a new field. Dense search uses learnt vectors to find docs by sense. It strains in niche fields, where the train mix parts from the target mix. Fit to a new field oft needs dear marks and re teach of query doc pairs.

Their find runs the next way from the norm. Squeeze of the vectors, to fewer dims, lifts fit to the new field. A smaller vector holds less of the old field's quirks. For search teams in law, care, or code, a cheap squeeze may beat a dear re teach.
arxiv-2601-13625: Zhenghui Li, Benchao Su, and Zhixiang Wu study the completed cohomology of quaternionic Shimura curves in 2026. These curves link to an indefinite quaternion algebra that is ramified at a prime p. The team uses methods first brought in by Lue Pan. They focus on the locally analytic vectors in that space. Such vectors are the parts that act in a smooth, calculus-like way. They often carry the key arithmetic data of the whole space.
arxiv-2601-13725:
Nikko John Leo Lobos studies spinning black holes through a lens of quantum gravity ideas in 2026. The frame is the Generalized Extended Uncertainty Principle, or GEUP. It adds two fixes to old rules: a smallest length at tiny scales, and large-scale fixes too. No full quantum gravity theory exists yet to test these ideas.

Lobos takes a metric-based path, working with the curved space form of the hole. He asks what traits such spinning holes would show in real data. Those traits are the phenomenology, the signs a telescope might catch. Clear signs would help future tests of quantum gravity.
arxiv-2601-14225:
Luke Coffman, N. L. Diaz, Martín Larocca, Maria Schuld, and M. Cerezo wrote this 2026 paper on quantum physics. It asks how a known tool for sorting quantum states works when states are drawn in quantum phase space. That tool splits a state into parts set by a symmetry group. Each part is a set piece called an irreducible representation.

Work before this paper showed that the split can show how much of a quantum resource a state holds. Phase space gives a second way to draw the same systems, so the group picture changes there. The authors study that change. Their aim is a clearer test for resource traits in the phase space view.
arxiv-2601-14325:
Li Tuobang examines universal rules in very large societies in this 2026 paper. It builds on the author's past research on the topic. The focus is the topological base that keeps shared rules in force. In graph terms, a small society can be a fully connected network, where all watch all.

In that small case, the paper finds two things can coexist. Absolute egalitarianism and the rule of law fit together through peer monitoring. The title frames the wider themes: scale, hierarchy, the cost of justice, and civilizational development. Readers get a theory of why shared rules need support as societies grow past the small scale.
arxiv-2601-14425:
Haley R. Stueber leads a team of thirteen authors on a distant galaxy cluster in this 2026 paper. The cluster is SPT-CL J2215-3537, at redshift 1.16. It is relaxed and has a cool core. Galaxy clusters serve as a unique laboratory for testing cosmological models. They also show astrophysics at the high-mass limit of structure formation.

Relaxed clusters are prized targets because their form and dynamics are simple. Past redshift one, though, very few such clusters have been identified. The team reports deep Chandra observations of this rare case. Readers get a close look at a calm cluster from when the universe was much younger.
arxiv-2601-14525:
Chenglei Si and five co-authors test automated AI research in this 2026 paper. Automated AI research holds great potential to accelerate scientific discovery. Yet current large language models often generate plausible-looking but ineffective ideas. A paper can sound right and still fail when run. Execution grounding may help, by forcing ideas through real runs.

Two questions stay open. Is automated execution feasible at all? And can models learn from execution feedback? The team's title states their stance: towards execution-grounded automated AI research. Readers get a study of whether running the code, and feeding back the results, makes machine-generated research more real.
arxiv-2601-14925:
Nicolás Arrieta Larraza and Niels de Koeijer work on cleaning up speech in small devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with single-channel speech enhancement, which lifts clear speech out of noise. Such tools run on embedded gear with tight limits on speed and power.

Many deep learning models have been put forward for the task in recent years. One recent model, ULCNet, ranks among the best of them. The authors present Fast-ULCNet, a faster and far lighter network in that line. The name itself points to the goal: low cost and low delay.
arxiv-2601-15025:
Marian Renz, Martin Günther, and co-authors report on the ExPrIS project, which helps robots read a scene. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with object recognition from sensor data. Deep learning has pushed the field far, but its answers can lack sense.

A purely data-driven system ignores what is already known about a place. ExPrIS tests a fix for that gap. Knowledge-level expectations, facts known ahead of time, serve as priors. Those priors guide how the robot interprets what its sensors report, so the labels it gives fit the scene it sees.
arxiv-2601-15325:
Chaojun Li and Hao Fang track communities in networks that change over time. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dynamic community detection. The task shows how group structures in a complex network evolve, merge, and split as time passes.

A common tool is nonnegative tensor RESCAL decomposition. In its classic form, the decomposition rank must equal the count of communities, which limits the model's freedom. The authors add a multilayer perceptron to the method. That enhancement loosens the rank constraint and gives the model more room to fit the changing data.
arxiv-2601-15425:
Lucas G. Barão and J. E. Horvath explain odd changes in a young pulsar's spin. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with PSR B0540-69, a spinning neutron star. Its spin-down rate, the pace at which it slows, has shifted in ways that need a cause.

How a pulsar's crust and magnetic field lines move together is much debated. The question remains unsettled after fifty years of work. New evidence has begun to confirm parts of the theory. The authors tie the spin-down changes to a drift of the magnetic axis, the line through the star's magnetic poles.
arxiv-2601-15625:
Zhiwei Zhang and a large team make language models better at using tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models can call tools well in clean conditions. Real runs are messier. A tool call fails, and smaller models often loop. They repeat invalid calls instead of reading the error and fixing course. That brittleness blocks reliable deployment, since errors in tool use are inevitable.

Their method is called Fission-GRPO, per the title. It teaches models to recover from execution errors. Recovery is a distinct skill from first-try success. Training for it should make agents steadier across multi-turn tasks. The work speaks to anyone building agents that act through software. A model that can absorb an error and adapt is worth far more than one that cannot.
arxiv-2601-15725:
Joana Figueira, Jordi José, Rubén Cabezón, and Domingo García-Senz model a recurrent nova's blast wave in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is U Sco. Recurrent novae erupt more than once. Their outbursts return on short timescales, from one to about a hundred years. Such pace demands extreme conditions. The white dwarf must accrete mass at a very high rate. Its mass sits close to the Chandrasekhar limit.

The star also starts with very high luminosity, the authors note. The study follows how the ejecta interact with two partners. One is the accretion disk feeding the dwarf. The other is the secondary star in the system. Those collisions shape how the eruption looks and fades. Modeling them helps observers read real nova light curves.
arxiv-2601-16125:
Tingyu Song and coauthors build a fine test for search by pic plus word change. Their 2026 preprint deals with composed image search. In that task, a query joins a base pic with a word change. Past tests use few query types. They miss the wide needs of real search by users.

The team builds a new test from real image edit cases. Edits give clear base pics, changes and true end pics. Fine groups let teams see where a model fails by type. A rich test can guide search tools to real world strength. The work stems from edits, not made up query sets.
arxiv-2601-16525:
Yi-Jie Wang, Geng-Dong Zhou, Hyunsung Jung, Seongyeon Youn, Seung-Sup Lee, and Zhi-Da Song study a quantum puzzle in graphene. Flat sheets of carbon, twisted at a magic angle, show odd traits. Pairs of charges form, and gaps open in strange ways. Small flaws in the sheet may drive these traits. Their 2026 preprint builds a theory for such flaws.

The flaws carry both spin and valley marks. The team maps the flaw to a known Kondo type task. They then solve that task with a tool called bosonization. The work splits into two clear cases. In one, a valley pair rules the flaw. In the next, a plain lone state rules it.
arxiv-2601-16625:
