dospassos-manhattan-transfer-1925:
Harper published Manhattan Transfer in New York and London, listing it among Dos Passos's early books. The list sets it beside One Man's Initiation, Three Soldiers, and Streets of Night. Its author was already known as a bold voice in American fiction by 1925.

New York City itself becomes the true hero of the novel. Dozens of lives flicker past in fragments and headlines: clerks, actors, newcomers, and con men. Together they paint the huge city as a machine that lifts people up and grinds them down. Bold in form and rapid in pace, the book stands as the great modern novel of Manhattan life.
dreiser-american-tragedy-1925:
Theodore Dreiser published An American Tragedy in 1925, a long novel based on a real murder case. Clyde Griffiths is a poor young man hungry for wealth and status. He works in a factory owned by rich kin and dreams of marrying into their world. He also courts Roberta, a factory girl under his charge.

When Roberta expects a child, Clyde sees his hopes collapsing. He takes her out in a boat on a lonely lake. The trial that follows fills the last part of the book. Dreiser studies ambition, class, and guilt on a vast scale. The novel is his most famous and most debated work.
eliot-hollow-men-1925:
T. S. Eliot published The Hollow Men in 1925, between The Waste Land and his religious poems. The short work runs in five parts, complete here. Its title joins a line from Conrad with the stuffed effigies burned on Guy Fawkes Day in England.

The hollow men are stuffed men, leaning together like scarecrows, unable to act or truly speak. They drift in a dead land between death and any real afterlife, afraid to meet the eyes that judge them. The poem ends with one of the most famous last lines in modern poetry. It captures the spiritual exhaustion of Europe after the First World War.
epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-oldfath:
W A Oldfather published Volume 1 of his Loeb Epictetus in 1925, the standard scholarly English translation. Epictetus was a Greek slave in Rome who won freedom and taught Stoic philosophy. His student Arrian wrote down the Discourses, and Oldfather's first volume holds Books 1 and 2.

Epictetus taught that events lie outside our control, but our judgments about them lie within it. Freedom, he said, is wanting things to happen as they do. The Discourses speak in a direct, searching voice, questioning students by name. Oldfather's Greek text and facing English made the Loeb set the core text of Roman Stoicism for scholars and general readers alike.
europmc-pmc10122825:
Salari and co-workers pool world studies to estimate how common heart attacks are, in a 2023 review. A heart attack, or myocardial infarction, is a sudden blockage of blood flow to the heart muscle. It remains a leading cause of sudden death, and full global figures help guide prevention work.

Their systematic review gathers rates from many countries and combines them into global estimates. The authors also review the complications that follow a heart attack. The paper gives health systems a clearer picture of the burden they face. It can guide staffing and prevention plans.
europmc-pmc10233625:
Agirre and a very large team describe the CCP4 suite, a software collection for macromolecular crystallography, in a 2023 paper. Crystallography reveals the three-dimensional shapes of proteins and other large molecules from X-ray patterns. CCP4 is a long-running British-led project that builds and shares the programs scientists use for that work.

The paper presents the suite as an integrated whole, from raw data to finished structure. It covers the shared interface and the many specialist tools inside. Generations of structural biologists have relied on this suite, and the paper is its current reference.
europmc-pmc10550825:
De Ceglia and a large team showed in 2023 that a special set of astrocytes can release a brain signal like neurons do. Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells in the brain. Whether they could fire out glutamate, the brain's main go signal, in fast bursts was long in doubt. Proof had been patchy and indirect.

The team sorted mouse hippocampus astrocytes into nine kinds by their gene profiles. One kind alone held the full kit for vesicle release of glutamate. De Ceglia filmed fast, pinpoint releases from that kind in live tissue. Cutting its loader protein, VGLUT1, stopped the events. The same cells shaped circuits for memory and movement, in health and in disease models.
europmc-pmc11462125:
Twyford and the Darwin Tree of Life Consortium set out a DNA barcoding framework for the project in this 2024 paper. The project aims to sequence reference genomes for every eukaryotic species in Ireland and Britain, meaning all species with a cell nucleus. Naming a specimen from looks alone can be unreliable. DNA barcoding, reading a short standard gene stretch, can confirm identity.

Barcode data from over 12,000 project specimens flagged up to 20 percent as needing extra verification. After checks, 2 percent of seed plants and 3.5 percent of animal specimens had their names changed. The standardised framework was adapted for diverse organism groups, from fungi to insects. The authors recommend new sequencing approaches and streamlined computing for the future. They present barcoding as a quality gate that genome projects rarely use but should.
europmc-pmc1247525:
Wasserman and colleagues tested arsenic in water and child intellect in Bangladesh in 2004. Arsenic harms adult nerves, but controlled child studies were lacking. The study covered 201 ten-year-olds in Araihazar. Their parents belonged to a long health cohort of 12,000 residents.

Home tube well water was tested for arsenic and manganese. Children took adapted Wechsler intelligence scale tests at a field clinic. Scores were built for verbal, performance, and full-scale domains. Urine and blood samples added exposure measures. Wasserman gives the first well-controlled look at arsenic and child thinking there.
europmc-pmc1262625:
Altan-Bonnet and Germain modeled how T cells tell friend from foe in 2005. T cells react within seconds to a few foreign markers. They ignore vast numbers of near-identical self markers. No prior model explained that sharp discrimination.

Measurements showed a key signal protein, ERK, switches in digital fashion. It flips fully on or stays off, with little middle ground. Competing feedback loops produce that behavior in their model. A positive loop based on ERK fights a negative loop through another protein. Altan-Bonnet shows feedback rivalry can yield near-perfect discrimination.
europmc-pmc1275525:
Holy and Guo recorded ultrasonic calls of male mice in 2005. Males call at 30 to 110 kilohertz when they meet females or scent. Those calls sit far above human hearing. The team asked whether the calls qualify as song.

Calls came in several distinct syllable types. Syllables formed repeated phrases in ordered sequences. Each male kept a personal syllabic and timing signature. Holy gives the first measured description of mouse song. Mice become a genetic model for studying song production. It appeared in PLoS Biology in 2005. Males sing when they catch the scent of a female mouse.
europmc-pmc1298325:
Town, Nikolic, and Tan reframed brain immune cell activation as a spectrum in 2005. Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain. They arrive during embryonic development from blood lineage. Calling them simply activated hides their range of states.

One end of the spectrum is the eating and clearing response. The other end is antigen presentation, a learned-immunity role. Which state appears depends heavily on the stimulus type. Stimuli reviewed include bacterial patterns, myelin pieces, and amyloid. Alzheimer immunotherapy also shifts microglia along the spectrum. Town argues stimulus-specific states should guide therapy design.
europmc-pmc1463025:
Learning a reach takes more than one kind of memory. Smith, Ghazizadeh, and Shadmehr showed in 2006 that two learning processes run at once, on time scales of minutes. One reacts weakly to errors but holds its gains well. The other reacts strongly but forgets fast.

Their model made an odd forecast. After training, if error feedback is held at zero, skill should partly bounce back on its own. Tests with human reaching confirmed it. Smith argues the two-process view also explains savings, where old skills return fast, and why new learning can clash with old. The brain seems to run two learners at different speeds.
europmc-pmc1564025:
Germs from sick patients can live for months on dry hospital surfaces. Kramer, Schwebke, and Kampf reviewed the proof in 2006. They gathered every study that timed how long ward pathogens persist on surfaces.

Most Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA and resistant enterococci, survive for months. Many Gram-negative species, like E. coli and Pseudomonas, also last months. A few, like the whooping cough germ, last only days. The fungus Candida albicans survives up to four months. Most cold and flu viruses persist a few days. Kramer ties these spans to how outbreaks spread within wards.
europmc-pmc1705825:
TV time and exercise may affect children's metabolic health through different routes. Ekelund and co-authors tested that in 2006 in 1,921 European children aged 9 to 10 and 15 to 16, for the European Youth Heart Study. Activity was measured by motion sensors, not self-report.

More TV viewing went with more body fat. Once activity was accounted for, TV's link to clustered metabolic risk faded, suggesting fatness carries the effect. Activity itself linked independently to lower blood pressure, glucose, insulin, and triglycerides, and to a lower overall risk score. Ekelund concludes the two habits are separate entities, not two ends of one scale.
europmc-pmc1831725:
Jegede examined in 2007 why three northern Nigerian states boycotted the polio vaccination campaign in 2003. Polio immunization drives aim to wipe out the disease, and the World Health Organization had led a global eradication push since 1988. A regional boycott put that goal at risk and let the virus spread.

Jegede drew on books, journals, news reports, and records on past vaccination efforts in northern Nigeria. The account traces how distrust of the program and its sponsors grew into an organized refusal. It sets out the harm the boycott caused, how the dispute was finally resolved, and the ethical issues it raised. The closing recommendations aim to prevent a repeat, stressing trust and local engagement before future campaigns.
europmc-pmc1853125:
Yu, Gerstein and co-authors argued in 2007 that the key proteins in a network are not always its busiest hubs. A bottleneck protein is one that many shortest paths cross, like a bridge on a highway map. Such proteins link network neighborhoods rather than collecting the most partners.

Bottlenecks turned out more likely than hubs to be essential, meaning the cell dies without them. In directed networks, such as gene regulation maps, bottleneck status predicted essentiality far better than connection count did. Bottlenecks also form the dynamic parts of the network. Their activity levels match their neighbors' levels poorly, unlike steady non-bottlenecks. The authors conclude that expression dynamics, the rise and fall of activity, is wired into the network's shape.
europmc-pmc2039825:
Harmsen and De Haard reviewed tiny antibody fragments from camels and llamas in 2007. These animals make antibodies without light chains, unlike most species. A single small domain, called a VHH or Nanobody, can still bind a target fully on its own. The review covers their properties, their production in microbes, and their medical uses, with a focus on yeast production.

These fragments are stable, dissolve well and are easily produced in microorganisms. Their small size suits building larger combined molecules. They also work well in display systems using phages, yeast or ribosomes, which select binders from huge libraries. Compared with conventional antibodies they are simpler to make and handle. The authors see strong promise for biotechnology and therapy.
europmc-pmc2126125: A medical paper on the lymphocyte in natural and induced resistance to transplanted cancer. The cancer-fighting cells. This article preserves that oncology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2130925: A medical paper on the respiratory response to carbon dioxide. The CO2 breath. This article preserves that physiology. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131225: A medical paper with studies on the etiology of heartwater, multiplication of rickettsia. The cattle fever. This article preserves that veterinary pathology. It waits for future eyes. Its place in history is secure. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131625: A medical paper on a paralytic disease of guinea pigs due to the tubercle bacillus. The paralyzed guinea pigs. This article preserves that pathology. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes.
europmc-pmc2140625: A biology paper with experiments on toleration of temperature by drosophila. The heat-proof flies. This article preserves that genetics. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2212625:
Meng and co-workers reported a new stem cell population in 2007 harvested from menstrual blood. The uterine lining rebuilds monthly and makes new blood vessels, suggesting resident stem-like cells. The team isolated adherent cells from menstrual blood and grew them in culture. They named the cells Endometrial Regenerative Cells. Their growth, markers and differentiation range were compared with umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells.

The cells doubled every 19.4 hours, faster than the cord controls, and kept growing beyond 68 doublings without chromosome abnormalities. They could mature into nine lineages, including heart muscle, nerve, liver, pancreas and bone cells. They also produced vessel-growth and signalling factors at levels 10 to 100,000 times higher than control cells. The authors propose them as an easily obtained alternative stem cell source.
europmc-pmc2222925:
Michael and a large team built a network discovery pipeline in 2008 to find daily timing patterns in plant gene activity. Correct daily phasing of gene expression gives plants an adaptive edge. The team analysed time-course data for the whole Arabidopsis nuclear genome under varied temperature cycles, light cycles and circadian conditions. They searched for regulatory modules, groups of genes switched on at specific times of day.

A striking 89 percent of Arabidopsis transcripts were cycling in at least one condition. Most genes peak at a particular time, which shifts with the environment. Temperature cycles on their own can drive half or more of all transcripts. Three distinct timing modules emerged, including a new midnight-specific one called PBX/TBX/SBX. Its PBX element alone could drive daily expression. All three modules are conserved in poplar and rice.
europmc-pmc2265025:
Mendez and Maier reviewed phytostabilization in 2008, using plants to lock mine waste contaminants in place. Unreclaimed mine tailings are a worldwide problem, with bare piles spreading pollution by wind and water, especially in dry regions. The review draws on literature about mine closure, revegetation, plant and microbial ecology, and tailings soil properties, from academic databases and agency publications. It focuses on arid and semiarid environments.

Suitable plants must be native and tolerate drought, salt and metals, while keeping metals out of their shoots. Harsh climate plus the tailings' own properties demand specific choices about growth stage, soil amendments and irrigation. The authors call phytostabilization a feasible, cheaper alternative to conventional cleanup. They also flag open questions impeding long-term success and call for more field trials on species and tailings chemistry.
europmc-pmc2289825:
Dowd and co-workers surveyed bacterial diversity in chronic wounds in 2008 using three DNA-based methods. Chronic wounds host biofilms where many bacterial species cooperate and persist. The team profiled diabetic foot ulcers, venous leg ulcers and pressure ulcers with pyrosequencing, shotgun sequencing and gel fingerprinting of ribosomal genes. They also compared molecular results with traditional culture-based diagnosis used in clinics.

Certain bacteria appeared across all wound types, including Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas and Serratia species. Each wound type also had marked differences. In pressure ulcers, 62 percent of the population were obligate anaerobes, bacteria that cannot tolerate oxygen. Some detected species were not recognised as wound pathogens before. Culture methods identified the main population correctly in only one wound type. The authors argue wounds must be studied and treated as multi-species communities.
europmc-pmc2361125:
Forbes and co-authors updated COSMIC in 2006, a public catalogue of gene mutations found in cancers. Somatic mutations are DNA changes picked up during life, not inherited, and some of them drive cancer growth. COSMIC gathers such changes from the published literature so researchers can search them in one place.

By 2006 about 350 cancer genes were known, and 311 of them carried somatic mutations. The catalogue held full data on 28 known cancer genes plus a systematic screen of 518 protein kinase genes, genes for switch-like enzymes often tied to cancer. Its total reached 538 genes. Just 25 genes were mutated in over 5% of tumors of some type, while 333 showed no mutations at all. A new section covered mutations found in 728 cancer cell lines.
europmc-pmc2438325:
You and colleagues released a bulk primer-design web tool in 2008. A primer is a short DNA piece that starts copying at a chosen spot, essential for genetic mapping tests. Big genome projects need thousands of primers at once, and most existing tools designed them one at a time.

Their program, BatchPrimer3, builds on the trusted Primer3 engine and reads sequences in batches. It designs several primer kinds: plain pairs, primers flanking repeat markers, and three specialised types for detecting single-letter variants. A scoring module picks primers locked to set positions when a test demands it. Inputs can be masked to force or bar regions. Output comes in spreadsheet-ready files to ease ordering. The team validated it on thousands of wheat and Brachypodium primers, a grass model, across several labs.
europmc-pmc2570625:
Friston presented in 2008 a general hierarchical model that unifies many statistical models used on brain and other continuous data. The framework stacks layers of dynamic models so that each layer's output feeds the next, forming a hierarchy. Special cases inside it range from the general linear model for still data to nonlinear models for time series with system noise.

Crucially, every model in the family can be fitted, or inverted, by one scheme called dynamic expectation maximization. Friston reviews how this single approach connects models that look unrelated. He then shows the inversion can be rewritten as a simple neural network. That casts the mathematics as a metaphor for how the brain itself might perform inference and learning.
europmc-pmc2660425:
Pesce and colleagues overturned in 2009 a common belief about a protein that marks a healing type of macrophage, a roaming immune cell. The protein, arginase-1, was thought to feed scarring and allergy-style inflammation by supplying building blocks for tissue growth. The team tested mice infected with a parasitic worm that drives exactly that kind of response.

Mice whose macrophages lacked the protein died faster after infection. Their livers showed worse inflammation, heavier scarring, and higher blood pressure in the veins feeding the liver. Allergy-style signal molecules rose, not fell. In dishes, normal macrophages stopped T cells from multiplying by draining away arginine, an amino acid T cells need. Without the protein, that brake failed. Arginase-1, the authors conclude, calms this inflammation rather than driving it.
europmc-pmc2664325:
Rao and colleagues ran a small trial in 2009 testing whether a probiotic drink could ease the anxiety that often comes with chronic fatigue syndrome. The illness brings deep, lasting tiredness and, in most patients, mood problems. Gut microbes differ in these patients, and animal work hints that gut bacteria can sway mood, so the team tried a friendly strain called Lactobacillus casei Shirota.

Thirty-nine patients drank either the probiotic or a dummy drink daily for two months. Stool tests showed helpful bacteria had risen in the probiotic group, as expected. More striking, their anxiety scores fell significantly, while the comparison group saw no such gain. Depression scores did not shift clearly. The authors treat this as early support for a gut-brain link, and call for larger trials to confirm the effect.
europmc-pmc2724425:
Xi and Li released BSMAP in 2009, a program to map bisulfite sequencing reads onto a whole genome for DNA methylation studies. Bisulfite treatment converts unmethylated cytosines, one DNA letter, to another letter, which reveals methylation at single-letter precision. Mapping those altered reads is hard because the conversion shrinks the alphabet, breaks strand matching, and expands the search space.

BSMAP combines genome hashing, a fast lookup method, with bitwise masking to align reads quickly and accurately. Against existing tools it proved faster, more sensitive, and more flexible, with workable memory and processor needs at genome scale. As the first general-purpose tool of its kind, it is freely available under an open license.
europmc-pmc2725325:
Claesson and co-authors compared in 2009 two high-throughput ways to profile gut microbes in older adults: deep pyrosequencing and a phylogenetic microarray, a chip that detects known groups. Gut community makeup links to many health states, but each method has biases. They used stool samples from four elderly people and read two variable regions of a bacterial identity gene.

Over one million seven hundred fifty thousand sequences still did not exhaust richness, though a fifth of the reads captured most diversity in two samples. One gene region classified far more accurately than the shorter other region. Chip and sequencing profiles clustered very similarly, and their abundance signals correlated strongly, which shows both methods are robust despite different grouping schemes.
europmc-pmc2793425:
Teschendorff and colleagues searched blood samples for a chemical pattern on DNA that flags active ovarian cancer. The marks, called DNA methylation, are added tags that do not change the DNA code itself. Their 2009 study profiled blood from one hundred thirteen women with ovarian cancer and one hundred forty-eight healthy women.

Across more than twenty-seven thousand measured sites, the team derived a signature that spotted active cancer in blind test sets with strong accuracy. It also held up in a second group of treated patients. Age and cancer shifted blood in alike ways, both favoring one white cell type. Most changed sites sat outside the dense tag clusters called CpG islands.
europmc-pmc2811725:
Wallace and Kelsey built the first math model in 2010 of the human ovarian reserve, the stock of resting egg follicles a woman is born with. That stock is set before birth and drains away until menopause near age fifty. The team fitted data from eight tissue studies covering three hundred twenty-five ovaries, from before birth to age fifty-one.

One curve shape fit best, matching the counts well across the whole span. The model estimates that by age thirty, most women keep only about twelve percent of their peak pre-birth stock, and by age forty only about three percent. Age alone explained most of the spread between women, and follicle use sped up until about age fourteen, then slowed.
europmc-pmc2818025:
Bhaumik and colleagues found in 2009 that two tiny RNAs act as a brake on the inflammatory output of aging, worn-out cells. Cells that stop dividing for good, called senescent, pour out signals named IL-6 and IL-8 that inflame nearby tissue. Screening human fibroblasts, a connective tissue cell type, revealed the two RNAs, miR-146a and miR-146b, rising during senescence.

Adding extra copies of these RNAs to young cells cut IL-6 and IL-8 release and lowered a relay protein called IRAK1. Blocking an upstream signal, IL-1 alpha, shut off both the RNAs and the cytokine output. The pattern forms a negative feedback loop, the authors argue, that keeps the senescent outpouring from running unchecked.
europmc-pmc2824625:
Goldstein and colleagues issued the International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on caffeine and sport performance in 2010. The stand sums up a large research base on how caffeine affects endurance, power, and alertness in athletes.

Low to moderate doses, about three to six milligrams per kilogram of body weight, improved performance in trained athletes, while doses of nine or more added nothing. Pure caffeine beat coffee for effect. Gains were clearest for endurance and time trials, and also showed in team sports mixing bursts with long play. Strength and power results stayed mixed. The panel found no proof that caffeine dehydrates athletes during exercise or harms fluid balance.
europmc-pmc2837025:
Ma and Kosorok proposed a new way in 2010 to find gene pathways, sets of genes working together, that predict breast cancer outcome. Single-gene hunts miss the coordination between genes, and older pathway methods judged fit rather than true forecasting power. Their method scores a pathway by how well it predicts relapse-free survival, using the joint effect of all its genes at once.

The method can also pool several studies with unlike designs, which older tools could not do. Run on four breast cancer prognosis datasets, it flagged ninety-seven pathways with real predictive power. Some of those pathways had been missed entirely by rival methods. The authors offer the tool as a sharper route to prognosis clues hiding in gene groups.
europmc-pmc2910725:
Collino and colleagues showed in 2010 that stem cells package selected microRNAs into tiny shed bubbles that other cells can pick up. The bubbles, called microvesicles, are a postal service between cells, and marrow and liver stem cells were already known to mail working messenger RNAs this way. The team asked whether microRNAs, the small gene-tuning RNAs, ride along and whether the cargo is chosen or random.

Profiling hundreds of known microRNAs, they found forty-one shared between the bubbles and their parent cells. Some microRNAs were concentrated into bubbles and vanished from the parent after mailing, while others were always kept home, proof of deliberate sorting. The bubbles also carried the RNA-handling proteins that load, stabilize, and deliver such cargo. Stem cells may tune distant cells' gene activity by post.
europmc-pmc2919425:
Griffin and co-authors built in 2010 a detailed simulation of falciparum malaria in Africa to test how far current and coming interventions can cut transmission. Their individual-based model tracks people and the three main mosquito vectors, and it was fitted to parasite data from thirty-four real transmission settings. Onto that engine they layered treated bed nets, house spraying, mass screening with treatment, and the leading vaccine candidate.

Six representative settings spanned low to intense transmission. Combined roll-out drove transmission down steeply in low and moderate settings, and the vaccine added a useful increment. In the most intense settings, though, even stacked interventions left substantial transmission running, because sheer mosquito pressure overwhelms each tool's partial effect. The model tells planners where elimination is realistic now and where new tools are prerequisites.
europmc-pmc2924325:
Halvorsen, Martin, Broadaway, and Laederach scanned in 2010 for disease mutations that do harm by changing the shape of an RNA strand, not a protein. Many disease-linked variants sit in the control stretches that flank a gene's code. RNA folds into a shifting set of shapes, so the team used a math method that weighs all the folds at once, not just the lowest-energy one.

They tested known disease variants from a large mutation database. In six diseases, several variants clearly warped the fold set of their RNA. The six were an iron and cataract syndrome, beta-thalassemia, cartilage-hair hypoplasia, retinoblastoma, chronic lung disease, and high blood pressure. Such shape-changing variants are missed by protein-based tests. The scan gives labs a ranked list of suspects to test.
europmc-pmc2955025:
Bustin led a group of specialists in a 2010 editorial setting out minimum reporting rules for a common gene measuring method, quantitative real-time PCR. Thousands of papers rest on this technique, yet many report too little detail to judge or repeat the work.

Methods details increasingly shrink into supplements or vanish, and the little shown often exposes sloppy practice. Their summary, a short form of the MIQE guidelines, lists the assay facts every paper should state. It runs from sample handling to analysis choices. It also advises papers whose whole point is checking reference genes. Journals are urged to enforce the checklist.
europmc-pmc2958125:
Pigati and co-authors showed in 2010 that breast cells release small regulatory RNAs selectively rather than in proportion to what they contain. Fluid-borne versions of these molecules are chased as cancer markers, on the assumption that outside levels mirror inside levels.

Comparing normal and cancerous mammary cells, they found two RNAs, miR-451 and miR-1246, were mostly shipped out by cancer cells but mostly kept back by normal ones. In other words, cells choose which molecules to release, and the choice shifts with malignancy. Marker hunters must therefore read fluid profiles on their own terms, not as cell copies.
europmc-pmc2993925:
Chew and Eysenbach mined Twitter during the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic in a 2010 content study, testing whether social posts can track public attention in an emergency. Surveys do that job slowly and at high cost.

They archived over two million posts mentioning swine flu or H1N1 across eight months. Use of the official H1N1 term climbed steadily from under a tenth to about two fifths of posts. Hand coding of a sample found resource sharing the commonest content and misinformation in a small minority. News sites were linked far more than health agencies, and automated searches matched hand coding well.
europmc-pmc2996325:
Wilham and co-authors described a lab test that counts prion seeding activity in about two days, in a 2010 article. Prion diseases resisted fast measurement, forcing slow animal tests to gauge tiny amounts of the infectious protein.

Their method seeds a shaking reaction that converts normal prion protein into fibrous clumps, watched in real time. Testing serial dilutions yields a dose estimate like classic animal end-point assays. Hamster brain samples gave values matching animal test sensitivity. Comparable speed and sensitivity could transform diagnosis and safety screening for blood and tissue products.
europmc-pmc2998425:
Bouffi and co-authors probed how mesenchymal stem cells calm joint inflammation in a 2010 mouse study of arthritis. These cells suppress immune responses and are chased for therapy, but the working ingredients in a living animal were disputed.

Comparing cells from normal mice with cells unable to make certain signals, they traced the effect. Suppression flowed mainly through a messenger called prostaglandin E2. Its release depended on another signal, IL-6, with nitric oxide playing a smaller part. In arthritic mice the cells helped only within a narrow treatment window, and cells lacking IL-6 failed to ease signs.
europmc-pmc3024225:
Zaehle and colleagues tested in 2011 whether weak electric currents applied to the scalp can change working memory, the ability to hold information in mind briefly. Volunteers received gentle direct current stimulation over the front left side of the brain while doing a letter memory task. Brain waves were recorded at the same time to watch the underlying activity change.

Earlier studies had hinted that one current direction could boost memory while the opposite direction could not, but the brain mechanism stayed unclear. The team tracked rhythms in the alpha and theta ranges, which are linked to holding items in mind. Their combined behavior and brain wave design shows how stimulation, task scores, and rhythms move together. The approach points to safer ways to study, and perhaps one day support, failing memory.
europmc-pmc3053525:
Shaikh and coauthors reviewed in 2011 drug delivery systems designed to stick to mucus lined surfaces inside the body. Holding a medicine in place on the moist lining of the mouth, nose, eye, gut, or other passages lets it release slowly where it is needed. Such routes also suit drugs that stomach acid destroys or that the liver strips out after swallowing.

Stickiness depends on both the tissue and the chemistry of the carrier material, and the review explains the forces involved and how they are measured in the lab. It then tours delivery designs for the mouth, nose, eye, digestive tract, and reproductive and rectal routes, with examples for each. Sticky systems raise how much drug reaches the blood and how long it acts. The authors see special promise for fragile large molecules such as peptides.
europmc-pmc3065425:
Sapone and colleagues compared in 2011 two gluten related conditions, celiac disease and gluten sensitivity, and showed they are distinct illnesses. Both make people ill after eating wheat and similar grains, but gluten sensitivity lacks the autoimmune markers and gut damage of celiac disease. The team measured gut leakiness and immune gene activity in gut samples from both patient groups and from healthy controls.

Celiac guts were leakier than normal, as expected. Sensitive patients, surprisingly, had tighter gut barriers than controls, with higher levels of a sealing protein. Their immune profile leaned on fast, innate defenses, while celiac samples leaned on the slower adaptive system, and a regulatory marker ran low in sensitivity. The authors conclude the two conditions arise through different mechanisms. That distinction supports diagnosing sensitivity as its own entity, not a mild form of celiac disease.
europmc-pmc3138025:
Wissem Mnif and colleagues reviewed farm chemicals that interfere with hormones in a 2011 paper in a public health journal. Such chemicals can disturb the body's signalling system in people and wildlife, and many pesticides belong to the group. People meet them at work and through food, water, soil, and air.

The review traces how widely these products spread since the nineteen thirties. Some linger in soil and water and build up through food chains, and the review weighs what health effects studies have tied to them. Benefits for crop protection and disease control are weighed against the risks. The authors gather current knowledge to guide safer use and tighter rules for hormone-disrupting pesticides.
europmc-pmc3149125:
Bruce Bacon and colleagues wrote the 2011 practice guideline on iron overload disease for the US liver association known as the AASLD, published in Hepatology. Passed down in families, the condition makes the body absorb too much iron, which slowly damages the liver and other organs. The guideline gives doctors a shared, evidence-based approach to finding and treating it.

Its advice covers diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, each graded by the strength of advice and quality of evidence under a standard scoring system. The authors stress the guidance offers preferred approaches, not rigid rules, leaving room for judgement in each case. The document rests on a formal review of world literature plus the authors' clinical experience, and it is meant for practising physicians managing this condition.
europmc-pmc3177825:
Ying Wang and colleagues charted gut bacteria across the life of the main African malaria mosquito in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Gut microbes shape mosquito fitness and immunity, and the mosquito passes them through water-dwelling young stages into flying adults. Mosquitoes were reared in semi-natural Kenyan habitats and sampled at each stage by gene sequencing.

Young stages carried guts dominated by light-harvesting bacteria, while adults shifted to two other broad groups with a stable core pair of families. Adult diet mattered greatly: blood meals crashed diversity and favoured gut bacteria equipped, as their genomes show, to handle the chemical stress of digesting blood. Field and laboratory adults ended with similar communities, suggesting the gut selects its residents firmly. The profile hints the microbes help the mosquito live with its bloody diet.
europmc-pmc3208625:
Trevor Dalton and colleagues built a mouse wound model carrying a mixed-species bacterial biofilm, reported in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Real chronic wound infections usually involve several bacterial species at once, yet most animal studies test only one. The team wanted a model that captures how species interact inside an infected wound.

They grew biofilms in the lab from four species, mixing Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria plus aerobes and anaerobes, then transplanted them onto mouse wounds. The mixed community persisted throughout the experiment. Compared with single-species infections, the polymicrobial wounds healed more slowly, and their bacteria tolerated antimicrobial treatment better. The results suggest cooperation between species helps explain why chronic wounds resist healing and antibiotics.
europmc-pmc3223525:
Cathy Price and Joseph Devlin set out their Interactive Account of how the brain reads, in this 2011 paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences. A region at the back underside of the brain responds to written words as well as to objects. Traditional views treat it as a word-form specialist; Price and Devlin propose a different picture of what it does.

In their account, perception mixes incoming sensory detail with predictions generated from experience. The region combines visual features with higher-level information such as speech sounds, actions, and meanings. Its apparent specialization for spelling therefore emerges from those interactions. It does not come from built-in tuning to letters. The authors show how the account explains normal reading, developmental dyslexia, and the effects of damage to the region.
europmc-pmc3257625:
Claudia Luevano-Contreras and Karen Chapman-Novakofski reviewed dietary advanced glycation end products and aging in this 2010 article in Nutrients. These compounds, called AGEs, form when sugars react with proteins without enzymes, both in cooked food and inside the body. Levels rise with age and are higher in several chronic diseases of aging.

The authors summarize two decades of work measuring AGEs in foods and in people, and the mechanisms by which some tissues get damaged while others are spared. Animal and human studies link AGEs to heart and blood vessel disease, Alzheimer's disease, and diabetes complications. Diets low in AGEs improved wound healing, insulin resistance, and heart outcomes in several studies. Such diets also extended lifespan in animals. The paper closes with suggestions for future research.
europmc-pmc3257725:
Maddalena Rossi, Alberto Amaretti, and Stefano Raimondi reviewed folate production by probiotic bacteria in this 2011 article in Nutrients. Folate is a vitamin many people lack, and certain gut bacteria can make it. The authors assessed which probiotic groups genuinely produce the vitamin, aiming at folate-enriched fermented foods and supplements that manufacture folate inside the colon.

The verdict differs by genus. Most lactobacilli cannot synthesize folate at all and actually drain it from fermented dairy products, though one species is an exception when a building block is supplied. Several bifidobacteria strains do produce and release folate, in widely varying amounts. Rats fed folate-producing bifidobacteria showed higher blood folate, and a human trial found more folate in feces, proof of production in the body.
europmc-pmc3338325:
Blacquière, Smagghe, van Gestel, and Mommaerts reviewed fifteen years of research on a popular insecticide class and bees, in a 2012 article. Neonicotinoid sprays and seed coatings control crop pests effectively, but they can also reach pollinators. The review gathers evidence on three fronts, contamination levels found in the field, harms seen in bees, and whether official risk assessment handles these chemicals properly.

Residues in plants, bees, and hive products generally sat below levels that kill or chronically harm bees outright, though data were thin and gathered for few crops. Lab studies found real effects on foraging, learning, and memory at sublethal doses, while field studies at realistic doses found none. The authors judge the existing risk scheme for systemic chemicals usable for these insecticides, and call for field realistic tests with molecular markers to sharpen future assessments.
europmc-pmc3377625:
Orenstein and colleagues examined arteries from children lost to Kawasaki disease in 2012 to explain its complex damage to blood vessels. Among children in rich countries, it is the leading source of heart disease that begins after birth. Earlier accounts described one bout of artery inflammation followed by healing, which fit the illness poorly.

Studying dozens of autopsy and transplant specimens, the team separated three linked processes. A brief, self-limited attack destroys the artery wall early and can form bulges that clot or burst. A longer inflammation follows, converting wall cells into scar-like builders that slowly narrow the channel. Untangling the three steps reshapes how doctors think about treatment timing.
europmc-pmc3460225:
Morris proposed in 2011 a smarter way to pool genome-wide association studies across ethnic groups. Such pooling finds the spots behind complex traits and zooms toward the causal variant, but most data came from European-descended groups. Mixing populations helps, because their local DNA correlation patterns differ, yet their genetic effects may also differ in ways standard pooling handles badly.

The new method expects similar effects in closely related populations while allowing distant groups to diverge. Across many simulated scenarios it beat both fixed-effect pooling, in raw power and in pinpointing the causal spot, and random-effects pooling when relatedness was modeled well. The payoff is sharper maps of trait genetics drawn from the whole species, not one branch of it.
europmc-pmc3464725:
Fan and co-authors reviewed the role of cardiac fibroblasts in heart disease for Fibrogenesis and Tissue Repair in 2012. Fibroblasts are the most common cells in heart muscle, and their main job is building the support matrix around other cells. When they grow too active, that matrix builds up as stiff scar tissue called fibrosis, which harms heart function.

The review covers where these cells come from and how their numbers rise in disease. Fan's group explains how fibroblasts both make and break down the matrix, guided by enzymes and their blockers. Lessons from mouse models with altered matrix proteins fill much of the paper. The authors show why these once ignored cells now sit at the center of heart research.
europmc-pmc3491025: Protists got a DNA-barcoding push. This 2012 paper pushes DNA barcoding beyond animals, plants, and fungi. The authors map the push. Their work guides taxonomy. Pawlowski's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped protist taxonomy.
europmc-pmc3552825: Gut germs got an estrogen link. This 2012 paper links gut microbes to estrogen levels. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides oncology. Flores's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped breast-cancer research.
europmc-pmc3556525: MRSA got a genome outbreak study. This 2013 paper traces an MRSA outbreak with full-genome sequencing. The authors reveal the tracing. Their work guides hospitals. Harris's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. The study shaped hospital screening.
europmc-pmc3556625: Radiation got a heart-disease review. This 2012 pooled study links low-level radiation to heart disease. The authors reveal the risk. Their work guides policy. Little's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It shaped radiation limits.
europmc-pmc3607725: Crops got a measuring manifesto. This 2013 paper sets rules for next-gen crop measuring. The authors map the strategies. Their review guides breeders. Cobb's paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped smart farming. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3630325: Dopamine got a flexibility review. This 2013 paper reviews how dopamine aids mental flexibility. The author maps the roles. Their review guides neuroscience. Floresco's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped ADHD research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3665925: STRUCTURE got a how-to. This 2013 paper explains STRUCTURE software for genetics. The authors map the uses. Their review guides researchers. Porras-Hurtado's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. Labs rely on it. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3667625: Memory got a protein-brake study. This 2013 paper shows releasing the protein-making brake boosts memory. The authors reveal the release. Their work guides drug design. Sidrauski's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It is a classic.

fitzgerald-great-gatsby-1925:
F. Scott Fitzgerald published The Great Gatsby in 1925, his novel of Jay Gatsby's green-light pursuit of Daisy Buchanan. The tale moves through the glitter and rot of 1920s Long Island,. It sold modestly then and rose after Fitzgerald's death to near the summit of American novels.

Nick Carraway, a bond salesman from the Midwest, rents beside Gatsby's mansion and is drawn into his parties and past. Gatsby, born Gatz, built a bootleg fortune to win Daisy, now wed to brutal Tom Buchanan of East Egg. A hit-and-run, a garage killing, and Gatsby's own murder drain the dream of its gold in the end at summer's close. Nick's narration weighs the careless rich and the dreamer who outshone them in a prose of rare lyric polish throughout. The green light across the bay remains America's emblem of longing.
ford-no-more-parades-1925:
No More Parades, published in 1925, is the second volume of Parade's End and its great war book. Christopher Tietjens now serves as an officer in France, holding a draft of men together under shelling, mud, and absurd orders.

Sylvia follows him to the front, trailing scandal, while his mind keeps returning to Valentine Wannop and the England that is vanishing. Ford, who served himself, writes battle as confusion, noise, and moral pressure rather than glory. The trenches are rendered as a modernist time-piece, memory and terror interleaved. Many judge this the finest volume of the four.
frus-1861-d125:
On 30 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton, his minister in France. The letter is document 125 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's end of May orders to Paris matched his stern line to London that month. Both envoys were told to block any step toward the South. The letter shows one policy worked through two capitals at once, each with its own risks. The stern May line worked, and neither capital took the step the South craved. The step the South craved, recognition, stayed unmade in both capitals all year.
frus-1861-d225:
Writing home was Mr. Fay's duty, and his letter of 7 June 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 225 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the opening months of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d25:
On 6 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford at the Brussels post. The letter is document 25 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's May orders went out as the Union blockade of Southern ports took shape. Envoys had to explain that step and defend its force in law. A letter to Brussels put those points in Sanford's hands, ready for use with the Belgian court and press. The blockade had been declared in April, and its law was now the front line of the paper war. Law, argued well, could hold a blockade that ships alone could not.
frus-1862-d125:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 August 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 125 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d225:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 August 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 225 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was acting for Lord Lyons at the British legation in Washington.

August opened with the war's center shifting back to northern Virginia, where a new campaign was gathering. Stuart's letters to Seward carried British requests and protests in the formal manner of the legation. Read with Seward's replies around it, this letter shows the two offices grinding through wartime business. They ground on even as armies moved within a few days' ride of the capital.
frus-1862-d25:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 28 February 1862. Congress received it as Document 25 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the winter of the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d325:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 12 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 325 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Five days later the armies met at Antietam, but in Paris the talk was of mediation drafts and Mexican reinforcements. Dayton's job was to keep those two files separate in French minds, so Mexico would not buy the South a friend. His report from this week sits in the file just before the battle news broke the pattern. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d425:
Horace J. Perry sent this report from the Madrid legation to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 August 1862. It is Document 425 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Mid-August 1862 found the Madrid mission in transition, with Gustav Koerner arriving to take over as minister while Perry stayed on as secretary. Perry's reports bridged the change, keeping Washington informed about Spanish policy without a gap. Spain still held the keys to Cuba's ports, and its stance in Mexico was settling into watchful distance from France. A reader gets from letters like this the steady, factual feed on which Seward built his Spanish policy.
frus-1862-d525:
On 5 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike. It is Document 525 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

November brought the dismissal of McClellan and France's proposal for joint mediation in the war, which the Union refused. Seward's orders that month repeated the refusal to every post, great and small, The Hague included. Pike's Netherlands had no part in the mediation scheme, but a single line held everywhere was the policy's strength. The dispatch is part of the late-autumn file of that year. In it the Union, bloodied but standing, told Europe plainly that the war was an American question. It said the war would stay one.
frus-1862-d625:
On 1 April 1862, the day after his previous order, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to Edward Joy Morris at Constantinople. It is Document 625 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Back-to-back orders to the farthest post in Europe suggest an enclosure or a second subject that could not travel in the same letter. The Ottoman file's business ran to the protection of American citizens and commerce in the Levant. There, consuls did the daily work. They did it under the minister's eye. Seward's paired instructions gave Morris the Department's mind on that business in full. Together the two letters show the care Washington took with a mission three months' post from home.
frus-1863p1-d125:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 12 March 1863, though the printed volume sets it after letters of 19 March. Adams was the American minister in London, writing to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 125 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Stray dates are a quirk of these printed files, where late or loose sheets were set where they fit. The work in the letter is Adams's own: a report from the post that tracked Britain's mind on the war. Read on its true date, it fills a gap in mid-March. Read in its printed place, it is a small lesson in how the record was built.
frus-1863p1-d225:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 July 1863. It is document 225 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d25:
This second letter of 5 January 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. It is document 25 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Paired letters like these are a mark of the exchange all through the volume.

Seward often split his orders so each sheet held one clear point. Adams, in turn, could act on each as its matter ripened in his talks with the British. This letter is the mate to document 24, written the same day. Together they open Washington's side of the London file for 1863, in the week the war took on a new cause.
frus-1863p1-d325:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 24 November 1862. It appears as document 325 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It comes from the autumn after Antietam, when Lincoln's first emancipation order had just raised the stakes for Britain. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d425:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 26 March 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d525:
Document 525, dated 22 May 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d625:
From Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 29 September 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d125: Harriman wrote to Hopkins again on November 13, 1943, a day after his previous letter in this series. The new message is Document 125 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Back-to-back letters from Moscow in the summit fortnight suggest fast-moving news, though the record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, among the last Moscow reports before Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d225:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Roosevelt a secret memorandum aboard the Iowa on 17 November 1943 about command of British and American forces fighting Germany. It carries two draft plans, Enclosure A and Enclosure B, and states plainly that the chiefs judge Enclosure A the sounder plan.

That plan argues the war in Europe has outgrown committee control. Operations in the Mediterranean, in northwest Europe, and the strategic bombing of Germany are tied so closely that a single commander should direct all three, under the Combined Chiefs of Staff. The chiefs urge an immediate appointment, warning that even a commander named now could not be working before the end of January 1944, and that delay risks confusion at a critical time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d25: Roosevelt and Churchill signed a joint message to Stalin on August 18, 1943, in the middle of their Quebec Conference. It is Document 25 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter in two names carried extra weight in Moscow, where Stalin had long complained of fighting the Germans nearly alone. The record names the three leaders and the date. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series as a marker of allied unity that August.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d325:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 400/1 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, on control of strategic air forces in northwest Europe and the Mediterranean. It answers the American plan to place the Eighth and Fifteenth Air Forces under one headquarters in the United Kingdom.

The British grant America's right to organize its own forces, but record their view that the plan's drawbacks far outweigh its gains. A big day-bomber mission needs up to twenty-four hours to prepare. European weather allows a launch decision only hours ahead. Attacks from bases as far apart as Britain and Italy therefore cannot truly be combined in detail. Switching forces between theaters would also demand duplicate airfields, runways, and depots, locking up men and gear. General coordination, they conclude, can be had under the present organization.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d425:
The Log of the President's trip resumes with the second Cairo stay, covering 2 to 7 December 1943, kept hour by hour by Lieutenant William Rigdon. It opens with the flight back from Tehran on 2 December.

The President's plane reached Cairo West airfield at twenty-five minutes past two, Cairo time, after a 1,290-mile flight, and Roosevelt returned to Ambassador Kirk's villa in the Mena district. That evening word came from Ankara that President Inönü would arrive on Saturday 4 December for talks with Roosevelt and Churchill. The next day's entries show the machinery turning. Major Boettiger flew to Adana at noon to meet Inönü and bring him to Cairo. The President signed a batch of bills and a Day of Prayer proclamation. He lunched with Marshall, Leahy, McCloy, Winant, and Hopkins. He met his Joint Chiefs at ten past five.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d525:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote to Secretary of State Hull from London on December 22, 1943. Winant was deeply trusted in Britain, where he had stood with Londoners through the Blitz. The State Department printed his message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Winant's reports carried a feel for British opinion that few envoys could match, because the British treated him almost as one of their own. A late-December message belongs to the period when London was digesting the Tehran and Cairo decisions and looking toward the invasion year. For readers, it offers the alliance's most sensitive listening post reporting home at Christmas time.
frus-1944-quebec-d125:
H. Freeman Matthews, deputy director of the Office of European Affairs, wrote to General McFarland of the Joint Chiefs on September 9, 1944. He enclosed a British Foreign Office telegram instructing London's ambassador in Moscow on a joint approach to the Russians. The subject was Allied plans for occupying northern Norway if German forces withdrew.

The British wanted Moscow told the plans were old, not improvised to block Soviet troops entering Norway. Norwegian pressure on Eisenhower's headquarters, help for Norwegian resistance, and a naval base for Russia convoys were the stated reasons. Matthews suggested similar instructions go to Ambassador Harriman, so General Deane in Moscow would have the political background.
frus-1944-quebec-d225:
Hopkins telegraphed Roosevelt on September 11, 1944, after discussing the Poland cables with the State Department and General Marshall. Warsaw's garrison was fighting on as the Soviet agreement to cooperate opened a narrow chance of relief. Hopkins proposed three coordinated steps for the president to set in motion at once.

First, a message to Poland's prime minister assuring him every possible step was being taken to bring Allied assistance speedily to Warsaw. Second, a message to Marshall asking that General Deane in Moscow explore the matter fully and urgently with British and Russian officers. Third, a State Department reply to Harriman, coordinated with Marshall's instructions to Deane. The Map Room corrected Hopkins's draft in one respect: the message went to the prime minister, not the president, of Poland.
frus-1944-quebec-d25:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 11, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, in the correspondence leading to the September conference.

Mid-August brought the invasion of southern France within days and the liberation of Paris within weeks. Roosevelt's letters then balanced the final campaigns against the approach of the Quebec meeting, where lend-lease and Germany's future awaited decision. For readers, this message shows the President steering the alliance toward its autumn summit while the greatest pursuit battle of the war ran its course in France.
frus-1945-50-intel-d125:
Admiral Leahy, the president's chief of staff and a member of the intelligence authority, wrote to Director Vandenberg on 12 August 1946. Leahy spoke with the president's nearness behind him. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A letter from Leahy in the middle of the August ruling week carried weight beyond its words. As the authority's presidential member, he linked the board to the White House that had created it. Vandenberg, pressing his group's claims hard that summer, had to heed the channel. Readers should place this paper among the settlement papers of the dispute. The board ruled, the bureau protested. The president's own man wrote to the director who had forced the question.
frus-1945-50-intel-d225:
On 26 September 1947 the First Meeting of the National Security Council sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. It survives in print as document 225 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. A new law was about to remap the whole field: the armed services, the National Security Council, and the CIA all hung on it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. The Council had been created by law only weeks before, and its first meeting set the pattern for how it would work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d25:
Admiral Ernest King, chief of naval operations and commander of the fleet, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 9 October 1945. King was the Navy's top officer and a formidable voice in any council. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A paper from King carries the weight of the wartime fleet behind it. The Navy's intelligence, above all its code-breaking and its Pacific networks, was a prize in the postwar argument, and King guarded naval prerogatives jealously. Readers meet the service chiefs' level of the fight here. Not drafting details, but fixed positions from men who had won a war and meant to keep their tools. Forrestal received few papers with more authority behind them.
frus-1945-50-intel-d325:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 11" heads a text dated 16 September 1947. The State Department prints it as document 325 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Central Intelligence Group knew its days were short, since the National Security Act would soon set up the CIA in its place.

Once a directive went out, staff worked to its terms, and later papers cite its number as their warrant. Staff could be held to each line, which is why the words were fought over before issue. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d425:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 2 was issued on 13 January 1948. It appears as document 425 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The low number with a later date tells its own story. The Council revised and reissued its early rules as the new system settled. Directives like this one set who did which work across the government. They are dry reading, but they map the real lines of power in early Cold War intelligence. A revised base rule shows the Council learning from the first months of joint work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d125:
Secretary of the Treasury Morgenthau sent Stettinius a sharp critique of British planning on 3 November 1944. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, forwards a memorandum on the British draft of a policy directive for Germany. A copy had gone to Lord Cherwell, with the War Department's approval, he says.

The enclosed critique finds the British draft wanting either way. If it is a long-range program, Washington is not ready to decide such issues. If it is an interim one, it prejudges them. Its ninety-seven pages of detailed instructions mix principles with office detail, and so give no basis for high-level decisions. Morgenthau urges talks confined to the major interim questions, leaving detail to staff work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d225:
“Russian Request for Financing of Acquisitions of Capital Equipment During and After the War” is a briefing book paper of 26 January 1945. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It states what Moscow asked, and the answer the State Department proposes.

The Russians seek a credit of six billion dollars at two and a quarter percent, with repayment ending in the thirtieth year. It would cover gear for now and for true postwar needs alike. The Department would answer through Harriman in set steps. No long-range equipment can go into production until the 3-C lend-lease terms, under talk since May 1944, are settled. Action on 3-C should come before the Fourth Protocol is signed, though Washington should not stand too hard on that point. Postwar credits are a separate matter.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d25: On 26 November 1944 Roosevelt wrote to Churchill again, continuing the near-daily rhythm of their fall correspondence. The message is document 25 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. By then the two governments were deep in preparation, and even short presidential notes could settle questions that lower officials had left open for weeks.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d325:
Settling two points before the afternoon's big meeting drove this Joint Chiefs session at Yalta on February 4, 1945. Admiral Leahy said the chiefs wanted Stalin to order his General Staff into full, free, and frank talks with the American and British staffs. They also wanted a direct channel for matching moves between General Eisenhower, Field Marshal Alexander, and the Soviet command.

General Marshall backed the plan, urging that the field commanders deal with each other through the Allied military missions in Moscow. The minutes show the chiefs rehearsing their asks hours ahead of the first plenary. Coordination with the Red Army was still more hope than fact.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d425:
Churchill urged patience in Hiss's notes of the plenary of February 9, 1945. Molotov had offered amendments to the American proposal on Poland. Churchill said he was glad to see advance, but he had something to say before the report went on. He referred to private talks about the Lublin government.

This matter cannot be hurried, he insisted. A complete meeting of minds might still be reached in the time left. Only 48 hours remained, he noted, and a day's latitude might be taken if needed. To leave without agreement on Poland, he warned, would mean failing on the most dangerous and tiresome matter of all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d125:
Secretary Byrnes invited Robert Murphy to Berlin and listed his full party in a telegram dated July 5, 1945. The message is document 125 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, was asked to see that proper arrangements were made for the group, due to arrive July 13.

The party totals thirty-six people. Below Byrnes stand Harriman and Murphy, plus Assistant Secretaries Clayton and Dunn. There are also specialists for every region on the agenda. They range from Bohlen and Thompson for Russian questions to Vincent for China and Dooman for the Far East. A staff of twelve handles administration and secretarial work. The roster shows the State Department arriving at Potsdam staffed for any subject the leaders might raise.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d225:
Ambassador Kirk relayed Churchill's dark mood about Russia in a telegram from Caserta on July 12, 1945. The message is document 225 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Field Marshal Alexander had confided what he had heard from the Prime Minister.

Churchill is very ill at ease about the Russians, Alexander said. Reports from Ambassador Clark Kerr's talks with Soviet officials left no doubt in Churchill's mind about Russia's ultimate intentions. Stalin was being amiable now to sweeten the atmosphere before the meeting, but several unpleasant things would likely be tabled, and even a fait accompli or two should not be ruled out. Alexander urged knotting together at once what could be salvaged of the Western way of life in Europe, Germany included.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d25:
Stalin listed his grievances at the second Kremlin conversation, on May 27, 1945, in Bohlen's memorandum. Hopkins opened by recalling that the Marshal had hinted at questions about the United States that worried him. Would he care to begin with them? Stalin said he would not hide behind Soviet public opinion. He would speak of the feeling created in Soviet government circles by recent American acts.

His concerns, as listed, ran wide. They covered Argentina's invitation to San Francisco, the reparations commission, and the Polish question. The curtailment of Lend-Lease and the disposal of German naval and merchant ships followed. Poland drew a heading of its own. The memorandum shows the mission turning, on its second night, into an accounting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d325:
Soviet views on freezing enemy assets in neutral countries are reported in a Washington cable to Ambassador Winant of June 30, 1945. Moscow's embassy messages had described the Soviet stand on assets held in Switzerland, Spain, Portugal, and Sweden. The assets belonged to Finland, Rumania, Hungary, and Bulgaria.

Because those states had declared war on the Axis, Moscow argued, their resources should go to rebuilding, so state assets should not be blocked. Private assets, the Soviets said, should be blocked, with control in the hands of the Control Commissions. The Department agreed on the private assets, but parted from Moscow on the state holdings.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d425:
British proposals on the coal famine come in an aide-mémoire from the British Embassy dated July 3, 1945. It refers to the recent exchange of messages between President Truman and Prime Minister Churchill on steps in Germany to relieve Europe's threatening coal famine. London's first point concerns consultation.

Procedure should at once be concerted, the Embassy says, for consulting the Soviet government on the question, as well as the French, whom Washington had already approached. It is common ground, London adds, that Germany should be administered as a whole, under policies agreed by the four controlling powers. The note then turns to amendments in the draft directive the President proposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d525:
Russian absence from Europe's economic bodies is the problem in a briefing book paper dated July 3, 1945. Its recommendation matches its title. It would obtain Soviet agreement to take part fully in four bodies. They are the Emergency Economic Committee for Europe, the European Coal Organization, the European Central Inland Transport Organization, and the United Maritime Authority.

The discussion admits how far matters stand from that goal. The Soviet Union has declined to participate in the first three bodies, all temporary advisory organizations for urgent continental problems. Negotiations to establish them began in the fall of 1944, and every effort was made to obtain Soviet participation. Failing that, the three were set up during May 1945 without Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d625:
From Moscow on July 10, 1945, reparations chief Edwin Pauley sent an urgent secret wire to Ralph Davies. Davies was deputy head of the Petroleum Administration for War. The wire is document 625 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam, with a copy to the White House.

Pauley asks Davies to rush him two sets of figures. First, the tanker needs for supplying Western and Mediterranean Europe from Anglo-U.S. oil sources. Second, the rough tanker saving if Austrian, Hungarian, and Rumanian sources could be used in full. He refers to Davies's letter of June 29, which had set out the western oil needs. The short wire is a working step in the push, seen across this file, to free East European oil for Allied use.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1025:
Philip Mosely wrote to William Clayton on July 21, 1945, about a Soviet proposal by Ivan Maisky. Maisky had urged immediate internationalization of the Ruhr. Mosely warns that the plan would revise the agreed occupation zones at Britain's expense. It would strip the larger part of the British zone's resources. That would come only weeks after America honored the zone lines.

He recalls that Truman refused Churchill's plea to hold the May advance line as a bargaining chip. America withdrew on its pledged word. Mosely's advice is to press Russia instead to start the agreed Control Machinery at once. Experience with that machinery, he argues, will teach more about lasting Ruhr control than a sudden new scheme.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1125: Acting War Shipping Administrator Conway wrote this internal note to Morse, aide to the War Shipping Administrator, on 20 July 1945. It belongs to the office that ran America's merchant fleet in wartime. The note is short staff business between two men in the same agency. Morse served as chief aide to Administrator Land, and Conway held the acting post under him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1225:
Sato, Japan's ambassador in Moscow, replied to Foreign Minister Togo on 18 July 1945. His seat gave him the hard side of the errand: Soviet doors were not opening. Moscow stalled, smiled, and said little that Tokyo could use.

Sato's reports home carried that cold news in careful words. He dealt with Soviet officials face to face and read their delays for what they were. Washington read his cables too, through its codebreakers, and learned that Japan's peace feelers were failing. This dispatch is the Moscow end of a dying hope, written by the man sent to keep it alive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1325:
The Economic Subcommittee issued its report of 1 August 1945, the summit's last full day. By then the money terms of the peace were nearly fixed. A closing report from the experts summed up the economic brief at the point of decision.
