The group's work had run through the whole conference: German industry, food, reparations, and trade. Its reports gave the ministers agreed facts to bargain over. This final one belongs to the endgame. It shows the staff layer finishing its task as the leaders finished theirs, and it closes the subcommittee's run in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1425:
The Soviet delegation put a proposal before the conference on 23 July 1945, in the run of late papers printed near the volume's end. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

By the second week at Potsdam, proposals were no longer opening bids; they were moves in a closing game. Each side knew the others' lines and drafted to shift them by inches. This Soviet proposal can be read against the final protocol of 1 August to see what those inches came to. The editors chose to print the drafting trail, not just the results. That choice makes the volume a record of negotiation rather than a trophy case.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-125:
Another staff memorandum from the United States delegation bears the date July 27, 1945. Two memos from the team on one day reflect the conference's late pace. Each handled a strand of business that could not wait. The paper joined the files later printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

What such a memo offers is a fixed point. It states what its writer held to be true or needed on that day. Later events can be measured against it. Readers tracing a topic through the volume will find these memos useful mileposts. They mark where thought stood before the final bargains were struck.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-25:
No official record survives of a garden talk on July 19, 1945, and the editors print a diary entry instead. The talk is covered by an editorial note in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Secretary Stimson's diary for that day supplies the only account.

Stimson writes that Lord Cherwell called at noon. The two men, with Harvey Bundy, sat out under the trees and talked over S-1. Cherwell was very reasonable on notifying the Russians, Stimson records. He felt about as doubtful on that question as the Americans did. Cherwell also reported Churchill much pleased with their luncheon together that week. The talk, he said, had much cheered the prime minister. The diary fragment is the only trace of a key side discussion on the atomic project at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d725:
Samuel Reber, special assistant to the director of European affairs, wrote this memorandum on July 18, 1945. Document 725 dates from the Potsdam Conference's second day. Reber was a career officer with deep European service. His memos carried the working knowledge of the Department's Europe hands. The paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

Staff memoranda like Reber's formed the briefs behind the briefs. Leaders read summaries; men like Reber wrote the layers beneath. Readers find in such papers the facts officials trusted. The memo shows the conference's first days being fed by quiet, expert work done far from the cameras.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d825:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Melbourne in Rumania on July 28, 1945, in document 825. Washington answered its acting representative in Bucharest in the conference's last days. The letter carried guidance from the home office. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Guidance sent this late had to reckon with the summit's results. Melbourne would soon work inside the settlement's terms. Readers see Washington preparing its man for that change. The document closes a circuit opened by his many reports. Facts had flowed up for two weeks; now direction flowed down, shaped by Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d925:
The United States submitted this final Pauley version of its reparations position to the Economic Sub-Committee on July 24 or 25, 1945. It presents a plan for exacting reparations from Germany in a practical way. The program of removals would run through the occupation machinery already set up in Germany.

The plan allows removals to start at once, as an interim scheme. It pairs west and east in a swap. Steel equipment from the Ruhr would go to the Soviet Union. In return, farm goods, fuels, timber, and potash from the east would flow to western Europe. The attached proposal text repeats the zonal removal rules, with imports paid before other removals.
gao-gaoreports-b-297225: Information Ventures took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297425: Prudent Technologies took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297825: Allied Protection Services took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Security firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-310725: This 2008 GAO ruling is about disposition of False Claims Act Recoveries at National Science Foundation. GAO's legal decisions tell agencies what federal funding law allows. Agencies follow these rulings when spending federal funds. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-310825: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by DRSC3 Systems, LLC. Decided February 26, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1025: The Kennedy Center was improving in 2006, and GAO's report says progress had been made on recommendations, though oversight challenges remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the nation's stage needed steady supervision. The progress had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-125: Navy Reserve manpower needed cost-effective planning in 2005, and GAO's report says assessments should consider the best mix. The findings demand the analysis. The report warns that the reserve sailors deserved smart staffing. The assessments had to consider the mix.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-25: No Child Left Behind needed clearer information in 2005, and GAO's report says improved access to Education's data could help states implement teacher provisions. The findings demand the clarity. The report warns that the schoolchildren deserved workable rules. The access had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-425: Junk fax enforcement was faltering in 2006, and GAO's report says weak procedures and performance management hindered the crackdown. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the fax spam should not win. The enforcement had to improve. The fax spam should not win.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-525: The IRS's tax settlement program was mixed in 2006, and GAO's report says performance varied, though better information and simplification could help. The findings balance the good and the gaps. The report warns that the debt deals deserved better management. The program had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-625: EPA grant reforms were progressing in 2006, and GAO's report says progress had been made, though implementation and accountability weaknesses remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the green grants needed steady handling. The reforms had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-825: Fighting human trafficking needed better data in 2006, and GAO's report says better data, strategy, and reporting were required for the overseas effort. The findings demand the tools. The report warns that the modern slavers should not operate in the dark. The effort had to be sharpened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-25: The next air-traffic system kept inching along in 2007, and GAO's report reviews the progress and the challenges of the transformation. The findings take stock. The report warns that the future of flight needed a surer flight plan. The skies' overhaul had to stay on course.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-425: Homeland Security's tech-hiring blueprint mostly matched the guidance in 2007, GAO found — but the doing lagged the drawing. The report says the department's plan for landing and keeping computer talent needed teeth and timelines. Paper plans do not staff a cyber watch; GAO wanted the follow-through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-825: Chemical safety, two rulebooks: GAO's 2007 report stacks America's approach against Europe's tough new law. The comparison shows where U.S. rules lagged on guarding against toxic risks. The findings landed as Congress weighed whether to toughen the home team's chemical game.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-925: Asian American and Pacific Islander students were hitting hidden walls in 2007 — GAO's report says colleges could crack them by sharing notes. The findings argue the ‘model minority' myth masked real struggles. The report's fix is humble: talk to each other, and the patterns emerge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-125: The Government Accountability Office dug into telecommunications: FCC Has Made Some Progress in the Management of Its Enforcement Program but Faces Limitations, and Additional Actions Are Needed in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-25: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report finding that trends in energy derivatives markets were raising questions about the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's oversight. New trading venues and products were growing faster than the regulator's grasp. GAO's analysis landed as energy prices surged — and as lawmakers began asking whether speculation, not supply, was driving what Americans paid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-325: The Government Accountability Office dug into military Transformation: DOD Needs to Strengthen Implementation of Its Global Strike Concept and Provide a Comprehensive Investment Approach for Acquiring Neede in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-525: The Government Accountability Office dug into information Security: Federal Agency Efforts to Encrypt Sensitive Information Are Under Way, but Work Remains in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-825: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on critical Infrastructure Protection: DHS Needs to Fully Address Lessons Learned from Its First Cyber Storm Exercise. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-925: GAO published its findings on information Technology: Agencies Need to Establish Comprehensive Policies to Address Changes to Projects' Cost, Schedule, and Performance Goals in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
ginza-rba-lidzbarski-1925:
The Ginza Rba, the Great Treasure, is the holy book of the Mandaeans, a small faith that survives in Iraq and Iran. Mark Lidzbarski's German rendering of 1925 is the standard scholarly version. The Mandaeans prize John the Baptist and hold light and life as twin first powers.

The book holds their tale of creation, hymns, prayers, and the soul's road through the worlds of dark and light. It tells how the soul must pass guards and rivers to reach its home on high. Lidzbarski spent a life on the Mandaean tongue to make this version. His work opened a whole scripture to the learned world.
gitlow-v-new-york-1925: Gitlow v. New York (1925) let free speech bind the states via the Fourteenth Amendment. Gitlow's manifesto lost, but liberty won. The Tower library holds the full opinion. It nationalized the First Amendment. Speech spread. States bound. Freedom grew. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
glasgow-barren-ground-1925:
Ellen Glasgow considered Barren Ground, published in 1925, her best novel. Glasgow wrote it after years of success with Richmond society stories. This time she set her story on worn-out Virginia farmland and made a working woman its hero.

Dorinda Oakley is betrayed in love as a young woman and flees to New York. She returns home determined to restore her family's ruined farm by science and sheer will. Across thirty years she drains, plants, and prospers, while love offers her a second, harder choice. Glasgow reverses the usual plot: the land, not a husband, is the prize worth winning. Barren Ground is a landmark of American regional fiction.
hemingway-in-our-time-1925:
Ernest Hemingway published In Our Time in New York in 1925, his first book with a major American publisher. Hemingway had built the collection from stories written in Paris, where he worked among the modernist writers of the Left Bank. The book made his reputation.

Nick Adams grows up across the stories: fishing in Michigan, wounded in the war, drifting through Europe after it. Between the tales, short brutal vignettes show bullfighters, soldiers, and refugees. Hemingway's style, short sentences and telling omissions, changed American prose at a stroke. Stories like Big Two-Hearted River and The Doctor and the Doctor's Wife remain classics. In Our Time is the founding book of his career.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol7-1925:
The seventh volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law appeared in 1925. Holdsworth's project, pursued at Oxford over decades, aimed to record the whole growth of English law. By the seventh volume the story had passed the age of revolution and entered calmer waters.

Volume 7 covers the eighteenth century, the age of Mansfield in the courts and Blackstone in the study. Holdsworth describes a law polished into system: commercial law modernized for a trading nation, and the great commentaries giving the whole a shape students could learn. It was the law's Augustan age, elegant and confident. Holdsworth treats it with the respect of a man who loved the tradition he chronicled. The volume remains a standard guide to the century that made the common law a world system.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol8-1925:
Holdsworth issued the eighth volume of his History of English Law in 1925. The history had grown from medieval beginnings through revolution and Augustan polish. Its author, by now the dean of English legal historians, turned to the century of reform.

Volume 8 covers the first half of the nineteenth century. Bentham's fierce attack on the old law opens the story, and the great reforms follow. Courts were rebuilt, procedures simplified, and whole fields of law cleaned of archaic clutter. Holdsworth tells of the law's modernization with the zeal of a historian who had lived to see its results. The old order is swept away in these pages, reform's triumph recorded act by act. The volume is essential reading on how Victorian England remade its law.
homer-odyssey-pope-1725:
Homer's Odyssey came to Augustan England in Alexander Pope's version of 1725 to 1726. Pope's Odyssey was the companion piece to his Iliad of the decade before in couplets. He shared the work with two helpers, Fenton and Broome, though his name crowned the title.

Odysseus sails through monsters and tempests toward Penelope and his rocky isle of Ithaca. Pope's couplets give the sea tale a smooth, bright, and courtly English polish and grace. The suitors' slaughter and the test of the great bow close the homecoming plot in Ithaca. Notes by Broome filled out the learning that Pope's verse wore so lightly for readers. Together the Pope Homers fixed Augustan taste for classical epic in English verse.
james-warning-to-the-curious-1925:
Late ghost tales by M. R. James fill A Warning to the Curious, his set from 1925. The lead tale warns a man who digs for a lost crown on the coast. Old lore guards the crown. Theft wakes a thin, grim shade that will not rest.

Each tale is lean, clear, and full of dread. James wastes no word. A small wrong step leads to a vast price. Fans treat the set as his ripe best work. It is the yardstick for the short ghost tale. The coast tales use flat sands, grey seas, and lone paths to fine effect. Place does half the work of fear in James's late craft.
jaufre-occitan-breuer-1925:
Jaufre is the great Arthurian romance of the troubadour lands, written in Occitan, the old tongue of the south of France. Hermann Breuer's 1925 critical edition prints the full poem, 10,955 verses in all. Its hero is a young knight who comes to Arthur's court seeking deeds.

Jaufre rides out to face giants, enchantments, and a proud foe who shames the court. The tale mixes high adventure with the wit and grace of the southern courts. No other Occitan romance of Arthur survives at this scale. Breuer's edition is the scholar's door into that lost shelf of song.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-25:
Death comes for Jogues in Volume 25, published by Thwaites in 1898. The book covers the years 1644 and 1645 across Iroquois and French lands. Mohawk men kill the peacemaker who had come to save them.

Fellow priests tell of his death with heartbreaking, plain simplicity. They count him a saint even as they write the sad news. Grief runs through the reports, yet the mission work goes on. Baptisms, burials, and brave journeys fill the months that follow. His blood, in their eyes, seals the mission he loved and served so well. Sorrow and pride fill the closing reports of this book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-arib-10225:
Ma'arib, the Jewish evening prayer, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The name comes from the prayer's first benediction. In Talmudic language it is called Tefillat Arbit. It stands as one of the three daily prayers, linked to David and Daniel in Scripture. Tradition credits the patriarch Jacob with founding it.

The article explores a puzzle about the prayer's status. Morning and afternoon prayers replaced daily sacrifices, so they became duties. Evening prayer began as voluntary, and its standing prayer was long omitted. Babylonian rabbis filled the gap with eighteen Bible verses naming God. Maimonides held that universal custom had made the prayer a duty in practice. The entry then gives the order of the service, from its opening verses to the Shema. It is a compact guide to how one daily service took its shape.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malbim-meir-lob:
Meir Lob Malbim, a Russian rabbi and Bible commentator, is profiled at length in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Volochisk, Volhynia, in 1809, he took his famous name from his initials. He served as rabbi at Wreschen and then at Kempen, where he stayed until 1860. He died at Kiev on September 18, 1879.

The article reads as a record of clashes with reforming congregations. As chief rabbi of Bucharest he fought the rich German Jews who wanted a reformed rite. Intrigues landed him in prison, and Montefiore's help freed him only on condition he leave Rumania. At Moghilef, richer Jews denounced him as a political criminal and had him expelled. Wilna's governor later blocked his election there for the same reason. Through it all Malbim wrote his commentaries on the code, the Pentateuch, and the Prophets. The entry honors a traditionalist whose learning never bought him peace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-henry-han:
Henry Hananel Marks, an English journalist and politician, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London on April 5, 1855, he was a son of Professor D. W. Marks. He studied at University College, London, and at Brussels. At sixteen he went to the United States to try journalism.

The article follows his return and his newspaper's rise. When his resources hit their lowest point, he came home in 1883. Soon after he founded the Financial News, starting in a very small way. He made the paper a power in the financial world. Politics followed the press success. Londoners elected him to the County Council for Marylebone in 1889. In 1895 he entered Parliament for St. George's, Tower Hamlets. He held the seat until 1900. The entry preserves a journalist who turned a struggling sheet into a seat in Parliament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-the-ess:
Menahem the Essene, a teacher of Herod's time renowned for prophecy, is profiled by Kaufmann Kohler in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Josephus tells the famous story: Menahem saw the schoolboy Herod and clapped him on the back. He hailed him as a future king. He would reign successfully, but without justice toward men or piety toward God. He would end as his crimes deserved. Years later Herod, at his zenith, sent for him and pressed him on the reign's length. "Yes, twenty; nay, thirty years," came the answer. Pleased, the king henceforth honored the Essenes.

The article identifies him with the Mishnah's Menahem, colleague of Hillel and predecessor of Shammai. Then it sifts the darker traditions. One says he "went out" to serve the king with eighty pairs of silk-robed disciples. Another says he apostatized altogether. Kohler lets the conflicting memories stand side by side.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mesquita-10725:
Mesquita was a Castilian Jewish family that scattered during the Inquisition to Holland, England, and America, traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906 by Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner. The article follows the name across three continents, from wealthy Amsterdam merchants to early settlers in Mexico, Jamaica, and New York.

Among its figures are David Bueno de Mesquita, a rich Amsterdam merchant of the mid-seventeenth century, and Luis de Mesquita of Segovia, tried in the Mexican Inquisition case of Gabriel of Granada. Benjamin Bueno de Mesquita reached New York by way of Jamaica, and his 1683 tombstone is called the oldest Jewish tombstone in that city. Later members appear in Jamaica and Nevis records into the seventeen hundreds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morse-godfrey-1:
Godfrey Morse was an American lawyer in Boston, and the brother of Leopold Morse. Cyrus Adler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wachenheim in Rhenish Bavaria on May 19, 1846, he came to Boston as a boy in 1854. He graduated from Harvard College in 1870 and from its law school two years later.

The entry lists the bars that admitted him, ending with the Supreme Court of the United States in 1879. In Boston he served on the school committee and presided over the common council in 1883. He later chaired the Massachusetts Gold Democrats and led charities, including the Leopold Morse Home for Infirm Hebrews and Orphanage. Such entries preserve the civic record of Jewish public men of the era.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-meir-of:
Moses ben Meir of Ferrara was an Italian tosafist of the thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry. The tosafists wrote glosses on the Talmud, and Moses worked in that tradition in Italy.

His own tosafot were used by the compiler of the Haggahot Maimuniyyot, a well-known gloss on Maimonides. In turn, Moses drew on the tosafot of Judah Sir Leon of Paris. Whether he was actually Judah's pupil, the entry says, is doubtful. The notice shows the web of teachers and texts that linked Italian and French Talmud study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munz-bernhard-1:
Bernhard Münz was an Austrian writer born at Leipnik in Moravia on February 1, 1856. Isidore Singer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He took his doctorate at Vienna in 1877 and studied philosophy further at Munich. From 1889 he worked in the library of Vienna's Jewish community, becoming its director in 1900.

His early books treat Greek thought: the seeds of the theory of knowledge before Socrates, and the ethics of the early thinkers. Later he wrote lives and studies of modern figures, from the philosopher Frohschammer to Moriz Lazarus. A book on Goethe as educator appeared in 1904. The entry shows a librarian who was also a steady philosophical author.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naresh-11325: Naresh was a Babylonian city near Sura, standing on a canal. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give it a short Jewish Encyclopedia notice. It may be the Nahar Sar of the Tigris. Its people had a name as thieves and rascals in the Talmud. Yet the town also produced teachers, called Narsheans, and a kind of beaver was found nearby.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nicodemus-11525:
Nicodemus was a wealthy member of the Sanhedrin. Schulim Ochser and Kaufmann Kohler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Jerusalem in the first century C.E. John's Gospel names him in three passages. He is there called a ruler of the Jews.

Nicodemus came to Jesus by night for teaching. He asked what rebirth could possibly mean. He feared being known as one of Jesus' disciples. Later he helped Joseph of Arimathaea bury Jesus' body. The entry links him to Nicodemus ben Gorion. That Talmudic figure was a popular saint of miracles. An apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus arose in the third century. It tells of Jesus before Pilate and the Sanhedrin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunes-da-almeyd: Manuela Nunes da Almeyda was a Spanish poetess. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote her brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in London, the record says. Her son was Mordecai Nunes Almeyda. He patronized the Spanish poet Daniel Lopez Laguna. Manuela wrote Spanish verses in praise of Laguna's work. Two gifted daughters shared that labor with her. They were Benvenida Cohen Belmonte and Sara de Fonseca. Sara had married Manuel Fonseca Pina by then. Their poems together form her small surviving fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-abrah:
Abraham Oppenheim was a German rabbi born at Mannheim. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Löb Oppenheim of that town. He died at Hanover on November 2, 1786. He had lived to a great age by then.

For many years Abraham held a paid post at Mannheim. That post was in the Klaus, a house of study there. He was called in the same role to Amsterdam. Later he was called on to Hanover in that role. He wrote notes on the Orah Hayyim, a code of law. One work treats the rules for the shofar horn. One gathers notes on Orah Hayyim and Yoreh De'ah. The second code treats food, mourning, and kindred rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pereyra-abraham:
Abraham Israel Pereyra was a Spanish writer and patron in Amsterdam. He was born at Madrid and died in 1699. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He fled the Inquisition by way of Venice.

Pereyra led the Spanish Portuguese community for several years. He gave a fortune to its Talmud Torah school. He also founded a Talmudic seminary at Hebron. Like many then, he believed in Shabbethai Zevi. He crossed Italy hoping to reach the false messiah. His books preach trust in God and scorn for worldly show.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phylacteries-te:
Phylacteries, or tefillin, are small leather boxes worn in prayer. Five scholars shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They were the Executive Committee, Julius H. Greenstone, and Joseph Jacobs. Ludwig Blau and Emil G. Hirsch also took part.

Four Bible verses ground the whole practice. The details, though, come from tradition and inference. No Jewish rite carries more clustered laws than tefillin. The boxes must be square and made of clean skins. One box binds on the arm, one on the head. Black straps fasten both boxes in place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pogorelsky-mess:
Messola Pogorelsky was a Russian doctor and writer born at Bobruisk on March 7, 1862. Herman Rosenthal and J. L. Lait wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at the University of St. Vladimir in Kiev. He finished his studies there in 1890.

That same year Pogorelsky became government rabbi at Kherson. He held the post until 1893. He wrote much on medicine and on Jewish themes. His works treat ritual circumcision and Jewish names in Bible and Talmud. One late work deals with syphilis as the Bible presents it. Another deals with occult science in Bible and Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popes-the-1125:
How the popes dealt with the Jews is the subject of an article by Gotthard Deutsch and Joseph Jacobs. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Church claimed no rule over people who were not baptized. So papal rules set the terms for Jewish life in Christian states. As rulers of the Papal States, popes also made laws for their own Jews.

At times Jews in danger asked the popes for help. Popes then spoke out as the highest heads of the Church. The article sets out the rules that guided this treatment. Jews were to be kept apart from Christians in daily life. No Jew was to hold power over Christians. Jewish worship was not to take a public form. These rules came down from the code of Justinian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-vii-sur:
Ptolemy Philometor was king of Egypt from 182 to 146 B.C. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the eldest son of Ptolemy the Fifth. With him, the writers say, power passed to poor hands. He was still a child when he took the throne.

A Jewish thinker taught the boy king, it is said. He was Aristobulus of Paneas, a man of note. News of the king's sole rule roused Antiochus the Fourth. That king was the great foe of the Jews. He took the news as a call to watch his own safety. The entry follows a reign of wars and weak rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-radner-david-12: David Radner was a Hebrew writer born at Wilna in 1848. Joseph Jacobs and Isidor Warsaw wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Wilna in 1901. He turned famed German works into Hebrew for his readers. He rendered Schiller's William Tell in 1878. He rendered Schiller's Don Carlos a year later. He turned a play of Mosenthal into Hebrew in 1880. He also turned a history of the Jews by Cassel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-redlich-henry-1:
Henry Redlich was a Polish copper engraver born at Lask in 1840. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Berlin on November 7, 1884. He studied first at Breslau, then at Warsaw.

The article follows his training in Munich and Dresden after a prize. He lived at Vienna from 1866 to 1873. In 1876 he joined the St. Petersburg Academy of Fine Arts. Denied a professorship because of his religion, he left for Paris. His engravings won a gold medal there. His best works copy Raphael, Brandt, Matejko, and Gerson. Illness took him to Berlin, where he died. The entry shows talent blocked by bias.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosales-jacob-h:
Jacob Hebræus Rosales, born Immanuel Bocarro Frances y Rosales, was a Portuguese physician, mathematician, astrologer, and poet. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born in Lisbon in 1588 or 1593 and died in Italy in 1662 or 1668.

Rosales studied medicine and mathematics at Montpellier, then won fame as a doctor in Portugal. In Rome he turned to astrology, and Galileo urged him to write on the subject. Living later in Amsterdam, he openly embraced Judaism and took the name Jacob. His books cover comets, astrology, and astronomy, and include long poems in Portuguese and Latin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubinstein-susa:
Susanna Rubinstein was an Austrian psychologist born at Czernowitz, Bukowina, on September 20, 1847. Isidore Singer and Regina Neisser wrote her entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. She was the daughter of an Austrian deputy of that city.

Rubinstein entered the University of Prague in 1870, a bold step for a woman then. She studied further at Leipsic, Vienna, and Bern, taking her doctorate in 1874. Her essays join psychology with aesthetics, the study of beauty and taste. Later books treat the inner world, the nature of movement, and pessimism. One volume profiles three thinkers of the will in metaphysics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salfeld-siegmun:
Siegmund Salfeld was a German rabbi born at Stadthagen on March 24, 1843. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1870 and became rabbi of Dessau.

In 1880 Salfeld was chosen rabbi of Mayence, where he still served in 1905. His studies include the Song of Songs among medieval Jewish interpreters. He wrote the history of the old Jewish cemetery at Mainz, in 1898. He also edited the martyrology of the Nuremberg Memorbuch that year. From 1902 he collaborated on The Jewish Encyclopedia itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-yarhina-:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel Yarḥina'ah. He is generally known as Mar Samuel. He was a Babylonian amora of the first generation. Born about 165 at Nehardea, he died there about 257. He was a teacher of the Law, a judge, a physician, and an astronomer.

Samuel's father was a silk merchant named Abba. A legend ties the boy's name to his father's respect for a spoken word. Samuel studied at Nisibis and then under Levi ben Sisi. He rose fast and soon dealt with his teacher as an equal. Beyond Bible and Law, he learned the sciences of his day. That breadth made him a leading voice of Babylonian Jewry. His rulings shaped the Talmud for later ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-13225:
Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on a later Saul. He was a Karaite leader, the son and successor of Anan ben David. Anan founded the Karaite movement within Judaism. Saul died about 780. Later Karaites styled him nasi, or prince. They also called him rosh hagolah, head of the exile.

Saul's own activity left a modest mark. Solomon ben Jeroham says he also commented on the Ten Commandments. He is quoted for a strict view of the sixth commandment. For Saul, adultery meant union with any woman not one's wife or concubine. Rabbinic law limited it to another man's wife. Saul also followed Gnai Baruch on when the yearly reading of the Law begins. The entry draws on Fürst's history of the Karaites and on Pinsker.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulhoff-juliu:
Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Julius Schulhoff. He was an Austrian pianist and composer. Schulhoff was born at Prague on August 2, 1825. He died at Berlin on March 15, 1898. Kisch and Tedesco taught him piano. Tomaschek taught him theory. He made his debut at Dresden in 1842.

Schulhoff then played at the Leipsic Gewandhaus. In Paris, Chopin urged him to turn professional. Concerts at Chopin's suggestion succeeded so well that he toured widely. He played across France and in London. He toured Spain in 1851 and Russia in 1853. Then he returned to Paris for composing and teaching. In 1870 he settled at Dresden, and later at Berlin. His works include a grand sonata in F minor. He also wrote twelve études and many smaller pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-senlis-hebrew-l:
Senlis, a town in France's Oise department, had Jewish residents by the twelfth century. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the town. A bishop passing through in 1106 debated religion there with a Jew named Leon. That story, true or not, points to an early community.

Tax records from 1202 and around 1300 show Senlis Jews paying large sums. They must have been many, rich, or both. The entry follows their place in a town known as a health resort. Readers get a small window on Jewish life in medieval France, built from taxes, travel tales, and church records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-si-a-leon-judah:
Leon Judah Aryeh Si'a, called Nasr al Din, was a physician at Constantinople before 1633. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He befriended Jewish learning and its scholars there. He rendered two classic Arabic works into Latin.

Those works were Judah ha-Levi's Cuzari and Bahya's Duties of the Heart. His friend Jacob Roman hoped to print them with Hebrew and Arabic. Si'a also knew Anton Leger, the Dutch embassy's chaplain. Through Leger he commended Roman to Buxtorf at Basel in 1633. In 1639 Prince Rakoczy made Si'a his court physician in Transylvania. Leaving Constantinople, he also left Judaism behind, Buxtorf reported. The entry traces a scholar between faiths, courts, and languages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-society-of-amer:
The Society of American Cantors was founded in Baltimore on May 14, 1895. Cyrus Adler and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Alois Kaiser himself founded the society that year. Its aim was to raise the cantor's profession in standing. It also sought cohesion among members and better synagogue music.

The society chose and arranged music for the Union Hymnal. That hymnal appeared in 1897 from the Central Conference. In 1904 it marked the hundredth birthday of Solomon Sulzer. It published a Friday evening service from his Shir Ziyyon. It also held a memorial service in New York city. Addresses were given there in Sulzer's honor that March.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sorani-ugo-1392:
Ugo Sorani was an Italian jurist and deputy born at Pitigliano in 1850. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on May 4 of that year. He studied law at Pisa, graduating in 1872. He then practiced law at Florence for many years.

He also served as secretary of the Jewish community of Florence. In 1900 voters sent him to the Chamber of Deputies. He represented Scansano, in the district of Grosseto there. He was reelected to that seat in 1904. His books dealt with political parties and the Bank of Italy. He also wrote on bills of exchange, bankruptcy, and women in law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-szterenyi:
Albert Stern was a Hungarian rabbi born at Nagy-Kanizsa in 1826. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Presburg and Ofen. He was son-in-law to Rabbi Hirsch Bär Fassel. He died in an asylum at Ofen on June 16, 1888.

Stern served as rabbi at Lengyeltoti from 1851 to 1867. He then moved to the rabbinate of Uj-Pest. His strong demands for Reform forced his resignation in 1884. He founded a German periodical that ran three volumes. In it he studied laws on proselytes and rabbinical seminaries. He also wrote on Jewish names and burial law. Seeking full assimilation, he changed his name to Szterényi. The entry tells a reformer's rise and fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stone-and-stone:
Sacred stones appear often across the Old Testament as markers of worship. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Jacob set up such a stone at Beth-el. Samuel raised the stone of help called Eben-ezer. Moses placed twelve stones near his altar at Sinai.

These standing stones were called maẓẓebot in Hebrew. The twin Temple columns Jachin and Boaz counted among them. Phoenician temples held similar columns as holy symbols. For a time they served as lawful signs of God. The Deuteronomic code later rejected them as foreign to true worship. Hosea and Isaiah still mention them in prophecy. The entry traces how one object moved from shrine to ban.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tammuz-assyrian:
Tammuz was a Babylonian god, called Dumuzi in Assyrian. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Ezekiel seems to name him in a vision of Jerusalem. Women there weep for Tammuz at the Temple gate. He was husband, or sometimes son, of Ishtar.

Each year Ishtar descended to the underworld for him. She stayed there from his month until spring. Tammuz thus embodied the spirit of spring growth. Babylonia mourned when growth stopped for the year. Some link the Jewish fast of the seventeenth to that mourning. The Greek Adonis myth may share the same root. Robertson Smith tied the cult to king-of-the-woods rites. The entry traces a foreign god's shadow inside Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-joshua-: Joshua Feiwel Te'omim was rabbi at Przemysl in Poland. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. His one known work is Panim Masbirot. It argues against Meïr ben Isaac Eisenstadt. The polemic appeared in 1715. Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue records the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todros-of-beauc:
Two men named Todros of Beaucaire share this entry from Montpellier. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. The first was a leading poet of the late thirteenth century. In 1277 he represented his community before James II of Aragon. The king granted its Jews a synagogue for a small yearly payment.

Abraham Bedersi ranked Todros among the great men of the age. They exchanged poems in verse letters. One poem read backward gives a wholly different sense. The second Todros was a rabbinical scholar around 1300. He backed Abba Mari against students of philosophy. He read out a ban on such study in synagogue. Scholars think the two men may be one person.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-troki-14525:
Troki was a Karaite family named for the city of Troki in Russia. Isidore Singer, Isaac Broydé, and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Abraham ben Aaron was a liturgical poet there in the 1500s. His poem for the Beshalah section entered the Karaite prayer-book.

Abraham ben Josiah served as physician to King John III Sobieski. He wrote medical works in Hebrew and in Latin. One Hebrew work, Ozar ha-Am, is named in the entry. Isaac ben Abraham Troki was the family's famed polemicist. Born in 1533, he learned Bible from Karaite teachers. Christian teachers gave him Latin and Polish letters. Debates with Christians pushed him toward religious philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unicorn-12725:
The unicorn of the English Bible renders the Hebrew word re'em, this article argues. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Aquila and Saadia read the word as rhinoceros. Bochart and others chose the oryx, or white antelope. The Revised Version prints wild ox instead.

Scripture calls the re'em wild, untamable, and mighty-horned. Job asks whether it will serve or plow. Those traits best fit the aurochs, the article holds. Assyrian rimu names the same great wild bull. The Talmud imagines a re'em too big for Noah's ark. It had to be tied outside by its horn. A one-horned beast in Hullin is allowed as food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valabregue-albi:
Albin Valabrègue was among the most prolific French dramatists of his day. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Carpentras in 1853, he wrote about two plays yearly. He also served as dramatic critic for L'Illustration in Paris. His first listed play, La Veuve Chapuzot, dates to 1879.

Most of his plays were written with collaborators. Paul Ferrier, Hennequin, and Ordonneau each partnered him often. Durand et Durand appeared with Ordonneau in 1887. Les Saturnales was an operetta with music by Lacombe. Titles like Le Bonheur Conjugal show his comic vein. Parisian households and marriage fill many plots. By 1893 his catalog already passed twenty-five plays. Few French stages lacked a Valabrègue piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-jacob-1482:
Jacob Weil was a German rabbi and Talmudist. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the first half of the fourteen hundreds. Little is known of his life story. He was a leading pupil of Jacob Mölln, the Maharil.

His teacher ordained him and cleared him for Nuremberg. Weil declined, to avoid offending an older rabbi there. He later served as rabbi of Erfurt. Communities near and far sent him their questions. His one surviving book collects his legal answers. Its appendix gives rules for slaughtering cattle. Those rules ran through seventy one editions. Later rabbis treated them as binding.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-victor-15:
Victor Worms (born 1853) was a French judge, the younger brother of Emile Worms. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Luxembourg, he took a law degree in 1878. He read law at both Paris and at Rennes.

In 1880 he won a post on a district board. At Rennes he met the statesman Waldeck-Rousseau there. When that chief joined the cabinet, Worms went as his aide. He served two terms in that close role. He then left board work for the bench in full. In 1886 he became a judge at Reims. Three years later he moved to Versailles in the same role. In 1904 he rose to vice chief of that court.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yozerot-15125:
Yozerot is the name for hymns set in the dawn rite on feasts. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. North rite Jews use them on feasts and choice Sabbaths. Each hymn takes its name from the prayer word near it.

One is called Yozer, one Ofan, and one Meorah in turn. More are called Ahabah, Zulat, and Geullah in the set. The first name, Yozer, came to name the whole class. It came to name that part of the rite as well. New use tends to drop the hymns from the rite. Their use makes the rite run too long, men say. Their tunes lack the fixed form of the older rite parts. That lack comes from their late start in the rite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeitlin-joshua-:
Joshua ben Aaron Zeitlin (1823-1888) was a Russian scholar and giver. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Kiev, he died at Dresden in the German lands. As a boy he moved with his kin to Chernobyl town.

There he kept close to the Hasidim in his youth. In time he turned to world books and Hebrew lore. He wed at Slutsk and read with a sage in that town. He then lived at Saint Petersburg and at Moscow in turn. In Moscow he won note as a friend to poor sages. In the Turk war he fed the Russian host with goods. The czar gave him a medal for that work in 1879. In 1883 he left Russia to live at Dresden in peace.
journal-of-discourses-vol-25:
Volume Twenty-Five, from 1886, stands near the great turning point. The discourses breathe strain as the Saints await a change they cannot see. Within a few years, plural marriage will end by church decree.

Nothing here names that surrender, yet tension fills every long sermon. Leaders preach obedience while the law closes each road around them. A people waits for deliverance with no clear sign of its form. Readers who know 1890's Manifesto feel the ground shifting below. The hardest choice in Mormon history gathers force in these tense pages. When the change came, this volume helped readers grasp its cost.
kafka-der-prozess-1925:
Der Prozess, The Trial, appeared in 1925, a year after Kafka's death, published by the Verlag Die Schmiede against his instruction to burn his papers. Josef K., a bank official, is arrested one morning for a crime that is never named.

K. fights through a court that sits in attics, works by rumor, and never states its charge. Lawyers, painters, and priests offer help that helps nothing. The novel ends with an execution 'like a dog'. In the original German, its bureaucratic nightmare reads at full chill. It is the defining novel of guilt without cause.
keith-antiquity-of-man-1925:
Arthur Keith, Britain's best-known anatomist of his day, published The Antiquity of Man in 1925. He surveyed every major fossil human find then known. His aim was to fix how long people had lived on earth.

Keith accepted the Piltdown skull as genuine and pushed Neanderthals to a side branch. Piltdown was later exposed as a forgery, which dates his conclusions sharply. Even so, his anatomical descriptions remain detailed and readable. The book preserves a field at its most confident, just before it was proved wrong. Keith wrote with the authority of a man who had handled many original fossils himself.
kroeber-handbook-indians-california-1925:
Alfred Louis Kroeber, a student of Boas, spent years recording the Native peoples of California for the Bureau of American Ethnology. His handbook, published in 1925, is a huge survey of those peoples. The work grew from more than two decades of travel, interviews, and museum study. It covers the tribes of the whole state, group by group.

Kroeber describes languages, homes, food, tools, dances, myths, and laws, with maps and drawings throughout. Much of what he wrote down came from elders whose worlds were fast disappearing. Scholars still treat the handbook as the basic reference on California's first peoples. Few single books hold so much firsthand record of a whole region.
laski-grammar-politics-1925:
A Grammar of Politics, published in 1925, is Laski's systematic political theory. It is the fullest statement of his pluralist thought and his democratic socialism. The state, liberty, equality, rights, and property are treated in turn, in the manner of a grammar: the elements and rules of the subject.

Laski argues that rights are conditions of social welfare. Liberty, he says, needs economic equality to be real, and government must be judged by the lives it makes possible. The book is dense with learning and warm with reforming purpose. It became the standard text of the British left between the wars.
lawrence-st-mawr-1925:
St. Mawr, published in 1925, is a novella of Lou Witt, a rich American woman in England. Her husband seems hollow to her, and her social world seems dead. At a country sale she buys St. Mawr, a magnificent stallion, and the horse changes everything.

The stallion stands for a wild, male vitality that modern England has lost, and Lou follows that force rather than the men around her. She ends at a ranch in New Mexico, choosing the desert and the horse's world over marriage. The tale is Lawrence's flight motif at its purest, and many call it his finest novella.
leadbeater-masters-and-the-path-1925:
Charles Leadbeater described the hidden guides of mankind in The Masters and the Path, printed in 1925. The book sets out the Theosophical Masters and the ranks of the occult order above men. Leadbeater was the most famed seer of the Theosophical Society.

He tells where the Masters dwell, how their pupils are trained, and what the path of initiation asks. Grades, robes, and festivals of the inner government are laid out in calm detail. For Theosophists of the 1920s, this was the standard map of the unseen rule of the world. The book states that age's esotericism at its fullest.
lewis-arrowsmith-1925:
Sinclair Lewis published Arrowsmith in 1925, turning from small-town business to American science. He researched the novel with a young bacteriologist, Paul de Kruif, who supplied the laboratory life. The book was awarded the Pulitzer Prize, which Lewis famously refused.

Martin Arrowsmith fights his way from a prairie town to medical school, country practice, and a great research institute. Everywhere, commerce, publicity, and careerism press him to sell his science short. A plague outbreak in the Caribbean tests his principles at the highest cost. Lewis makes the researcher's purity both heroic and impossible to keep clean. Arrowsmith made the scientist a tragic American hero and remains the classic novel of the profession.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-1-1925:
Frantisek Lexa published the first volume of his great French study of Egyptian magic in 1925. The work traces magic in Egypt from the Old Kingdom to the Coptic period. Volume one lays out the whole system in an extended survey.

Lexa asks who practiced magic, how rites worked, and what words could do. Priests, private magicians, and the gods themselves all have roles here. He treats magic as a serious Egyptian science rather than mere superstition. The survey was the fullest of its time on the subject. Egyptologists still respect its learning and scope. Volume two supplies the translated texts behind the survey.
lexa-magie-egypte-antique-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Frantisek Lexa's study of ancient Egyptian magic appeared in 1925, in French. The first volume explained the system; this companion gathers the actual texts. Magical writings from across three thousand years stand side by side here.

Pyramid spells, coffin texts, and everyday charms appear in French translation. Readers move from theory to raw material in the magicians' own words. Lexa selects texts that show magic at work in temple, tomb, and home. The sourcebook remains unmatched for following his survey volume. Students of ancient spells can test every claim in volume one here. Together the pair forms a landmark of Egyptology.
locarno-pact-1925:
Germany, France, Belgium, Britain, and Italy signed these treaties in 1925. Their rulers acted through named envoys with full powers. The preamble recalls the scourge of the war of 1914 to 1918. Peoples who suffered it desired security and protection afterward.

Belgium's old neutral status had been ended before this pact. Europe's frequent conflict area needed fresh guarantees of peace. Article One guarantees the land status quo together and separately. Germany's frontiers with Belgium and France stand declared inviolable. The League of Nations framework bounds the supplementary guarantees. Frontiers fixed by existing treaties remain untouched by Article One. Each side signed in the names of its king or its republic.
locke-new-negro-1925:
The New Negro, published in 1925 and edited by Alain Locke, is the landmark anthology of the Harlem Renaissance. Locke, a Howard philosopher, gathered the movement's fiction, poetry, essays, and art. His aim was to present a people remade in its own image.

His title essay declares that the Negro is no longer an object of history but a maker of it. The people, he argues, are moving from the rural South to the modern city. Work from the era's rising writers and artists fills the volume with argument and display. The book served as the movement's manifesto and showcase in one. Its influence on American culture is still unfolding.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-1-1925:
R. A. Nicholson was the great English sage of Persian verse. His Mathnawi of Jalaluddin Rumi, Book One, came out in 1925. The book gives Books One and Two of the Mathnawi with the Persian text at hand. Rumi was a Sufi sage of the 1200s in Turkey.

The Mathnawi is a vast poem of tales, told to bare the soul's path to God. A reed's wail for its lost home opens the whole grand work. Kings, fools, and saints crowd its tales of love and loss. Nicholson's set is the stock full dress of the poem in English.
mellon-ms-28-alchemical-miscellany-1525:
Mellon MS 28 is a small paper manuscript from north Italy. The copy is dated about 1525, and may come from Bologna. White leather, stamped in blind tooling, covers its paste boards.

John Dastin's Rosarius of the philosophers leads the texts inside. A short piece on the four elements adds a chart for mixing colors. A work ascribed to Hermes, Merlin, or Rasis closes the set. One scribe wrote the main texts in a small, neat humanistic hand. Pale red marks set off heads, tables, and some verse. Linen ties once held the small book shut on all sides.
mellon-ms-29-lumen-luminum-etc-1525:
Mellon MS 29 holds the Lumen Luminum, or Light of Lights. Elias of Cortona, a Franciscan friar, is named as its author. This north Italian paper copy is dated about 1525.

The record says the work was said to be made in 1315. That date, the record warns, is wrong for the piece. Its matter came from Saracen and Hebrew sources, turned into Latin. A text in cipher and some recipes in Italian stand with it. Gilt edges with a knot work stamp mark this copy's care. Part of the text hides its sense in a cipher code.
mendel-experiments-plant-hybridisation-b:
Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk who crossed pea plants and counted how their traits passed to the next crop. He read his results to a local science society in 1865, but few people noticed them at the time. William Bateson later translated the paper into English, and this edition came out in 1925.

Mendel found that traits such as tall or short stems appear in clear ratios, not blended halfway. He argued that hidden factors, now called genes, carry each trait from parent to child. The paper was ignored for decades, then rediscovered around 1900. It is now read as the founding work of genetics, the science of heredity.
moore-defence-of-common-sense-1925:
George Edward Moore published A Defence of Common Sense in 1925, and it became his most famous short work. Moore, a Cambridge philosopher, wrote against skeptics who doubted the plain truths of everyday life. His method was disarmingly direct: state what we all know, and hold it more firmly than any theory that denies it.

The essay lists truisms Moore claims to know with certainty, such as that the earth existed long before his birth. In its best-known passage, tied to his lectures of the period, he proves an external world by holding up one hand, then another. The plain statement shook philosophy because it refused the skeptic's terms altogether. The piece is often called the shortest revolution in thought ever written, and it still anchors debates about knowledge.
nasa-tm-19710007896-simulated-space-envi:
Engineers at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland ran this test, reported in February 1971. A module of twenty-five cadmium sulfide thin-film solar cells faced a simulated space environment. The run lasted for almost two thousand hours.

The test checked the strength of the module's mechanical and electrical links. It also taught the team how the module behaves as a power source. During the run, the module was loaded as it would be on a spacecraft. No breakdown could be found in the links between cells, the report states. Its power output and current traits were tracked through the test.
openalex-w1966648825:
George Schoneveld, Laura German, and Eric Nutakor studied biofuel farms. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Society in 2011. Africa's biofuel sector grew fast in those years. Plantations promised jobs and rural development to villages. Opinion on the sector was sharply divided, they note.

The team grounded its analysis in local field evidence. It measured real impacts of feedstock plantations in Ghana. Land deals can shift food, work, and forest access. Promises of development must face village reality, they argue. Their findings weigh gains against losses for local people. The study guides fairer land investment policy in Africa.
openalex-w2046416025:

The review explains how antioxidant claims should be tested. Lab tests must come before claims of benefit. The authors survey compounds from traditional remedies. They discuss how these substances may neutralise harmful molecules. They also consider protection of affected tissues. Clear testing standards matter before medical use. The paper maps a research path for natural anti-ulcer agents.

The team used data from forest plots across Amazonia. They compared species' shares of stems and carbon flows. The hyperdominant species handled a large share of carbon uptake. They also held a large share of stored carbon. Rare species contributed little to totals despite their numbers. Protecting common species matters for the carbon balance. Diversity still matters for other forest functions.
openalex-w2286612125:

openalex-w2593913025:

They compare several research models: everyday mindfulness, brief inductions, full programs, and expert meditators. From brain science they discuss how top-down and bottom-up control of emotions interact during practice. Clinicians, they argue, have not clearly separated mindful emotion regulation from other strategies. The authors propose splitting these strategies into top-down and bottom-up kinds. They also offer an embodied framework linking body, brain, and behavior. The review aims to sharpen how mindfulness treatments are understood and tested.
openalex-w2760911225:

Nobody had counted the deforestation mining causes beyond its own fences.

The team found mining significantly increased forest loss up to seventy kilometers beyond lease boundaries. Mining drove over eleven thousand square kilometers of deforestation in the study period. Roads, towns, supply chains, and displaced farming spread the damage outward. Current licensing, though, ignores off-lease and cumulative impacts. The authors argue impact assessments must widen their view dramatically. Otherwise the Amazon keeps paying for minerals with forest that official accounts never record.
openalex-w2794463825:
Richard Patterson, Eoin McNamara, and Marko Tainio lead a team pooling sitting-time research in the European Journal of Epidemiology in 2018. The authors adjusted for physical activity, which often confounds such studies.

They combined thirty-four prospective studies covering over 1.3 million people. For total sitting, the link to early death was non-linear: risk crept up, then rose faster past about eight hours daily. Heart disease mortality followed a similar bend. The message is not simply move more; very long sitting days carry their own penalty.

The team combined microbe, gene activity, and epigenetic analyses to explain the effect. Early exposure left lasting marks on immune genes, reprogramming how they switch on. openalex-w4386522125:
Mariana Leguía, Alejandra Garcia-Glaessner, Breno Muñoz-Saavedra, and colleagues track highly pathogenic bird flu, H5N1, in Peru's wildlife, in Nature Communications in 2023. Some sea lion viruses from southern Peru grouped with Chilean viruses, evidence of spread across the border. Two carried a mutation linked to easier spread among mammals. One sat close on the tree to a virus later found in a person in Chile. Such tracking shows why wildlife die-offs are watched as pandemic early warnings.
openalex-w7204840425: Are we free because we choose, or do we choose because we understand? The count weighs more than outlay and price. A green stamp can lift what a box of eggs earns, but it adds checks and costs of its own. Small farms live or fall on sums like these. openalex-w7213964825:

openalex-w7214234825:

Drug treatment alone, they argue, rarely keeps weight off. openalex-w7214457325:

Their work mixed a literature review with field research among patients at local family health units, including people with diabetic foot problems, and examined the nurse's role in the process.

Most patients used their medication, the team found, but few kept to diet and exercise plans. Forgetting doses and side effects hurt adherence, and many patients also lived with high blood pressure or thyroid problems. Foot self-care was only partly satisfactory. The authors argue nurses matter through health education, a trusting bond with patients, and care fitted to each person, sustained over time rather than given once.

Across the studies they survey, exercise helped control body weight and improved fitness, metabolic health, and quality of life. The authors present exercise as a central strategy, strongest when joined with adequate food and healthy daily habits. Their review gives families and schools a compact case for moving more, earlier.

Five books sort the tales by theme, from lost friends to war and peace. Lions, jackals, and doves act out greed, trust, and quick wit. Short verses state the morals, and tales nest inside tales. Ryder's sprightly prose keeps the humor and bite of the source. Its frame puts statecraft first and mere fun second.
pirenne-medieval-cities-halsey-1925:

Pirenne argues that the Arab conquests closed the Mediterranean and stalled Europe's trade. Cities faded until commerce revived in the 1000s. Merchants then built new towns and won charters of freedom.

This is the Pirenne thesis in its urban form. Burghers, guilds, and communes remade European society from below. The lectures are short, bold, and clearly argued. Later research qualified the thesis, yet its frame still organizes debate. The book is the best short entry into Pirenne's thought. It shows economic history at its most vivid.

Mary Magdalene asks most of the questions in the dialogue. Jesus explains the fall and rise of Pistis Sophia, a spirit who repents. Strange heavens, powers, and passwords fill the teaching. Schmidt's edition gave scholars a firm text to study. The work remains a key, hard source for anyone tracing early Christian mystics and their rivals. Few texts show that world so fully.

plos-pbio-0020225:
Livia de Hoz, Stephen J. Martin, and Richard G. M. Morris explored lost memories in rats for PLOS Biology in 2004. A rat that learns where things are can seem to forget over time. The team asked whether the memory is truly gone or just hard to reach.

A reminder cue brought the lost spatial memory back. That means forgetting was a failure of retrieval, not of storage, at least in this case. The result matters for how memory loss is understood. If traces persist but cannot be reached, then prompts and cues may restore more than expected. The study gives a neat animal model for telling stored memories apart from reachable ones.
plos-pone-0000025:
Bahjat Al-Ani, Peter Hewett, Suborna Ahmed, and co-authors reported in 2006 on a chemical route to growing new blood vessels. Angiogenesis, the sprouting of fresh vessels, is wanted for healing wounds and starved hearts, and unwanted when it feeds tumors. Nitric oxide, a small signaling gas, was already known to be involved.

The team showed that nitric oxide released from compounds called S-nitrosothiols promotes angiogenesis. Pinning the effect to a releasable source matters, because a drug that donates nitric oxide at the right place could coax vessels to grow where they are needed. The finding adds a usable lever to a process medicine has long wanted to control.
plos-pone-0000125:
Neil J. Gemmell and Jon Slate published this short genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It addresses heterozygote advantage, the idea that carrying two different copies of a gene can beat carrying two matching copies. Here the trait under study is fecundity, how many offspring an organism produces.

Heterozygote advantage is one classic way that genetic variety stays in a population instead of being weeded out. The authors weigh the evidence for this effect on reproductive output. The question matters well beyond one species, because it helps explain why populations keep diversity that looks, at first glance, like it should disappear.
plos-pone-0000225:
Annika C. Karlsson, Astrid K. N. Iversen, Joan M. Chapman, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. CTL responses are attacks by killer T cells on virus-infected cells. The authors track how these responses broaden, one target after another, in early HIV-1 infection. They link that broadening to viral escape, mutations that let the virus dodge attack.

Early immune responses shape the whole course of HIV infection. As each new T cell target appears, the virus mutates away from it, in a chase the authors document. Understanding that race informs vaccine design, which aims to aim the immune system at targets the virus cannot easily change.
plos-pone-0000325:
Xiang Jia Min and Donal A. Hickey published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. DNA barcodes are short, standard gene stretches used to identify species. The authors show that barcodes also provide a quick preview of a species' mitochondrial genome composition. One small piece summarizes features of the whole molecule.

A preview from a barcode saves the cost of sequencing whole mitochondrial genomes for every specimen. The authors test how much information the barcode region carries about the rest. The result adds value to the vast barcode libraries being built for species identification.
plos-pone-0000425:
Sol Efroni, Carl F. Schaefer, and Kenneth H. Buetow sorted cancers by the biological pathways active in them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Two tumors can look alike under the microscope yet behave differently. Instead of cataloging single genes, the team analyzed pathway activity to identify the key processes underlying cancer phenotypes, the observable traits of each tumor.

Grouping cancers by the processes they depend on could reveal shared weaknesses that cut across tumor types. A drug aimed at a process, rather than at one gene, might then serve several groups at once. The approach reflects a shift in cancer research from lists of mutations toward maps of how cells are rewired.
plos-pone-0000525:
R. David Hawkins and colleagues profiled gene activity in healing ear tissue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Some animals can regrow inner ear sensory tissue, the hair-cell-bearing epithelia whose loss causes deafness in humans. The team produced large scale gene expression profiles of regenerating inner ear sensory epithelia.

A profile taken during regrowth lists the genes the tissue switches on to rebuild itself. Comparing that list with the mammalian ear, which does not regenerate, highlights what is missing. Deafness research uses such profiles as a parts list for attempts to wake the same program in human ears.
plos-pone-0000625:
Farooq Kiani, Sonja Schwarzl, Stefan Fischer and colleagues built three-dimensional models of a faulty enzyme, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme is G6PD, and losing its function is the most common inborn error of metabolism in the world. The authors cite an estimate of 400 million people affected. In Germany, though, the condition is very rare.

Working from known G6PD crystal structures, the team modeled variants found in people of German ancestry. A 3D model shows how a changed enzyme part might break its working shape. Such models help explain why some variants cause severe disease while others stay mild.
plos-pone-0000725:
Odile Launay, Christine Durier, Corinne Desaint and colleagues compared two routes for delivering an HIV vaccine in the ANRS VAC16 trial. Their 2007 PLOS ONE objective was safety and cellular immune response. Healthy, HIV-uninfected volunteers received a candidate vaccine called LIPO-4, built from HIV lipopeptides. One group got it intradermally, into the skin; the other intramuscularly, into muscle.

The trial was randomized and open-label, run in France at six sites with 24 weeks of follow-up. Intradermal delivery is dose-sparing, stretching limited vaccine further. If skin delivery with less vaccine matches muscle delivery, vaccination campaigns gain reach. Cellular responses, T cell reactions, were the measure that mattered here.
plos-pone-0000825:
Ann-Charlotte Lundstedt, Shane McCarthy, Mattias C.U. Gustafsson and colleagues proposed a genetic reason some people suffer the worst urinary infections. For unknown reasons, urinary tract infections cluster in certain individuals. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper proposes a new, gene-based cause of susceptibility to acute pyelonephritis. That is the most severe form of UTI, the kind that reaches the kidneys. The IL-8 receptor, CXCR1, was identified as a candidate.

A receptor for IL-8 helps summon white blood cells to fight bacteria in the urinary tract. If inherited variants blunt that summons, kidneys may be left undefended. A genetic basis would explain family clustering, and could flag patients who need aggressive prevention.
plos-pone-0000925:
Richard Ortega, Peter Cloetens, Guillaume Deves and colleagues pictured iron stored inside dopamine vesicles at nano scale, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Disturbed metal balance in the brain is suspected in nerve cell death. Until now, no tool could map metals inside neurons finely enough to test that idea.

The team developed a chemical nano-imaging setup for the job. With it, they could see iron held within the tiny vesicles that store dopamine, a key brain signal chemical. A clear picture of where iron sits in healthy cells sets the baseline. Later work can then ask what changes when neurons begin to fail.
plos-pone-0001025:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang offered a safer way to relax small molecules into their bound shapes on a computer, in PLOS ONE in 2007. When a drug molecule settles into a protein pocket, it takes a bound conformation, a specific folded shape. Computer minimization finds such shapes by lowering the molecule's energy.

The catch: a shallow energy dip may not stop the process, and the molecule folds wrongly. Their procedure watches the minimization with normal mode analysis, a check on the molecule's vibration patterns. A monitored stop should give shapes that match how molecules really sit in pockets. Drug modelers need exactly that reliability.
plos-pone-0001125:
Stress during development can leave lasting marks on the brain. Xia Wang, David Green, Stephen Roberts, and co-authors tested one form of stress, heat, in the fruit fly Drosophila, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on the mushroom body, a brain region flies use for smell-based learning.

The study asks whether thermal stress disrupts how the mushroom body develops and how well adult flies learn odors. Earlier work had shown that many kinds of stress disturb brain development in every model system tried. This paper ties a specific stress to a specific brain structure and a measurable behavior, smell learning.
plos-pone-0001225:
Some blood cancers hide chromosome damage that standard tests cannot see. Lukasz Gondek and colleagues applied SNP arrays to patients with atypical myeloproliferative and myelodysplastic syndromes. Their study appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. SNP arrays are chips that read hundreds of thousands of single-letter DNA variants.

The authors show that SNP array karyotyping detects uniparental disomy. In that condition, both copies of a chromosome segment come from one parent. It also detects cryptic chromosomal abnormalities that older methods miss. They studied patients with and without the JAK2 V617F mutation, a common driver in these diseases. Finer karyotyping can change diagnosis and treatment choices.
plos-pone-0001325:
Certain short peptides can assemble themselves into coatings and scaffolds, making them attractive nano-biomaterials. Hong Yang, Shan-Yu Fung, and Mark Pritzker studied one model peptide, EAK16-II, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Ionic-complementary peptides carry alternating positive and negative charges that drive their assembly.

The authors present evidence that the peptide can assemble on and coat both hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces, water-loving and water-hating alike. Such coatings could engineer biosurfaces for implants, sensors, and cell culture. A single peptide that coats both surface types is a versatile tool. The peptide assembles on its own once applied.
plos-pone-0001425:
Enrique Caviedes-Vidal and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how bats take up food from the gut. Bats tend to have less gut tissue than like sized mammals that do not fly. A small gut saves weight, which helps flight. The team asked how bats still get enough food from that small gut.

They show that bats let a large share of food pass between gut cells, not just through them. That route breaks the usual mammal pattern. It lets a small gut act like a much larger one. The finding recasts how flight shaped the bat body, gut included, over time.
plos-pone-0001525:
Joshua Herbeck and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on whether HIV is growing more or less harsh. Past cohort data and lab tests had given clashing answers, with claims of falling, flat, and rising harm. The team tested the change claim in North American data. They used set marks of virus strength over time.

They found a lack of proof for a shift in HIV strength in this region. A flat verdict from sound data still counts. It means care and spread plans need not chase a moving target on this front. It also shows how weak methods can breed false trends.
plos-pone-0001625:
Cédric Patthey, Lena Gunhaga, and Thomas Edlund studied how the brain, spinal cord, and sense organs begin to form in the early embryo. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article focuses on two signal families, Wnt and BMP, that cells use to tell nearby cells what to become. The central nervous system grows from the neural plate, while the peripheral system grows from cells at its border.

For the senses to work, these two systems must grow in step, so that circuits form in the right places. The authors trace how Wnt and BMP signals coordinate the growth of neural plate, neural crest, and placodal cells. The full text gives the embryo experiments and the signals they recorded. The work helps explain how a flat sheet of early cells turns into a wired nervous system.
plos-pone-0001725:
Gregory P. Bisson, Tendani Gaolathe, Robert Gross, and their co-authors warned that HIV treatment success may be overstated, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tracking how well global antiretroviral therapy scale-up works is a health priority. In resource-limited settings, though, many patients are lost to follow-up after starting treatment, and their true outcomes are unknown.

If many of those lost patients have died, published survival figures will look too good. The authors examined definitive outcomes of lost patients and what they imply for reported survival after HAART. The full text gives the tracing results and the corrected survival estimates. Honest numbers decide whether scale-up is truly working or needs fixing.
plos-pone-0001825:
Daniel A. Beard, Kalyan C. Vinnakota, and Fan Wu worked out detailed enzyme kinetics for a core metabolic enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Citrate synthase runs the first step of the citric acid cycle, the cell's central energy pathway. The paper analyzes the compulsory-ordered ternary mechanism used by two-substrate, two-product enzymes.

Their treatment accounts for inhibitors binding to each of the four enzyme states and keeps the kinetic constants consistent with the reaction equilibrium constant. The full text gives the derivations and the worked example. Rigorous kinetics of this kind, called biochemical species kinetics, improves computer models of metabolism used in drug and biofuel research.
plos-pone-0001925:
Mathias Gehrmann and co-authors asked why tumor cells, but not healthy cells, show a stress protein on their surface, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, Hsp70, is the main stress-induced member of its family. When it sits on a tumor's outer membrane, it flags a worse or better outlook in some cancers, such as leukemia.

The team traced the display to a fat-like molecule in the membrane called Gb3. As the title states, Gb3 enables the tumor-specific placement of Hsp70 on the surface. That detail matters because surface Hsp70 can draw immune attack. A drug that shifts Gb3 might make more tumors show the flag.
plos-pone-0002025:
