Lina Dahl and co-authors studied a gene that keeps young blood cells dividing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. How the blood system expands in the fetal liver, stem cells and all, is largely unknown. The gene Lhx2 was a candidate driver, since it is active in that setting.

The team grew embryonic stem cells into embryoid bodies, small balls that mimic early development, and switched Lhx2 on. As the title states, its expression promoted self-renewal of a distinct early blood progenitor cell. A gene that keeps blood precursors young could help labs grow blood stem cells for therapy.
plos-pone-0002125:
Phuoc Tran and co-authors asked what happens when two cancer genes are switched off at once. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lab models had shown that tumors need a cancer gene to stay switched on, a trait called oncogene addiction. Most real cancers, though, are driven by several gene changes at once, which makes it hard to tell which ones the tumor truly needs.

Working with lung adenocarcinomas and lymphomas in mice, the team turned off both MYC and K-Ras together. Doing so reversed tumor growth in their models. The finding supports the idea that hitting more than one driver gene at once could be a stronger way to treat cancer.
plos-pone-0002225:
Allan Reiss and co-authors scanned the brains of people whose laughter can knock out their muscles. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cataplexy affects some people with narcolepsy, roughly 1 in 2,000 people overall. Strong feelings, above all laughter, can trigger a brief loss of muscle tone that leaves a person limp but awake.

The study aimed to find how the hypothalamus, a small brain region tied to sleep and emotion, responds to humor in these patients. Its responses looked anomalous next to those of healthy subjects. The work helps explain how an emotion can flip a switch in the brain and cut the body's strength.
plos-pone-0002325:
Wei Zhang, Song Liu, and Yaoqi Zhou presented an improved program for recognizing a protein's fold, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Predicting which known shape a new protein sequence will fold into is a central challenge in protein science. The team had built a series of methods, called SPARKS and SP2 through SP4, that score how well a sequence fits a known structure.

Their new method, SP5, adds torsion angle profiles, the twist patterns along the protein backbone, and a smarter penalty for gaps. Better fold recognition means more proteins of unknown shape can be assigned a likely structure from sequence alone, guiding experiments that follow.
plos-pone-0002425:
Faça and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Vitor M. Faça, Aviva P. Ventura, Mathew P. Fitzgibbon, among others. Its subject is proteomic Analysis of Ovarian Cancer Cells Reveals Dynamic Processes of Protein Secretion and Shedding of Extra-Cellular Domains. Elucidation of the repertoire of secreted and cell surface proteins of tumor cells is relevant to molecular diagnostics, tumor imaging and targeted therapies.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002525:
Takata and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Norio Takata, Hajime Hirase, among others. Its subject is cortical Layer 1 and Layer 2/3 Astrocytes Exhibit Distinct Calcium Dynamics In Vivo. Cumulative evidence supports bidirectional interactions between astrocytes and neurons, suggesting glial involvement of neuronal information processing in the brain.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002625:
Jürgen Konczak and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of haptic perception of object curvature in parkinson's disease. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jürgen Konczak, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The haptic perception of the curvature of an object is essential for adequate object manipulation and critical for our guidance of actions. A further point appears in the abstract. This study investigated how the ability to perceive the curvature of an object is altered by Parkinson's disease (PD). Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002725:
In 2008, Karlijn I. van Aerde and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about prelimbic and infralimbic prefrontal cortex interact during fast network oscillations. The catalog record names Karlijn I. van Aerde first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The medial prefrontal cortex has been implicated in a variety of cognitive and executive processes such as decision making and working memory. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002825:
In 2008, Jerome J. Weis and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was effects of algal diversity on the production of biomass in homogeneous and heterogeneous nutrient environments: a microcosm experiment. Authorship is credited in the record to Jerome J. Weis and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. One of the most common questions addressed by ecologists over the past decade has been-how does species richness impact the production of community biomass?. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002925:
Thomas Fanshawe, Andrew Lynch, Ian Ellis and colleagues tackled a statistics problem in breast cancer grading in 2008. Pathologists grade tumor samples to guide care, yet past studies found only moderate agreement between raters. Missing ratings and many raters make judging that agreement harder still.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out a way to assess agreement when rating data are incomplete. They apply it to a large but partial dataset of breast tumor grading. Better agreement measures help hospitals know how much weight a grade deserves and where training or review is needed most.
plos-pone-0003025:
Eliana Marengo, Luciana de Moraes, Marcella Faria and co-authors gave a leprosy heat shock protein to lupus-prone mice in 2008. Heat shock proteins guide protein assembly and transport and are highly conserved across life. The Hsp60 family is expressed at high levels and interacts with the immune system.

The treatment used Hsp65 from Mycobacterium leprae, the leprosy bacterium. It interfered with the progression of murine lupus, an autoimmune disease, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, a bacterial protein calming autoimmunity is counterintuitive but fits the idea that immune tuning can treat immune excess.
plos-pone-0003125:
Jean-Michel Benoist, Ivanne Pincedé, Kay Ballantyne and colleagues address a basic problem in pain research in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tests of pain response in rats use reaction time, the gap between the start of a stimulus such as heat and the animal's response. Yet skin cannot be heated at once by normal means, which makes that timing hard to read.

The authors work out what parts of the reaction come from the body surface and what parts come from the central nervous system. Readers get a careful approach to psychophysics in the rat. It helps others judge what a simple reaction time can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0003225:
Ting-Hua Huang, Meng-Jin Zhu, Xin-Yun Li and colleagues catalogue pig microRNAs in muscle in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs play critical roles in many important biological processes such as growth and development in mammals. In this study, the team identified hundreds of porcine microRNA candidates through computer prediction and analysed their expression in developing skeletal muscle using further methods.

Readers get both a discovery list and a developmental profile for pig muscle. Pigs are a major farm animal and a medical model, so their microRNA map has dual value. Muscle microRNAs may also guide breeding for meat traits.
plos-pone-0003325:
Alexander O. Vargas, Tiana Kohlsdorf, John F. Fallon and colleagues study digit identity in the bird wing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Comparative morphology identifies the digits of the wing of birds as one, two and three, but they develop at embryological positions that become digits two, three and four in other amniotes. A hypothesis to explain this is that a homeotic frame shift of digital identity occurred in bird evolution.

The authors examine evolution of HoxD-11 expression in the bird wing, with insights from Alligator mississippiensis. Readers see gene expression used to test a classic anatomy puzzle. Alligators, as bird relatives, provide the comparison that makes the test possible.
plos-pone-0003425:
Liran I. Shlush and co-authors checked a claimed longevity marker in this 2008 study. Studies in northern Italy and Finland tied one mitochondrial DNA group to long life. That group, haplogroup J, appeared more often among people past one hundred. The team tested the claim in Ashkenazi Jewish centenarians.

Their long-lived group showed no extra share of haplogroup J. The marker's link to long life did not hold in this population. Negative results like this keep longevity genetics honest. A marker found in one group may mean little in another. Long life likely rests on many small factors rather than one marker.
plos-pone-0003525:
Boris Schmid, Can Keşmir, and Rob J. de Boer modeled HIV escape and human diversity in this 2008 paper. MHC class I molecules vary greatly between people. That variety lowers the chance a virus arrives pre-adapted to a new host. Still, HIV might dodge shared steps of antigen processing instead.

Processing parts like the proteasome and TAP are near-identical in everyone. The model shows MHC diversity blocks global adaptation anyway. An escape that works in one person fails in the next. Diversity thus caps how far the virus can evolve ahead.
plos-pone-0003625:
Joann Mudge, Neil A. Miller, Irina Khrebtukova, and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It searches for the roots of schizophrenia, a serious mental illness that runs in families. The team used mRNA sequencing on brain tissue taken after death, focusing on the cerebellum.

By combining gene sequence data with other genetic evidence, the study found changed activity in genes for synaptic vesicle transport. Those vesicles are the tiny sacs that carry chemical messages between brain cells. The result points to faulty message handling as one part of how schizophrenia develops.
plos-pone-0003725:
Brian B. Gowen, Donald F. Smee, Min-Hui Wong, and colleagues published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2008. A growing list of arenaviruses cause viral hemorrhagic fever, a severe illness with leaking blood vessels. Ribavirin is the only licensed drug for some of these infections, and it has limits.

The team tested the drug T-705 in an animal model, treating late stage disease. T-705 worked against the infection and showed reduced toxicity compared with ribavirin. The results suggest an alternative for infections that are usually treated only after they are already advanced.
plos-pone-0003825:
Tzvia Abramson, Hassya Kedem, and David A. Relman published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Bordetella pertussis is the bacterium behind whooping cough. One of its surface proteins, filamentous hemagglutinin, helps it attach to airway cells. The authors asked what that protein does to host immune signaling.

They report that filamentous hemagglutinin modulates the NF-kB pathway, a master switch of immune responses. Tuning that pathway can damp or redirect the host's defenses. The result shows one way the bacterium shapes its reception while it settles into the respiratory tract.
plos-pone-0003925:
Masashi Tachikawa modeled how changing conditions split species in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Living systems always face swings in their surroundings. Species evolve under those swings and often end up robust to them. Diversity in nature also grows through evolution under change.

The author asked how swings themselves shape that growth of diversity. His mathematical model of an ecosystem shows fluctuation driving evolutionary branching. In branching, one lineage splits into distinct forms over time. The model suggests changeable worlds may breed diversity faster than stable ones. It offers theory that field studies can test against real ecosystems.
plos-pone-0004025:
Abdullah Al Mahmud, Gabriele Amore, and Giorgio Bernardi studied genome makeup and gene control in sea urchins in 2008. Gene activity is usually credited to regulatory DNA regions alone. Those regions are built from modules of transcription factor binding sites. The authors questioned whether wider genome composition also matters.

Their PLOS ONE article reports compositional contexts affect gene control in embryos. The base makeup around a gene can sway its activity. That adds a background layer to the modular control picture. Sea urchin embryos give a clear system for testing such effects. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004125:
Carlos Driscoll and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks where the extinct Caspian tiger came from and how it relates to the living Amur tiger. The Caspian tiger once lived in river forests across Central Asia, in a range cut off from other tigers. Hunters drove it to extinction by 1970.

Because it vanished before modern genetic tests existed, its place among the tiger subspecies stayed unclear for over a century. The team read mitochondrial DNA, passed down through mothers, to place it on the tiger family tree. The study settles a long taxonomic puzzle using samples from a tiger no longer alive.
plos-pone-0004225:
Stefan Maas and Willemijn Gommans published this RNA study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells edit some RNA messages after they are written, changing single letters in the code. This A-to-I editing adds much of the variety in the mammalian transcriptome and can recode proteins, changing what they do.

The authors report a novel exon, a coding segment, in the mammalian ADAR2 gene, one of the genes for the editing enzymes themselves. The new segment extends the gene's open reading frame, the stretch that can be read as protein. Even the editors, it turns out, had an unread page in their own instructions.
plos-pone-0004325:
Chadi Touma and colleagues published this depression model study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, the stress hormone system, plays a key role in mood disorders such as major depression. Further hallmarks of depression include disturbed circadian rhythms in behaviour, hormones, and sleep.

The team studied mice selected for extremes in stress reactivity, bred to be high or low responders. They tracked behavioural, endocrine, and sleep changes resembling endophenotypes of major depression, traits that can be measured, which underlie the illness. Such mice offer a living model of the depressed body's daily rhythm gone wrong. The mice were bred to react strongly or weakly to stress.
plos-pone-0004425:
Wolbachia bacteria live inside many insects and can rig reproduction in their favor, a puzzle explored by Arnulf Koehncke, Arndt Telschow, John Werren, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. When an infected male mates with an uninfected female, her eggs often fail to hatch. Biologists call this cytoplasmic incompatibility, and it helps the bacteria spread through a host population.

From an evolution view, the trick raises a hard question: why would hosts not evolve ways to block it? The authors model the life and death of a creature they call an influential passenger. They trace how host genes that modify the effect can appear and spread. The result helps explain how a hidden microbe and its host shape each other's evolution over time.
plos-pone-0004525:
A drink of glucose can reveal early metabolic trouble in the body's chemical profile, show Suzan Wopereis, Carina Rubingh, Marjan van Erk, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Overweight is rising worldwide, and low-grade, long-term inflammation in overweight people is thought to help drive later disease. New tools are needed to see these processes early.

The team used metabolic profiling, a broad scan of small chemicals in the body, around an oral glucose tolerance test. In that test, a person drinks glucose and the response is tracked over time. The profiling detected subtle metabolic changes that standard measures can miss. Catching such changes early could flag people heading toward diabetes long before plain blood sugar readings turn abnormal.
plos-pone-0004625:
A toolkit for building glowing reporter genes in worms is presented by Baris Tursun, Luisa Cochella, Ines Carrera, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reporters made from large genomic clones, held in fosmid vectors, let scientists visualize when and where a gene is active in a living animal. Because these reporters cover large genomic regions, they likely capture all the control elements that govern the gene.

Making such reporters used to be slow, bespoke work. The authors describe a toolkit and robust pipeline for generating them in the worm C. elegans. A standard, dependable method spreads reporter technology to many more genes and labs. Watching genes switch on and off in a transparent animal remains one of the clearest windows into development.
plos-pone-0004725:
Patrick Jansen and colleagues showed that a skin defense protein in blood tracks psoriasis activity, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Defense proteins in skin can kill germs and draw in immune cells. One of them is made in large amounts in the sore, scaly skin of psoriasis.

The team asked if blood levels of the protein match how bad the disease is. They also checked levels in the sore skin itself. Blood levels did track activity and reached meaningful levels in lesions. A blood test like this could help doctors grade psoriasis without repeated skin samples. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004825:
Patricia Opresko, Gregory Sowd, and Hong Wang showed that the Werner syndrome helicase and exonuclease processes mobile D-loops, in PLOS ONE in 2009. RecQ DNA helicases are critical for preserving genome integrity. Of five RecQ members in humans, only Werner protein possesses exonuclease activity. Loss of WRN causes the progeroid disorder Werner syndrome marked by cancer predisposition and premature aging features.

Mobile D-loops are recombination intermediates needing resolution. Branch migration and degradation by WRN clear them. Failure may destabilize genomes. The step links aging, cancer, and DNA repair. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004925:
Watching another person act seems to wake up our own movement areas. That hints at a mirror neuron system in humans. James Kilner, Jennifer Marchant and Chris Frith tested the idea in PLOS ONE in 2009. They tracked beta brain waves in the primary motor cortex. Volunteers watched actions while the team recorded.

The researchers varied the viewpoint of the observed action. The fading of the beta rhythm changed with viewpoint. That pattern fits a genuine mirror response, not simple attention. The results sharpen how scientists test for mirror-like activity in the human brain. They also clarify what motor cortex signals can and cannot prove.
plos-pone-0005025:
Hepatitis C virus is a major risk factor for liver cancer. Yet mice carrying the whole virus do not develop tumors. Naama Klopstock and colleagues asked why in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared mouse strains with different genetic backgrounds. The virus's tumor-promoting effect was the focus.

The same virus turned dangerous only in certain strains. Host genetics decided whether it pushed the liver toward cancer. Chronic infection inflames human livers, but the mice lacked that picture. The finding reframes how researchers model this virus. Strain choice can make or break a model. It also hints that human genetic background helps decide who develops cancer after infection.
plos-pone-0005125:
Tumors signal with chemokines, chemical messengers for cells. The receptor CXCR4 appears on most tumors. It drives their growth and spread. Katia Beider and colleagues studied its cross-talk with another pathway in PLOS ONE in 2009. That pathway centers on CCL20. Its role in tumors was less charted.

The two pathways interact to regulate tumor growth. Neither acts alone. CXCR4's ligand comes mainly from cancer-associated cells around the tumor. The partnership reveals a joint control system. Blocking both routes could hit tumors harder than blocking one. The finding warns against single-pathway thinking. Tumors network their signals. Therapies may need to network their blocks in return.
plos-pone-0005225:
Gene chips that scan single-letter DNA variants are now cheap and cover most of the genome. Some regions tied to disease still get thin coverage, though. Saccone and colleagues addressed that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009, using addiction as their test case.

Addiction is shaped by many genes interacting in complex ways. The team designed added chip content for regions tied to addiction biology and showed the supplement improves coverage. The same strategy can patch chips for other diseases where key regions would otherwise be missed. The same fix could help chips made for other hard traits, where a few key gene regions matter more than the rest of the genome.
plos-pone-0005325:
CD1 molecules display fat-based antigens on cell surfaces for inspection by specialized T cells. Many lipid species were thought able to bind them, but the actual cargo was unclear. Cox and colleagues determined which cellular lipids sit on human CD1d in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Knowing the real cargo defines what the immune system can see through this route. The lipid list also shows which fats the cell chooses to display. That knowledge guides work on vaccines and on immune disorders where lipid presentation goes wrong. Fats are the food of some germs and the flags of others. So a full list of the fats shown to T cells gives vaccine teams raw parts they can test one by one.
plos-pone-0005425:
Amynah Pradhan and colleagues studied pain-related receptors in living animals for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many drugs work by switching on receptors that sit on the surface of cells. After a drug switches one on, the cell often pulls the receptor inside, which changes the drug's effect.

The team focused on the delta opioid receptor, one target for pain drugs. They showed that whether this receptor moves inside the cell shapes how the drug changes behaviour. That finding matters for making pain drugs that work well for longer, with fewer unwanted effects over time.
plos-pone-0005525:
Nilesh Banavali and Alexander MacKerell presented a method for studying shape changes in large molecules, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When cells copy DNA, read genes, or build proteins, the molecules involved bend and twist. Those shape changes can be traced to bends in the molecule's backbone.

Their method maps the energy cost of bending in just the region that changes, rather than across the whole molecule. A local map is faster to compute and easier to read. It can help drug makers see how target molecules move. Cheaper computing also lets more labs study motions that once needed a large machine and weeks of time.
plos-pone-0005625:
Philippe Schyns, Lucy Petro, and Marie Smith studied how faces carry emotion in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Social animals have to read the feelings of others quickly. In primates, the face has evolved to broadcast inner states, and the receiver's brain has evolved to decode them.

The team paired behaviour tests with brain measures to trace which facial cues carry which feelings. They argue that signal and decoding shaped each other over evolution. That helps explain why some expressions are read so fast and so accurately across people. Fast reading of faces guides talk, trust, and mating choices, so its roots reach deep into social life.
plos-pone-0005725:
Christopher Stephens and co-authors used networks of species interactions in 2009 to forecast biodiversity patterns and disease outbreaks. A network maps who eats, hosts, or lives with whom across a whole community. Most past networks only charted links seen directly in the field.

The team went further, using known links to predict links not yet seen. Good predictions can flag where new diseases may jump between species. They can also show which species hold a web together. Such forecasts help managers act before a crisis, rather than after. The work treats ecology as a web that can be read ahead.
plos-pone-0005825:
Cyril Rakovski and Daniel Stram fixed a flaw in a standard gene-hunting test in 2009. Genome-wide studies compare cases and controls to find disease genes. The Armitage trend test is a workhorse for that job.

Hidden family links and subtle ancestry differences between groups can fake positive results. So can small, uneven genotyping errors. Their kinship-based version of the test corrects for those traps. Cleaner tests mean fewer false leads chased by costly follow-up studies. The paper is a statistical repair with wide use, since the same traps lurk in most large genetic datasets.
plos-pone-0005925:
Cells that repair the airway may also travel in the blood. Derek Nickerson, Angela Presson, Stephen Weigt and colleagues tested that idea in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They measured a marker called cytokeratin 5 in the blood of healthy people and of patients who had received a lung transplant.

The marker comes from airway lining cells, so its level in blood can hint at repair work under way. A simple blood measure of this kind could help doctors track lung healing without invasive tests. The paper sets a baseline in healthy people and opens a route to watching transplant patients over time.
plos-pone-0006025:
A kinase that helps cells move must also get into the nucleus to do some of its jobs. Christine Lightcap, Gabor Kari, Luis Arias-Romero and colleagues traced that trip for Pak1 in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs Pak1 with LC8, a small part of the dynein motor, and tests the pair in cells and in zebrafish.

Contact with LC8 is required for Pak1 to enter the nucleus, the title states, and the partnership is indispensable for zebrafish development. A fish that cannot run this step cannot grow normally. The work links a motor's light chain to a growth signal's address, a small fact with reach into both development and cancer biology.
plos-pone-0006125:
Switching a gene off in one tissue, at one time, and passing that control to offspring is a tall order. Mei Dong, Yan-Fang Fu, Ting-Ting Du and colleagues achieved it in zebrafish embryos in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper presents heritable and lineage-specific gene knockdown, answering a need in the study of development genes and tumor suppressors whose reduced levels drive disease.

A knockdown that can be aimed in space and time, and inherited, lets researchers test one gene's job in one cell line without breaking the whole animal. That precision is what embryo science had been missing. The method also serves cancer gene studies, where half-silenced genes are often the realistic case.
plos-pone-0006225:
Farmers need new ways to control the beet armyworm, a caterpillar that eats many crops. Honggang Tian and colleagues fed the pest bacteria carrying gene-silencing instructions, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The method, RNA interference, turns off a chosen gene when the insect eats matching double-stranded RNA.

Earlier feeding successes had focused on gut genes; this work targeted a gene outside the gut. Silencing it disturbed the pest's development. Success beyond the gut widens the list of genes farmers could attack. The approach hints at pest control sprays built from bacteria rather than broad poisons.
plos-pone-0006325:
Plant oil-body proteins can be borrowed as anchors for mammalian cell engineering. Laurent Pons and colleagues used oleosin, a plant protein found on lipid droplets, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their idea was to tether chosen secreted proteins to the inner side of the endoplasmic reticulum in mammalian cells.

As a demonstration, they sequestered transcobalamin, the vitamin B12 carrier protein, inside cells. Anchoring changes where a protein ends up and what it can do. The trick offers a general tool for studying secretion and storage. It may also serve production of therapeutic proteins.
plos-pone-0006425:
Radmila Lyubarova, Brandon Itagaki, and Michael Itagaki examined United States heart research funding in a 2009 PLOS ONE article. At the time, the National Institutes of Health budget had grown as part of an economic stimulus plan. Yet how NIH funding relates to cardiovascular disease research was poorly understood. The authors set out to map that link.

Their study weighs what extra public money is likely to do to the field. Heart disease research depends heavily on grant support, so funding shifts shape what gets studied. The analysis gives policy makers evidence instead of guesses. It also helps research teams plan around the funding climate.
plos-pone-0006525:
Michelle Dawson, Dan Duda, Sung-Suk Chae, and colleagues studied a growth factor receptor in lung metastases for PLOS ONE in 2009. The role of VEGFR1 in tumor metastasis remains incompletely characterized. Recent reports suggested that blocking VEGFR1 might help. The team tested its activity in growing lung metastases, where tumors seed the lungs.

Their title reports a split result: VEGFR1 activity modulates myeloid cell infiltration in lung metastases. Yet it is not required for spontaneous metastasis itself. Such nuance prevents wasted effort on the wrong target. It redirects attention to the immune cells the receptor does control.
plos-pone-0006625:
Mark Schütte and co-authors built tools to detect a fungus that harms weak patients in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aspergillus fumigatus is a common mold in the air. It often causes invasive disease in people whose immune systems are weak, and the outlook is poor. The team found a variant form of a fungal protein called Crf, made by a splice change. They then built lab-made antibodies to detect the fungus with care.

Good, fast detection is the weak point in care of this disease. Antibodies aimed at one fungal protein could speed tests on patient samples. Faster tests mean faster care, which is the main lever for survival. Their antibodies are a step toward a test clinics can use.
plos-pone-0006725:
Sang Soo Cho and Antonio P. Strafella used magnets to shift a brain chemical in PLOS ONE in 2009. The chemical is dopamine. It helps control movement, focus, reward, and learning. It also plays a key role in Parkinson's disease and in drug addiction. Work in animals had shown that brain pulses can change dopamine levels a lot.

The team pulsed the left front of the brain with a magnet coil. This method is called rTMS, and it needs no surgery. Dopamine then changed in two deep brain areas on the same side. Both areas help guide choices and reward. The work shows a surface pulse can reach deep brain chemistry.
plos-pone-0006825:
Diana Stralberg and colleagues projected how climate change will reshuffle California's birds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Species shift their ranges independently as climate warms. Independent shifts can build communities never seen before. Novel assemblages challenge species' ability to coexist and adapt. The authors borrowed a multivariate method from paleoecology to quantify the change.

They mapped future distributions for California bird species. Many future communities had no modern analog. A no-analog future means conservation plans built on today's communities may fail. Protected areas could end up guarding the wrong species mixes. The forecast argues for planning that expects reshuffling, not stability.
plos-pone-0006925:
Nikolaus Maier, Genela Morris, Friedrich Johenning, and colleagues presented a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their topic was sharp wave-ripples, a fast activity pattern in the hippocampus. Among hippocampal network patterns, these were the least understood at the time. Reliable study needed accurate detail on how the participating neurons interact.

The authors set out an approach for studying these ripples in the laboratory dish. Their method aimed at repeatable, trustworthy recordings of the events. That matters because sharp wave-ripples are tied to memory processes. A dependable in vitro system lets researchers test how the network produces them, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0007025:
Ikechukwu Okoli, Jeffrey Coleman, Emmanouil Tempakakis, and colleagues screened for antifungal drugs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Candida albicans is the most common disease-causing fungus in humans. It can set up a lasting, lethal infection in the gut of the worm C. elegans. That worm infection had already been adapted into a drug screen.

The team improved the high-throughput version of that assay. Then they used it to find compounds active against the fungus. Screening in a whole animal filters out drugs that only work in a dish. New antifungals are badly needed as resistance grows.
plos-pone-0007125:
Fabrice Armougom, Mireille Henry, Bernard Vialettes, and others checked gut germs by body weight in PLOS ONE in 2009. Work on gut floras had shown shifts in the main germ groups in obese patients. Counts of set groups in stool samples might show clear profiles for each weight state. The team tracked the gut flora of obese and anorexic patients.

They found more Lactobacillus in obese patients. Methanogens, germs that make methane gas, rose in anorexic patients. The two weight extremes carried opposed signs in the gut. Such profiles might one day help doctors spot, or even treat, weight disorders via the gut.
plos-pone-0007225:
Line Olsen, Mikkel Klausen, Lone Helboe, and colleagues mapped small RNA patterns in rat brains in 2009. The brain is a major site of microRNA gene expression. Yet the spatial patterns of those microRNAs inside the brain were not fully covered when the study began.

The authors profile microRNA expression across five distinct regions of the adult male rat brain. One region they name is the amygdala, involved in emotion. They find patterns where different microRNAs show mutually exclusive expression. Their map helps neuroscientists link specific microRNAs to specific brain areas.
plos-pone-0007325:
Hiranmoy Das, Jon C. George, Matthew Joseph, and colleagues tested gene-enhanced stem cells for heart repair in rats in 2009. They use human cord blood stem cells expanded on nanofibers. The cells are genetically modified to overexpress two growth genes, VEGF and PDGF, which promote blood vessel growth.

The authors transplant the cells in a rat model of heart attack. They monitor heart function every two weeks for a period after treatment. They report improved cardiac function with the modified cells. Their PLOS ONE study tests whether adding growth genes strengthens stem cell therapy.
plos-pone-0007425:
Andréa da Silva and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on dengue virus type 3, a mosquito-borne virus spreading through tropical regions. Dengue vaccine work has been slowed by a real danger. Immune memory from a vaccine might make a later natural infection worse instead of milder. The team worked to reduce that risk at the design stage.

They mapped the short stretches on the virus envelope protein that human antibodies actually recognize. These stretches are called continuous B-cell epitopes. Knowing exactly which patches the immune system sees lets vaccine designers favor protective responses. It also helps them avoid responses tied to harm. The map is a practical step toward a dengue vaccine that protects without backfiring.
plos-pone-0007525:
Bryan Clay and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the immune cells behind asthma and allergy. Th2 lymphocytes drive the airway inflammation in these conditions. A surface switch called ICOS, the inducible costimulator, regulates how those cells function. A variant in the human ICOS gene is tied to higher allergy rates. The team studied how ICOS expression controls the inflammation itself.

They found ICOS regulates the sheer number of Th2 cells that accumulate. More Th2 cells mean stronger airway inflammation. So the switch acts as a volume control on the allergic response. Because ICOS is reachable by drugs, it is a promising immunotherapy target. Calming it could reduce the cell buildup that makes airways twitchy. The study ties a genetic clue to a concrete cellular mechanism.
plos-pone-0007625:
Martine Hausberger and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 asking whether work itself can disorder a horse's behavior. In people, work stress leads to durable problems like anxiety and depression. Horses, unusually among animals, also work daily alongside humans. They are submitted to routines, demands, and confinement set by their jobs. The team compared horses under different work conditions and looked for behavioral disorders.

Horses' work routines were linked to problems such as stereotypies, the repetitive behaviors of stressed animals. The parallel with human occupational stress is hard to miss. Treating the horse as a fellow laborer changes how its welfare is judged. Stables and trainers may need to audit the job, not just the horse. The study widens occupational health beyond our own species.
plos-pone-0007725:
Michael Anderson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns the common cuckoo, a bird that lays its eggs in other birds' nests. A cuckoo chick hatches blind and naked. It then heaves its nestmates' eggs or chicks out of the nest.

That effort removes rivals for the foster parents' food and care. The authors show the effort also carries a cost for the chick itself. The chick pays in growth or survival, a form of virulence cost. Yet the authors argue the cost can be recovered as the chick grows alone.
plos-pone-0007825:
Hironori Nishitsuji and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uncovers a helper HIV borrows from human cells. HIV's integrase protein is best known for stitching viral DNA into the host genome. Evidence had also tied integrase to reverse transcription, the step that copies viral RNA into DNA.

The team studied a host factor called SIP1, also named Gemin2, that binds integrase. That interaction boosts reverse transcription inside the cell. Blocking it proved critical to infection in their tests. A host helper the virus cannot do without is a tempting target for new drugs.
plos-pone-0007925:
Mona Loutfy and colleagues surveyed women living with HIV in Ontario for PLOS ONE in 2009. Their cross-sectional study asked women of childbearing age whether they wanted children and whether they planned to try. The question mattered because better treatment had made pregnancy far safer than before.

Answers showed real demand for family planning help shaped to these women's lives. Many wanted children, yet worries about health, drug safety, and passing the virus to a baby weighed on their plans. The authors urge clinics to offer clear guidance and care that treats childbearing as a normal goal, not an afterthought.
plos-pone-0008025:
Hilary Moffitt and colleagues hunted for protein clumps across the body in a Huntington's disease mouse in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease comes from a stretched repeat in one gene, which makes a protein with a long tail of one building block. Those proteins pile into clumps in the brain.

The mouse, built to carry the same fault, formed clumps in many tissues outside the brain as well. Muscle, liver, and other organs all showed them. Care that aims only at the brain may thus miss much of the disease, and body-wide checks could track it better.
plos-pone-0008125:
Sagar Indurkhya and Jacob Beal made a standard reaction simulator far faster in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Gillespie method plays out chemical reactions one event at a time, which suits cases where some players are vanishingly scarce. On large systems it crawls, since each step rescans the whole set.

Grouping like reactions together, and refreshing only the parts a step actually changed, cut the work sharply. Big cell models that once needed special machines can now run on ordinary ones. Faster runs mean more ideas tested per day for everyone modeling living chemistry.
plos-pone-0008225:
Ulisse Garbin and colleagues studied young heavy smokers in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Smoking is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis, a chronic inflammatory disease of arteries. The reasons for that effect remain unclear. One idea is that water-soluble parts of smoke drive oxidative stress in blood vessels. A protective pathway called Nrf2/ARE normally helps cells resist such stress.

The team measured that pathway in blood cells from young heavy smokers. Smoking appeared to block the protective expression of the pathway. That failure would leave cells open to inflammation. The findings help explain how smoking harms arteries early in life.
plos-pone-0008325:
Pei-Gang Wang and colleagues built dengue virus-like particles in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cells infected with flaviviruses produce both infectious virions and smaller subviral particles. Both forms assemble from the prM and E envelope proteins. They are believed to mature in the same way. Dengue has four distinct serotypes, each able to cause disease.

The team produced recombinant subviral particles for all four serotypes. They used the native prM and E proteins for efficient assembly and secretion. Particles without a genome cannot infect, so they are safer research tools. They could also serve as vaccine candidates.
plos-pone-0008425:
Vladimir Voynov and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about why some drug proteins clump. Many key drugs are antibodies, and most such proteins wear a coat of sugar chains. The bond with those sugars helps set the shape and work of the protein. The team asked what takes place if that bond is weak or breaks. They watched the bond shift and move as time went by.

They found that this fast shift and move helps proteins stick to each other and clump. Clumps are a big flaw in drug making and in shelf life. If firms can calm that move, drugs may stay clear and safe for more time. The work ties small-scale motion to a large cost in drug plants.
plos-pone-0008525:
Wei Liao and co-authors map brain networks in epilepsy in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The resting brain shows coherent low-frequency fluctuations across regions. Those fluctuations define functional connectivity networks. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy affects deep structures vital for memory. Little was known about how it rewires whole-brain connectivity. The team scan patients at rest and build their networks.

They find altered connectivity and a changed small-world organization. Small-world networks balance local clustering with short global paths. Epilepsy shifts that balance in their patients. Such network measures may become markers for diagnosis or surgical planning in temporal lobe epilepsy.
plos-pone-0008625:
Magdalena Wisniewska and co-authors solve chaperone structures in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The 70-kilodalton heat shock proteins, Hsp70s, are chaperones with central roles in protein remodeling. Each Hsp70 has two major functional domains. The N-terminal domain binds nucleotides and has ATPase activity. The C-terminal domain grips the client polypeptide. The team determine crystal structures of the ATPase domains of four human Hsp70 isoforms. They are HSPA1L, HSPA2, HSPA6, and HSPA5, also called BiP.

Comparing four isoforms reveals how small changes tune ATP handling. Those differences may adapt each chaperone to distinct tissues or stresses. Structures of the ATPase domain guide inhibitor design. Hsp70 inhibitors are sought in cancer and neurodegenerative disease.
plos-pone-0008725:
Miriam Canavese, Fiorella Altruda, and Lorenzo Silengo tested blockers of a skin alarm signal in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. CCL5 is a chemokine, a chemical call that draws T cells into skin. Those cells drive eczema, psoriasis, and allergic contact dermatitis. Blocking the call might calm the reaction at its source.

The team gave mice drugs that block CCL5 and watched their skin reactions. They measured swelling, cell entry, and immune signals in the skin. Calmer reactions would support chemokine blocking as a treatment idea. The work adds detail on how CCL5 steers skin inflammation.
plos-pone-0008825:
Myriam Rai, Elisabetta Soragni, C. James Chou, and colleagues tested drugs that raise a missing protein in Friedreich's ataxia. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is the most common inherited ataxia in Caucasians. A repeated DNA stretch inside the frataxin gene muffles its output. Patients make far too little frataxin protein. Drugs that unblock silenced genes, called HDAC inhibitors, offered a remedy.

Two new inhibitors kept frataxin levels up over time. The effect held in patient cells and in a mouse model. Sustained raising is what a real therapy would need. The pair now merit deeper preclinical testing.
plos-pone-0008925:
Flaviano Martins, Guillaume Dalmasso, Rosa Arantes, and colleagues tested a probiotic yeast against a gut-invading germ. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salmonella Typhimurium invades gut cells and triggers strong inflammation. The yeast Saccharomyces boulardii is sold as a probiotic for gut troubles. Whether it directly protects against Salmonella was worth a firm test. Mice and cultured human gut cells, called T84, formed the two test beds.

The yeast protected mice from the infection's worst effects. It also changed how T84 gut cells answered the germ. A probiotic with measured effects beats one sold on hope. The results support careful clinical trials of this yeast.
plos-pone-0009025:
Olivo Miotto and co-authors scanned the whole bird flu protein set for changes that fit it to humans, in PLOS ONE in 2010. H5N1 avian influenza worries health officials worldwide. It infects people rarely and does not yet pass between them well. That missing skill would need specific adaptive mutations in the virus.

The team mapped known adaptive changes across every flu A protein. They judged which mutations might enable human-to-human spread. The resulting chart highlights the genome spots watchers should monitor. Surveillance can then focus sequencing effort where a pandemic risk would first show.
plos-pone-0009125:
Clett Erridge and co-authors measured bacterial alarm molecules in inflamed mouse guts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inflammatory bowel diseases flare where gut bacteria meet immune sensors. Toll-like receptors are sensors that detect bacterial products. Products that trigger TLRs 2, 4, and 5 were the team's focus.

Mice were given colitis or ileitis, inflammations of colon and small intestine. Intestinal levels of those TLR stimulants rose markedly. The inflamed gut is flooded with more alarm molecules, not just more sensitive. That surge may feed the cycle that keeps bowel inflammation going. The measurements came from the inflamed tissue itself.
plos-pone-0009225:
Jan Kostecki, Haiming Li, Raymond Turner, and co-authors published this bacterial study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines the twin-arginine translocation pathway, a shipping route in bacteria. Unusually, this route exports proteins that are already fully folded. Studies in Escherichia coli had found many brief contacts between the route's parts.

The team used protein fragment complementation to watch those contacts directly. Two halves of a reporter protein were attached to pathway parts, lighting up only when the parts met. That let them visualize interactions all along the pathway in living cells. The method turns fleeting handshakes between proteins into something researchers can actually see.
plos-pone-0009325:
Aaron Marley and Mark von Zastrow published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dysbindin is a protein best known for building special cell compartments related to lysosomes. It had also been reported to lower the surface levels of D2 dopamine receptors in neurons. Those receptors belong to a huge family of drug targets.

The team showed that dysbindin sorts such receptors toward lysosomes after they are pulled inside. Lysosomes are the cell's shredders, so sorted receptors are destroyed rather than reused. That sorting job makes dysbindin a traffic controller for receptor numbers. It could matter wherever these receptors guide health or disease, well beyond dopamine.
plos-pone-0009425:
Ophélie Philipot and co-authors published this muscle study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Core Binding Factor, or CBF, is a gene switch made of two subunits. It was first known for running blood development. The team found it also works in skeletal muscle.

In muscle, CBF holds back the final step of differentiation. Lowering CBF lets muscle cells complete their maturation. A brake on the last step may keep a pool of cells in reserve until needed. The finding adds muscle to the list of tissues this versatile switch controls, and warns that its roles reach beyond blood.
plos-pone-0009525:
Frederic Heymans and colleagues screened sinus patients for bacterial toxin genes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus makes toxins that can act as superantigens, stirring the immune system hard. Such toxins were suspected of driving chronic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps. Those conditions clog and inflame the sinuses for months. The team tested patients for the toxin genes.

Carrying those genes showed no link to having the disease. It also showed no link to how severe the disease was. A null result like this still does real work. It steers the search for the true drivers of chronic sinus disease away from this suspect.
plos-pone-0009625:
Chen Xu and co-authors searched for antibodies against a tumor protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, CAIX, covers many human tumors of the surface tissue type. Healthy tissues of the same kind do not carry it. That contrast makes it a prized drug target. The team used phage display, a method that sifts huge libraries of antibody pieces, to find ones that bind CAIX's working domain.

The antibodies they found showed unusual and useful traits in tests. Binding the catalytic domain may do more than just tag the tumor. It could block the protein's acid handling work that tumors rely on. The study delivers candidate molecules for cancer therapy aimed with high precision.
plos-pone-0009725:
Cells tag worn-out proteins with ubiquitin so they can be cleared away. Zhuojin Xu and colleagues found an enzyme that removes those tags and linked it to another protein. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The enzyme is a deubiquitinating enzyme, one that strips ubiquitin tags off proteins. Tests showed it binds AGS3, a protein tied to signaling and cell division control. The pairing connects the cell's tag system with AGS3's signaling routes. New pairings like this help map how cells coordinate cleanup and division. AGS3 was known before, but this partner was new.
plos-pone-0009825:
As brains age, they change shape and lose some volume. Adriaan van Es and colleagues asked how total blood flow to the brain relates to those changes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain depends on steady flow to work well.

Total cerebral blood flow is the full stream of blood the brain receives. The authors compared flow levels with age-related changes seen in the brain. Blood supply and brain structure may rise or fall together with age. Understanding that link helps doctors read brain scans in older adults.
plos-pone-0009925:
The visual brain draws maps of what each eye sees, and those maps can sharpen with experience. Spencer Smith and Joshua Trachtenberg tested a surprising way to sharpen one eye's map in adult mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Retinotopic maps lay out the visual field point by point on the brain. Ipsilateral names the eye on the same side as the brain area studied. Removing the dominant contralateral eye increased the refinement of the other eye's map. Adult brains, it seems, keep more flexibility than once thought.
plos-pone-0010025:
The authors were Daniele Marmolino, Mario Manto, Fabio Acquaviva, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered Friedreich's ataxia, an inherited nerve disease. Cells from patients make too little of some antioxidant enzymes. They also fail to raise those defenses when harsh oxygen stress hits.

The team focused on a helper protein called PGC-1alpha, which was turned down in these cells. They linked that drop to the weak antioxidant response that may drive the disease. If the link holds, restoring that helper could be a route toward treatment worth testing further.
plos-pone-0010225:
The authors were Anneleen Daemen, Marco Signoretto, Olivier Gevaert, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study improved medical decisions drawn from microarray data. Microarray studies had been criticized for noise and poor overlap between gene signatures. Two labs could study the same disease and name different marker genes, which weakened trust in the method for diagnosis.

The team encoded known gene interaction data as graphs and fed them into their models. Adding prior biological knowledge as side information improved decision support. More accurate models could make gene tests for diagnosis and prognosis more dependable in the clinic.
plos-pone-0010325:
Michael Weisenhaus, Margaret Allen, Linghai Yang and co-workers wrote for PLOS ONE in 2010 about a brain protein named AKAP5. The protein acts like a scaffold inside nerve cells. It holds signaling molecules in place on the thin branches that receive messages. Among its partners are enzymes that add or remove chemical tags. Together they form tidy signaling groups near the cell surface.

The team changed the AKAP5 gene in mice and watched what followed. Without a normal scaffold, those signaling groups fell apart. Nerve cells then behaved oddly in electrical tests. The mice also acted differently in behavior tests. The study ties one scaffold protein to both cell signals and whole-animal behavior.
plos-pone-0010425:
Joel Miller and colleagues studied what students did when flu closed their school in PLOS ONE in 2010. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, many schools shut to slow spread. Closing only works if students actually stay apart. If they gather elsewhere, the benefit leaks away. The team surveyed behavior during one such closure.

They asked where students went and whom they met while school was out. Answers feed models that predict whether closures are worth their disruption. Families' real choices, not official hopes, decide that value. The study gives modelers grounded numbers instead of guesses. It may also guide advice to families in future closures. Public health plans work best when built on observed behavior.
plos-pone-0010525:
John James Wilson judged which gene regions best reveal moth and butterfly family trees in PLOS ONE in 2010. Butterflies and moths are hugely diverse, yet their bodies look frustratingly alike. That sameness gives taxonomists few traits to work with. DNA sequences have therefore become the main tool for sorting their relationships. Wilson compared DNA barcodes, short standard gene stretches, with other priority gene regions.

Not all gene regions carry equal signal about deep relationships. Choosing the wrong ones can build confident but false trees. Barcodes excel at naming species but may falter at deeper branches. This study helps researchers pick regions matched to their question. It also informs the global barcode library effort with a reality check.
plos-pone-0010625:
Victoria Horner and colleagues asked whether chimpanzees copy high-status group members, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People clearly do this: we imitate leaders, elders, and celebrities more than strangers. That bias was long claimed to be uniquely human.

Two model chimps were trained to open a puzzle box in different ways. One model had high rank and long group experience. Observers copied the respected model's method far more often. Prestige, it seems, guides ape learning too. The finding pushes a supposedly human habit much further back in our family history.
plos-pone-0010725:
Marie Beaume and colleagues mapped every RNA message made by MRSA across its daily cycle, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Staphylococcus aureus causes infections from skin boils to deadly blood poisoning. Its drug-resistant form, MRSA, is a hospital scourge. Gene use shifts as the bacteria grow and face stress.

The map records which messages appear, which strand they come from, and when. Messages rose and fell in waves tied to growth phase and stress. The full atlas exposes control points that stay hidden in single snapshots. Drug hunters can mine it for weak spots that only appear at certain hours of the bacterial day.
plos-pone-0010825:
Lynden Miles, Katarzyna Karpinska, Joanne Lumsden and others reported this psychology experiment in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was mental time travel, the human habit of drifting in thought into the past or the future. They wondered whether a feeling of moving through space could steer that inner journey, since thought and body motion may be closely linked.

Volunteers did a dull watch-keeping task meant to invite daydreaming while a display created vection, the illusion of self-motion. When the illusion moved them backward, their wandering thoughts leaned toward the past. Forward motion instead brought more thoughts about the future. Miles and colleagues show that a bodily sense of travel can push the mind's own travel through time, linking perception and imagination in a direct, testable way.
plos-pone-0010925:
Hervé Colinet, Siu Fai Lee and Ary Hoffmann published this insect study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called Frost switches on when fruit flies are stressed by cold, but no one had shown what it actually does for the fly. Candidate genes for temperature tolerance are often named without such proof, and the authors set out to supply it.

They confirmed that Frost activity surges during recovery from chill coma, rising manyfold within a couple of hours. Then they knocked the gene down in adult flies and timed how well the insects recovered after half a day in the cold. Weakening Frost impaired that recovery. Colinet and colleagues establish a rare, direct link between a named gene and whole-animal cold tolerance, a model for how insects may adapt as climates shift.
plos-pone-0011025:
Christine Akimana, Souhaila Al-Khodor and Yousef Abu Kwaik published this tularemia study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Francisella tularensis is a highly infectious bacterium, spread between mammals by biting arthropods, that escapes its initial cell compartment and multiplies freely in the cytosol. Bacterial genes needed for that escape were known, but the host factors, in both insects and mammals, were not.

The team ran a genome-wide RNA interference screen in fruit fly cells, silencing host genes in turn from a library of tens of thousands, to find which ones the bacterium depends on. Akimana and colleagues used the fly as a stand-in for both arthropod and mammalian hosts. Identifying host accomplices can reveal drug targets the bacterium cannot easily mutate away, a valuable strategy against a potential bioweapon agent.
plos-pone-0011125:
Von Kraus, Sacktor and Francis tested memory erasure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was not facts but learned movements, the kind stored as skill and habit. A protein called PKM zeta had been tied to keeping such memories in place over time.

Blocking that protein erased the stored movement memories in their tests. That result supports the idea that one molecule helps maintain long term memory. It raises hopes for treating disorders where bad memories drive symptoms, such as trauma related illness. It also raises care questions, since erasing memory in people would need great caution.
plos-pone-0011225:
Bojang, Akor, Bittaye and colleagues ran a malaria trial in children for PLOS ONE in 2010. Young children in high risk regions need preventive treatment before malaria strikes. The trial compared three drug combinations given at intervals, weighing safety, tolerability and how well each prevented illness.

Head to head data let policy makers pick a combination with the best balance for children. Preventive schedules only work if families can tolerate and complete them. The results guide malaria policy in the regions where the trial ran. Protecting children during peak season can save many young lives at modest cost.
plos-pone-0011325:
Pau, Okin and Gillespie tracked Hawaiian forest leaves in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tropical forests time their leaf growth to seasons, and drought can shift that timing. The team examined how leaf phenology in Hawaiian forests responds to seasonal drought and to the stronger droughts tied to El Nino events.

Different parts of the forest responded on different schedules rather than in step. That asynchrony reveals how sensitive tropical trees are to water stress, unevenly across a landscape. Climate science can use such detail to predict forest futures more honestly. Uneven responses also mean some trees may cope while neighbors fail.
plos-pone-0011425:
Christoph Schmid and Philipp Bucher reported in 2010 that leftovers of ancient viruses in human DNA can still serve the immune system. Nearly half the human genome came from viruses that settled into our ancestors' DNA long ago. One repeat family, MER41, was filed as junk until the team checked what proteins bind to it.

They found that MER41 repeats carry binding sites for STAT1, a switch protein that turns on immune defense genes, and those sites become active when the immune system is alerted. In other words, fossil virus DNA has been recycled into working immune wiring. The finding changes how genome leftovers should be judged. Sequences inherited from old infections may hold real control functions, and cataloguing them could reveal immune switches that standard gene maps have missed.
plos-pone-0011525:
Robert Caesar and co-authors compared mouse fat depots in 2010 with two profiling methods at once. Fat is not one tissue: fat under the skin, fat around the reproductive organs, and fat in the gut lining behave differently and carry different health risks. The team combined gene activity profiling with lipid profiling, a census of fat molecules, across the three depots.

The combined view revealed marked functional differences among depots that either method alone would have understated. Where fat sits thus changes what it does, at the level of both its genes and its chemistry. That explains a clinical fact doctors have long seen: belly fat predicts disease far better than the same weight carried under the skin. Weight research that ignores depot identity, the paper argues, averages away the very differences that drive risk.
plos-pone-0011625:
Fahmy Aboul-Enein and co-authors used advanced brain scans in multiple sclerosis patients, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In this disease, insulation around nerve fibres is lost and the fibres themselves decay. Damage can hide in white matter that still looks normal on standard scans, a region doctors call normal-appearing white matter.

With a strong three-tesla scanner, the team measured a brain chemical called NAA, which falls when nerve fibres are injured. Levels were reduced in the normal-looking tissue, and the drop marked disease progression. Measuring this chemical gives doctors a way to track hidden damage and judge whether patients are worsening.
plos-pone-0011725:
Rodrigo Oliveira and co-authors simulated chemical neighbourhoods inside neurons, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The messenger cAMP and its main partner, protein kinase A, are vital for synaptic plasticity, the strengthening of connections behind learning. For precision, cAMP must activate its partner only in tiny local zones, despite spreading very fast.

Large-scale stochastic simulations showed that type 4 phosphodiesterase enzymes, which break down cAMP, create those microdomains. By chewing up the messenger at the edges, the enzymes fence it into pockets. The models reveal how cells achieve precise signalling with a fast-moving molecule.
plos-pone-0011825:
Cornelia Kiank and co-authors traced a chemical path from mental stress to weaker defences, in PLOS ONE in 2010. It is more and more clear that mental strain shapes both inflammation and mood. The team asked whether stress, given as sound plus restraint, switches on an enzyme called IDO1 that breaks down the amino acid tryptophan.

They found stress-driven, IDO1-based breakdown of tryptophan, with clear links to immune damping in mice and in humans. Loss of tryptophan leaves immune cells short of a fuel they need. Charting this path may suggest practical ways to protect stressed patients from serious infection.
plos-pone-0011925:
Mariana Bollo and co-workers reported in 2010 on a rescue circuit that eases stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment. When misfolded proteins pile up in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell answers with the unfolded protein response, which first slows new protein making. Calcium release is part of that early response, but its helpers were unclear.

The team found that calcineurin, a calcium-driven enzyme, partners with PERK, a stress sensor, and removes a phosphate from calnexin, a folding helper, thereby relieving the stress. The same relief circuit appears in both mammals and frogs. A pathway shared across such distant animals is likely an old and core part of cell survival.
plos-pone-0012025:
Amy Maher and co-workers found in 2010 a clear sex difference in the fat-burning machinery of human muscle. Women are known to oxidize more fat during endurance exercise and to resist some fat-related metabolic faults better than men. Several groups had reported differences in gene messages for fat-burning enzymes.

The team measured the enzymes themselves and found women's skeletal muscle carries more of the beta-oxidation proteins, which burn fatty acids for energy. Protein levels are the step closest to actual capacity, so the result firms up the explanation for women's endurance advantage. It also argues for sex-specific thinking in exercise and metabolic disease research.
plos-pone-0012125:
Wenming Bai, Fen Xun, Yang Li, and colleagues studied grass roots on the Inner Mongolian steppe for PLOS ONE in 2010. How long a root lives decides how well a plant gathers water and nutrients and how much carbon stays in the soil. Most past work looked at non-clonal plants, but this grass spreads through underground stems that link many shoots into one network.

Cutting those underground links changed the roots' fate: severed roots lived longer. A root cut off from the network may be kept alive as the plant's own lifeline rather than being shed. The result matters for managing grasslands that feed livestock and store carbon across a huge region of Asia.
plos-pone-0012225:
Arunava Dasgupta, Kamakshi Sureka, Devrani Mitra, and co-authors studied a peptide transporter of the tuberculosis bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. The germ's genome carries two such transporters, pumps that pull small protein pieces into the cell. Transporters in this family share a standard design of membrane parts, energy-burning parts, and a catcher that grabs the cargo.

The team showed one of these transporters also shapes how infected immune cells respond, changing the alarm signals they release and whether they die. A pump that doubles as an immune manipulator is a richer drug target than a pump alone. Tuberculosis treatment is long and failing more often, so each weakness of this kind counts.
plos-pone-0012325:
Kristel Kemper, Marc Tol, and Jan Paul Medema catalogued the message variants of a stem cell marker in mouse tissues, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prominin-1 is best known as a badge worn by stem cells, including cancer stem cells, but it also appears on many mature cells. The mouse gene is heavily spliced into eight known variants, and which tissues use which variant had not been systematically mapped.

Knowing the variant map matters because antibodies used to fish out stem cells may see only some variants and miss others. A marker misread is a stem cell population miscounted, which can bend the conclusions of cancer and regeneration studies alike. Reference work like this keeps a whole field's sorting honest.
plos-pone-0012425:
Carolina Del Debbio, Sudha Balasubramanian, Sowmya Parameswaran and colleagues coaxed support cells in the retina to rebuild light sensors, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Müller cells keep the retina healthy, and in fish they can also spawn new neurons after injury. Mammals mostly lack that gift, but signals named Notch and Wnt might wake it.

Working in adult mammalian retina, the team showed these signals can push Müller cells to produce new rod photoreceptors, the cells used for night vision. Regrowing rods from the eye's own cells is a long-sought goal for treating blindness from retinal disease. The study marks which signals to tune next.
plos-pone-0012525:
Jeanne Serb, Megan Orr, Heather Greenlee and colleagues used ancient shared gene modules to sharpen big gene studies, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Large expression studies were expected to reveal the networks behind complex traits, but the flood of data often blurred the signal. Modules of genes conserved across evolution — old, trusted circuits — might serve as anchors.

The team used those conserved modules to structure queries of high-throughput expression data, recovering clearer network patterns. Borrowing evolution's quality control is a smart filter for noisy modern data. The strategy can help any field drowning in gene lists, from crop science to medicine.
plos-pone-0012625:
Santos, Arroyo-Rodriguez, Moreno and co-authors measured what forest cutting does to the family tree of trees. In Brazil's Atlantic Forest, clearing has left small, broken patches with long exposed edges. Their 2010 study used a large plant survey from one badly fragmented landscape.

They asked whether the tree species left near edges are a random sample of the original set, or a skewed one. Losing whole branches of the tree family tree means losing unique traits built over ages. Their findings help planners judge which fragments most need protection and repair.
plos-pone-0012725:
Soanes and Talbot compared whole genomes to ask whether fungi carry a class of immune sensors found in plants and animals. In both kingdoms, proteins with leucine-rich repeats spot germ features and raise the first line of defence. Their 2010 search through fungal genomes looked for the same pattern-recognition family.

They report this sensor class is absent across the fungi. Fungi must therefore guard themselves by other means, a real puzzle given their constant contact with microbes. The gap reshapes how scientists think the defence systems of each kingdom evolved.
plos-pone-0012825:
Hedborg, Fischer-Colbrie, Ostlin and co-authors showed that low oxygen can push a childhood tumour toward a hormone-making form. Neuroblastoma grows from early sympathetic nerve tissue and can mature into milder forms. A high power to differentiate is one of its known hallmarks.

Their 2010 study found that when growth is slowed by limited diffusion and oxygen, the cells switch on a secretory protein, NESP55, and other marks of the chromaffin cell type. Tumour surroundings can thus steer the cancer's character. That steering may be usable in treatment design.
plos-pone-0332725:
Arman Khosravi and Seyed Jafar Sadjadi built an investing framework meant to survive its own forecasting errors. Classic portfolio maths wobbles badly when return guesses are slightly off and tends to pile into a few assets. Their model plans over several periods, assumes returns live inside a budgeted range of doubt rather than at a point. It adds an entropy term that mathematically forces the money to spread out.

Rebalanced over six years on sixty large American stocks across all major sectors, the framework matched strong benchmarks on risk-adjusted returns. It dodged their worst habits: far less concentration than tail-risk models, far less frantic trading, and shallower falls in crashes and wild recoveries. The authors pitch it to institutions that need a portfolio rule both cautious and practical to run.
plos-pone-0336725:
Marzena Syper-Jędrzejak and colleagues surveyed four hundred forty-six young Poles aged nineteen to twenty-two, the oldest edge of Generation Alpha, about what they expect from employers. Mountains of writing cover earlier generations at work; the youngest entrants are nearly unstudied. The 2026 survey weighed two expectation families, good pay and workplace well-being, and asked whether feeling personally in control links them.

Respondents wanted both: solid earnings and an employer who protects well-being, and the two wishes were indeed connected, with those chasing good pay also hunting for healthy workplaces. A strong sense of personal agency, however, could not be confirmed as the bridge between them. The study sketches priorities for employers hiring the newest generation.
plos-pone-0339225:
Huajie Xiong and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on steering swarms of drones through unknown, obstacle-filled places when the drones cannot talk to each other. Communication limits and small onboard computers make swarm navigation hard, exactly in the disaster settings where swarms would help most. Their framework splits the job in two: an upper planner charting global routes with classic search, and a lower layer where each drone navigates and dodges alone.

The lower layer uses a strengthened feature network trained in two stages, traditional optimization then reinforcement learning, so drones learn robust avoidance. In simulations built on the standard ROS robotics framework, multiple drones navigated complex unknown environments autonomously with no inter-drone communication at all. The authors report clear advantages over existing approaches. Swarms, the design suggests, can stay capable even when radios fail or are jammed, if each drone is smart enough alone.
plos-pone-0341525:
Mahdi Hamzaoui led a team of five authors building vision AI for fish farms, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fish farms need reliable eyes underwater, where light is poor and pens are crowded. Their framework, YOLO-CBNet, adds attention to a fast detection model to recognize fish in aquaculture settings.

Hamzaoui's model keeps working in murky water and dense schools, where ordinary vision systems give up. Reliable fish detection supports counting, health checks, and feeding control, all of which decide a farm's profit and the fish's welfare. Attention helps the model focus on fish rather than nets, shadows, and debris. Farms produce a growing share of the world's fish, so tools that work in real pen conditions matter well beyond one lab.
plos-pone-0343425:
Shervin Mossavarali and his team checked more than twenty-four hundred old folk in Iran. All took part in a health plan for the old in Bushehr. The team built three scores from fat, blood sugar, and blood fats. Each score is meant to flag a deep fault in how the body uses food fuel. They then set the scores next to tests of mind and recall.

Near two in three showed some loss of mind skill. One score, tied to deep belly fat, flagged loss in men. In women, the same score at a mid rank looked like a shield on one test. The team calls that clash a sign that more than fuel faults drive loss of mind.
plos-pone-0344925:
Kang Leng and colleagues built a risk score for the most common kind of kidney cancer out of genes tied to natural killer cells, the immune system's roving tumour hunters. Single-cell data from tumours and nearby tissue revealed how the tumour neighbourhood is remodelled and which killer cell groups talk most to their surroundings. A network method distilled twelve core genes, and a survival model was trained and checked in separate patient collections.

One gene stood out as the engine. Silencing it in kidney cancer cells slowed their growth and movement in the lab, and its levels tracked with how immunologically visible the tumours were. The twelve-gene score predicted patient outcomes reliably across datasets. The authors offer both the score and its lead gene as tools for sorting patients and designing targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0345125:
Afridi Rahman Bondhon and Emon Kumar Dey built an explainable system for labeling three-dimensional laser scans of terrain and cities, point by point. Stacking several classifiers usually lifts accuracy but buries the reasoning. Their framework stacks multiple base learners under a simple final model and then applies explanation tools to show which features drove each decision.

On two benchmark datasets the stack labeled points with accuracy above ninety percent. The explanations also revealed which input features could be dropped, cutting training time by at least seven percent without losing accuracy. For city planning and environmental monitoring, a segmentation tool that can justify itself is easier to audit and trust than a slightly stronger black box.
plos-pone-0345325:
Gabrielle C. Smith and three co-workers charted past work on the kin who care for women with ovarian cancer. This cancer kills more women than most womb-area ills. Yet the kin who nurse these women are oft left out of the tale. The team sifted scores of finds and kept thirty-two. They read each one with care and drew out the themes.

Three themes stood tall. First, the health of the kin's own minds, with grief and stress ills in the mix. Next, the loads they bear: more care tasks, cash strain, lone days, and poor self care. Last, the aids that help, chiefly faith and the backing of kin and friends. The team calls for aid built for these carers.
plos-pone-0346625:
Emelie Stotzer and colleagues interviewed eighteen managers in Swedish maternity care about leading their units through the third wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. Managers had to reorganize care for a new disease, limit infection spread, and keep services running despite severe staff shortages. The interviews took place in spring 2021 across units at different levels.

Managers described inventing new routines quickly, often with little information and no time to think decisions through. Support from peers helped them cope with the pressure. Reading their accounts through an implementation framework shows which parts of the system bent and which held. The lessons apply to any hospital service that must keep delivering care during a crisis.
plos-pone-0346925:
Sainadh Singh Kshatri and colleagues asked whether new wide-bandgap semiconductors, silicon carbide and gallium nitride devices, make solar inverters last longer than conventional silicon switches. Inverters are the weak link in rooftop solar systems.
