Their 2026 study simulated a three-kilowatt inverter under a full year of real Indian sunlight and temperature, minute by minute, and ran thousands of randomised lifetime trials.

The advanced devices cut switching losses by about forty percent against standard transistors, promising both higher efficiency and longer service life before ten percent of units fail. The authors argue that reliability, not just efficiency, should drive inverter design as solar spreads through hot climates.
plos-pone-0347925:
Caixeta, Oliveira, and de Melo used DNA barcoding to survey deep-sea fish off southern Brazil in a 2026 study. The deep sea holds a large share of fish kinds, yet sampling is hard and many groups are poorly known. Samples came from research cruises over the continental slope, from shallow slope depths down to much deeper water.

Gene reads covered more than one hundred species across many families and orders. Most samples could be named to species, and the rest at least to group. Genetic gaps between species were wide, which helps tell look-alike fish apart. The team also provided first gene records for some kinds, filling blanks in the map of Atlantic deep-sea life.
plos-pone-0348125:
Aboubacar Cherif and colleagues used a national American readmissions database to see whether rectal cancer patients can safely leave hospital within three days of major bowel surgery. Roughly forty thousand patients who had the operation between 2016 and 2021 were split into early and routine discharge groups, with statistical balancing to make the comparison fair.

About a quarter went home early. After adjustment, those patients were readmitted less often and cost the system several thousand dollars less per case, with no sign of higher death rates. Early leavers tended to be younger and to have had keyhole surgery. The authors support wider use of fast-track recovery pathways for suitable patients.
plos-pone-0348625:
Erika Hurtado-Salgado and colleagues surveyed adults and health workers in three Mexican states about what they know and do regarding adult vaccination. Vaccines protect at every age, yet adult coverage lags worldwide, partly from thin knowledge and hesitation. More than eleven hundred adults and over two hundred health professionals answered in late 2024, with questions on diseases including shingles, flu, whooping cough, and RSV.

Almost all adults agreed vaccines are important, a strong foundation to build on. The survey dug into where knowledge thins and how answers differ by age, sex, and other traits, and health workers were asked the same questions. Campaigns fail when they guess at the gap; measuring knowledge, attitudes, and habits on both sides of the clinic door shows where the real barriers sit.
plos-pone-0349025:
Hari Krismanuel and Purnamawati Tjhin ran a natural experiment on a decade of breathing polluted city air. They compared healthy older Indonesians who had lived at least ten years in a high-pollution Jakarta neighbourhood with peers in a cleaner rural area. All one hundred and one participants were non-smokers of normal weight, a filter meant to isolate the air itself. Standardised breathing tests measured how much air their lungs could move.

City dwellers scored significantly lower on both main lung measures, while the ratio between them stayed normal, a pattern pointing to stiffened, smaller-volume lungs rather than blocked airways. Where a person lived was the only clear predictor once other factors were adjusted. The authors frame the work as precision public health: proof that chronic fine-particle exposure quietly erodes lung capacity in later life.
plos-pone-0349225:
Yan Qin and a large team surveyed nearly six hundred art students at a Chinese university about why some of them succeed in English while others stall. Art majors often struggle with English, squeezed by studio training and different study habits. The team tested a chain of ideas from motivation theory: students who see real value in English engage more, procrastinate less, and finally achieve more.

The chain held up. Valuing English did not lift grades directly, but it raised engagement, engaged students delayed less, and less delay led to better results. Confidence strengthened the link, since engaged students who believed in themselves procrastinated least. Procrastination alone carried no effect. The authors advise teachers of art students to build engagement and confidence first, rather than simply preaching the value of English.
plos-pone-0349625:
I. Noureen and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One theoretical physics paper on building mathematical models of charged, ultra-dense stars in a modified theory of gravity. In f(R) gravity, Einstein's equations gain extra terms, and finding exact stellar solutions requires clever constraints. The authors model the star's interior with pressures that differ by direction, impose a linear relation between pressure and density, and add two geometric conditions.

Those conditions reduce the system to a single generating equation for the energy density, from which pressures and the pressure imbalance follow. A standard equation transformation then lets whole families of solutions be generated from one known solution. The paper is a methods contribution, giving relativists a systematic recipe for charged star models in this gravity theory.
plos-pone-0349825:
Jesus E Juarez Casillas and colleagues trained deep learning on prostate scans to forecast spread of prostate cancer. A special PET scan lights up prostate tissue. Models learned from the main tumour alone to spot hidden spread present at diagnosis, on the logic that early later spread comes from disease already seeded. Scan patterns were joined with clinical and imaging data.

Combined models reached discrimination near eighty two percent for present spread and about eighty four percent for later spread. Scan learning carried the largest weight in the combined score. Forecasting spread from the main tumour alone could help doctors choose stronger first treatment for men whose scans look local but whose risk runs high.
plos-pone-0350025:
Kyung-In Joung and colleagues piloted a diabetes program run by community pharmacies in South Korea, built around continuous glucose monitors. Thirty adults with type 2 diabetes that was not well controlled, all on oral medicines, joined the twelve-week program at eleven pharmacies. Pharmacists combined medicine advice with exercise and nutrition coaching, guided by live glucose data.

Everyone finished the program, and just over a third hit the combined goal of good average sugar, a meaningful drop, and most time spent in the target range. Average blood sugar fell clearly and time in range rose. A pilot this small cannot settle the model, but it shows pharmacy-led care with glucose sensors is workable and promising.
plos-pone-0350125:
Tanja Tomašević, Vladimir Petrović, and co-authors analyzed binge drinking among adults in Serbia's Vojvodina province using a new regional risk-factor surveillance system. Heavy episodic drinking drives injuries and chronic disease, yet local data were thin. Their 2026 study surveyed nearly four thousand health center users across all forty-four primary care centers in the province during 2024, with questions adapted from an American survey system.

About nineteen in every hundred adults reported binge drinking. Men had more than four times the odds of women, and younger adults far outdrank those over sixty-five. Among women, never having married, poorer material status, and smoking all raised the odds, while physically active men also drank more heavily. The authors back continuous regional surveillance to keep these patterns in view.
plos-pone-0350325:
Meenu Mariya James and colleagues mapped dengue fever across Indian districts from 2010 to 2022 by climate zone. Dengue has grown steadily in India, yet district level climate patterns were unclear. Districts were grouped into climate types, trends were fitted over time, and map tests hunted for clusters and hot spots of cases.

Spread varied sharply between districts. Fastest growth appeared in some cool zones, including tundra like and mild summer zones, with yearly rises near or above doubling in the steepest fits. Warm tropical zones kept high burdens too. Dengue pushing into cooler districts, the authors warn, means control plans built for hot lowlands alone will fall behind.
plos-pone-0350625:
Isa Spiero and colleagues compared Dutch language models for pulling signs and symptoms from primary care notes. Health records hold rich detail in free text, but hand coding is slow. Two local models were trained as direct classifiers on hand labelled notes about chest infections, with training sizes varied to find how much labelled data is enough.

Direct classifiers scored well, led by the medical tuned model. Prompt style use scored poorly for both models. Rare symptoms and missing mentions dragged scores down. About eight hundred labelled examples marked the floor for solid results. Local language models, the work shows, can unlock Dutch record text for research when labelled data are sufficient.
plos-pone-0350825:
Lauren Wakefield and co-authors built a computer tool for a hard problem on deer farms. A wasting disease spreads fast among penned deer. Once it takes hold, it is nearly impossible to remove. Testing only part of a herd can miss it in the early stage. A clean test result can leave false comfort.

Their tool works backward from a farm's own records. It uses herd makeup, animal movements, and past test results. From these it estimates the chance that disease hides in the herd unseen. That turns a bare negative result into a graded risk judgment. Farmers and officials can then decide about sales and movement with clearer eyes.
plos-pone-0350925:
Yisheng Yang and colleagues offer a smarter design method for the heavy pressure vessels inside wind tunnels. Tunnels that test aircraft at high speed need vessels that hold huge pressure without needless weight. Older design leans on habit and heavy safety margins, while pure data models falter when conditions change. Their method blends written design rules into a layered prediction model.

On a real tunnel section, the method cut vessel weight by about one quarter while keeping strength, and ran each design loop vastly faster than full simulation. Rule guided sampling and mixed quality training data drove the gains. Builders of test rigs and other pressure gear could design lighter, faster, and with more confidence.
plos-pone-0351125:
Msila and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask small-scale farmers in South Africa's Limpopo Province what would move them to change how they use water as the climate shifts. Most of the surveyed maize growers farm for their living, many are older, and most have some secondary schooling. Intentions were read through a standard behavior model with three drivers.

All three drivers mattered. A positive attitude toward adapting was the strongest push, followed by social norms, meaning what farmers believe people around them expect. Feeling able to adapt helped too, but less. In plain terms, farmers who saw adaptation as wise, felt backed by their community, and believed they could manage it were the ones planning to change. The authors advise climate programs to work on attitudes and community backing, not only on handing out technology, since intention is the doorway to action.
plos-pone-0351425:
Retirement reshapes health, mood, friendships, money, and purpose all at once. Yasin M Yasin and colleagues lay out a plan, in PLOS One in 2026, for an umbrella review that gathers earlier systematic reviews on what shapes well-being among retired older adults.

No findings are reported, because this is a protocol. The team will search five major databases for reviews published since 2015, then check their quality with an established checklist. Two reviewers will screen and extract data separately. The finished synthesis aims to show which factors and which kinds of support most deserve attention from planners and communities.
plos-pone-0351625:
Luca Alessandri and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One archaeology study dating an ancient salt production site near Rome by reading the magnetism locked into its kiln and pottery. Radiocarbon dating fails at this site because its age falls on a flat stretch of the calibration curve, and its plain jars offer few clues. Magnetic measurements gave two possible windows in the early first millennium BCE.

Combined with pottery styles and radiocarbon results, the magnetic dates let the team split the site's main area into three occupation phases spanning roughly two centuries. The authors argue that archaeomagnetic dating deserves wider use at sites where radiocarbon goes blurry, especially when several methods can be cross-checked against each other.
plos-pone-0351725:
Hamidreza Farzan and Maryam Koushkie Jahromi test a single dose of a medicinal mushroom extract on young men's brains and bodies around hard exercise, in this 2026 PLOS ONE trial. Twelve recreationally active men cycled to exhaustion twice, once after a gram of Cordyceps militaris extract and once after a starch placebo, in random order a week apart. Reaction time on a colour-word task and oxygen use were measured before and after each ride.

After exercise, reaction times were significantly faster on the mushroom day, while accuracy stayed at ceiling in both. Resting oxygen uptake also ran higher with the extract, though peak exercise values did not change. One dose, the authors conclude, sharpens the post-exercise mind without touching endurance itself.
plos-pone-0351925:
Jiale He and colleagues simulated what happens when farmers water dry fields with groundwater rich in arsenic, a poison that builds up in soil. Their test soil came from the Kuitun River Basin in Xinjiang, China. By changing evaporation, acidity, and salt in the water, they watched how arsenic moved through the soil profile, using special membranes to picture its spread.

All three water traits steered the arsenic. Under weak evaporation it traveled farther, both down and sideways, through the topsoil. More alkaline and saltier water pushed it deeper from the surface layer. For dry regions that must irrigate with tainted groundwater, the results flag which water conditions let arsenic sink toward roots and groundwater, and argue for managing water chemistry, not just water quantity.
plos-pone-0352025:
Sue Jordan and co-authors study in 2026 whether children in Europe born with major birth defects die more often when their families are poorer. Linked records from registers in seven countries covered tens of thousands of such children, followed to age one and to age ten. Social position was measured by mother schooling or by area hardship, depending on country.

Death was more common among the most deprived than the least deprived at both ages, and the gap was stronger after infancy than in the first year. Clear gaps reached statistical strength in only some registers. Children of mothers from outside the European Union also died more often. More support for the poorest is urged.
plos-pone-0352325:
Nana Zhou and four colleagues teach ground robots to label scenes they have never been trained on. Their 2026 study targets unstructured environments: rubble, scrub, disaster ground. Ordinary segmentation models need retraining for each new setting. Their framework instead leans on a vision-language model that already links images to words. Deep prompt tuning nudges the image encoder toward rough terrain. The zero-shot ability of the base model survives the tuning.

An ensemble of text prompts, tailored to wild settings, sharpens the matching. Global and local features from both encoders are combined to align words with the right pixels. Vehicles that can segment an unseen hillside into rock, brush, and path without new training data are far more deployable. The design aims squarely at rescue and exploration robots, which never know what terrain waits around the next bend.
plos-pone-0353125:
Hadj-Abo and colleagues, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, compare people with type 1 diabetes who use automated insulin delivery with those who do not. These systems link a glucose sensor to a pump that adjusts insulin on its own. Research has often checked blood sugar outcomes while asking less about daily distress.

About one hundred seventy people answered a survey on blood sugar control and diabetes distress, and twelve were interviewed in depth. Users of the automated systems had lower long-term blood sugar readings and lower distress on every scale measured. The biggest gaps were in feeling burdened by daily management and feeling powerless. Interviews suggested the systems ease the constant mental work of dosing. Distress about low blood sugar differed less, which the authors link to wide use of glucose sensors in both groups. They argue that judging diabetes technology should weigh peace of mind alongside numbers.
plos-pone-0353525:
Wang and colleagues tested a drug for sepsis-linked lung injury in rats in a 2026 study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, often floods and scars the lungs. Rats given the drug at three dose levels were compared with untreated sick rats and healthy controls.

Treated rats survived at higher rates, and the benefit grew with dose. Lung swelling, injury scores, and inflammatory signals fell at medium and high doses. A cell-death pathway driven by iron also weakened, tied to a protective gene chain the drug switched on. Low doses helped only a few measures. The dose pattern supports further study of the drug for this lung complication.
plos-pone-0353725:
An editorial note from The PLOS One Editors in 2026 addresses a cancer study about a platinum drug and cell death in a rare chest cancer. Readers should note this flag before trusting the original findings. After publication, concerns were raised that several figure panels seemed to overlap with one another or with panels in related papers.

Editors reviewed the original underlying images supplied by the authors. Following that review, the journal states that it considers the concerns resolved. The note also records that raw data files were not shared as the article's data statement had promised. Readers get the full list of questioned panels, so they can judge the record for themselves.
plos-pone-0354125:
Emily Eichenlaub and co-authors test in 2026 whether neck posture and neck braces change how young healthy adults keep balance while walking. A stiff or forward bent neck is common in an ageing spine disease that also harms walking. Volunteers walked in braces set to different neck shapes while a treadmill jolted them or while they stepped sideways to a target.

Jolts shrank stability in all conditions, but only braced walking tipped into measured instability in one direction. Side stepping stayed accurate except when the brace bent the neck forward and the target lay far away. The authors advise fall risk teaching for people given neck immobilisation.
plos-pone-0354425:
Fumiyo Nakagawa led a team of eight authors mapping how people who live with HIV in Britain use health services, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. With good treatment, HIV is now a long-term condition, but not everyone uses services equally. The team compared use across social and demographic groups.

Nakagawa's patterns reveal who is underserved, by age, background, or circumstance. Unequal use can mean missed chances to keep the virus suppressed and catch other illnesses early. The NHS aims for equal care, so maps like this show where outreach must reach further. The study gives service planners UK-specific evidence instead of assumptions imported from other health systems.
plos-pone-0354525:
De Herdt and colleagues, in 2026, study a drug target that may help repair myelin, the coating that speeds signals along nerve fibers. Loss of myelin is a core harm in multiple sclerosis. A receptor called GPR17 stays switched on in young myelin-making cells after injury, and that may block them from maturing.

The team first checked human brain tissue from people with multiple sclerosis and found more of these receptor-marked cells near damaged areas. They then gave mice with toxin-caused myelin loss a new drug that blocks GPR17 by mouth. Treated mice showed faster repair in key brain and optic nerve areas. Their memory and visual signals also recovered. The results point to blocking this receptor as a possible route toward repair-focused treatment, though the work is still in animals.
plos-pone-0354725:
Mushuai Hao, Haonan Qi, Liang Zhao, and Wei Han published this 2026 training study on how the lowering speed of a squat shapes strength gains. Thirty sports students trained twice weekly for eight weeks at one of three tempos: a slow four-second lowering, a two-second lowering, or a self-chosen rhythm. Strength, sprinting, and jumping were tested before and after.

All groups grew stronger, and the two-second tempo showed the friendliest trend, boosting explosive jumping most. The slow group actually lost some spring-based explosiveness despite gaining strength. Hao advises matching tempo to the quality being trained.
plos-pone-0354825:
Uchhwas Banik and five colleagues published this 2026 study turning waste plastic into fuel in Bangladesh, where plastic use keeps climbing. They heated four common plastics without oxygen, a process called pyrolysis, and tuned the temperature for each type to draw off the most liquid oil and char.

Polypropylene gave the richest oil yield, and the liquids resembled familiar fuels in their carbon makeup. The leftover char was checked for industrial uses as well. Banik presents tuned pyrolysis as a practical route for cutting plastic waste while recovering energy from it.
plos-pone-0354925:
Lixia Lin and five colleagues published this 2026 plant study on a valued Chinese medicinal herb that wilts in heat. They grew the plant at four temperatures, from mild to severely hot, and tracked leaf health, chemistry, and protein changes to see how it copes and where it fails.

Heat cut photosynthesis, lowered green pigment, and raised signs of cell damage. Hundreds of proteins shifted, including ones for daily rhythms, antioxidant defense, and the cell's recycling system, which seemed to protect tissue. Lin's findings give breeders and growers a starting map for raising heat tolerance in a crop that warming summers now threaten.
plos-pone-0355125:
Victoria Ballén led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of drug-resistant E. coli in Barcelona's water treatment plants. They collected well over a hundred resistant strains across two wastewater plants and one drinking water plant, then read their genomes and tested drug resistance, film-forming ability, and virulence genes.

Treatment lowered bacteria counts, yet most strains still resisted several drugs, and some dangerous clones survived into reclaimed water. One resistant strain even appeared at the drinking water plant's inlet. Ballén argues water systems belong inside resistance surveillance, not outside it.
plos-pone-0355625:
Masaaki Kuwajima and colleagues built a new lab animal for brain research: a rat missing a protein called synaptopodin. Their 2026 paper explains that the protein helps organize tiny structures inside nerve cells that support learning signals. Mice without it existed already, but rats offer steadier timing for when learning circuits switch on, which can make experiments cleaner.

The engineered rats lived and kept normal kidney function, though they grew slightly smaller than usual. Under strong microscopes, their brain cells lacked two small internal structures that depend on the protein, and a key learning signal in the memory region ran weaker. Kuwajima and co-authors present the rat as a shared tool for studying growth, behavior, and memory.
plos-pone-0355725:
Li-Feng Hung and four colleagues track drug-resistant gut bacteria in emergency department patients across the rise and fall of Taiwan's COVID-19 Omicron wave, in this 2026 study. Their hospital's records covered more than eight hundred adults with bloodstream infections from a bacterial family that includes E. coli, about a third of them multidrug-resistant. The team divided the year into pre-peak, peak, and post-peak stages and searched broadly for stage-specific risk factors.

Which variables accompanied resistance changed with the stage: advanced age and red-cell measures early on, liver and platelet values at the peak, and white-cell measures afterward. Resistance trends also split by species, one notorious pathogen gaining ground against a key antibiotic while E. coli's resistance eased against several drugs. The authors argue stewardship and risk checks should adapt as a pandemic moves through its phases.
plos-pone-0356725:
Dipo Aldila and coauthors published a 2026 mathematical modeling study in PLOS ONE on hepatitis B and D, two linked liver viruses. Hepatitis D cannot spread on its own; it infects only people already carrying hepatitis B, through what is called superinfection, and it makes outcomes far worse. Their model splits a population into susceptible, vaccinated, infected, recovered, chronic, and doubly infected groups, with vaccination and liver transplantation as controls.

The analysis shows familiar threshold behavior: when the basic reproduction number sits below one, the disease-free state is stable and infection dies out. Above it, two kinds of settled states appear, with and without hepatitis D. A global sensitivity analysis found vaccination coverage and vaccine strength dominate that threshold number. Transplantation does not move the threshold, but it shrinks outbreaks and delays their peaks. Vaccine effort, they argue, is the master lever, with transplantation buying time and sparing severe cases.
plos-pone-0356825:
Ravian Wettstein and colleagues follow adults with attention deficit disorder for years. Their trial had added talking therapy to medication and education. The question now is whether the therapy pays off late, in quality of life. Early results had shown no added benefit right after treatment, but coping skills might ripen slowly. From the original cohort of several hundred, about a quarter completed the long follow-up survey several years later, rating life quality on a standard scale.

Life quality rose sharply by the end of the original treatment in both groups, then eased back over the years while staying above the starting point. No measure separated the therapy group from the education-only group at any point. Wettstein and colleagues conclude this dataset gives no sign of a delayed therapy dividend, though early gains themselves partly lasted.
plos-pone-0357025:
Marjolijn Carolien Sales and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting right heart failure after a patient receives a durable left ventricular assist device, a heart pump. When the heart's right side fails after surgery, patients can crash, so surgeons lean on risk scores rarely validated head to head. They applied six established scores to just over a hundred patients at one center, using a standard registry definition.

About one patient in five developed moderate-to-severe right heart failure. The established scores discriminated weakly to moderately; one scored worse than chance, while a postoperative version performed best of them. An exploratory five-variable model built by the team, using sickness level, liver markers, and pressure measurements, appeared much stronger, and held up after internal bootstrap checks. Derived and tested in the same small cohort, it needs outside validation before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0357125:
Hanizah Mohd Yusoff and coauthors published a 2026 nationwide survey in PLOS ONE on how Long COVID harms the working lives of factory workers in Malaysia. Close to eight hundred workers who had previously caught COVID filled in questionnaires on lingering symptoms, quality of working life, productivity, and safety. The authors then looked for which personal, symptom, job, and workplace factors tracked with poor work outcomes.

About a quarter of workers with Long COVID reported poor quality of working life. Roughly two in five admitted working while sick, about one in eight had taken sickness absences, and a small share reported safety problems. Risk rose with older age, smoking, more symptoms, shift work, chemical handling, confined spaces, noise, and manual lifting. Factories without a sickness absence policy fared markedly worse. The authors argue employers need formal absence policies and hazard controls aimed at this group, not just general wellness advice.
plos-pone-0357625:
Anqi Hu and seven colleagues compare gut microbes in giant pandas that pace and sway repetitively with those that do not, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such stereotypic behavior troubles captive pandas, and gut microbes are known to influence the brain in other animals. The team watched fifteen captive pandas, then sequenced the bacteria in their droppings using two methods to build both a species list and a functional profile.

Pandas showing the behavior carried a distinctly different gut community, a pattern the authors describe as imbalance. One Serratia species was far more common in them, several Clostridium species trended upward, and a friendly Enterococcus species went the other way. Some of the shifted bacteria touch pathways that make brain signaling chemicals. The panda findings cannot prove cause, but they open a new angle on managing a stubborn welfare problem in zoos.
plos-pone-0357725:
Carla Blázquez-Fernández, Paloma Lanza-León, and David Cantarero-Prieto published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on social isolation and health behavior across generations in Europe. Isolation is a known health risk in old age, but its effects on the young are barely studied. Using the latest European Social Survey from twenty-four countries. The authors related five isolation measures, from rarely meeting others to lacking emotional support, against inactivity, smoking, drinking, and body weight. They did this generation by generation.

Isolation tracked with worse health behavior in every generation. Rarely meeting socially, for instance, raised the odds of physical inactivity across all ages. Generation X appeared as a bridge group, mixing traditional and modern patterns of connection and habit. Anti-isolation policy, they argue, should be age-specific and start young, because disconnection's health costs accumulate across a lifetime; social connection itself is preventive medicine.
plos-pone-0358125:
Jingwang Liu led a team of eight authors testing a drug's protective effect in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When blood flow returns to a limb cut off from circulation, the return itself injures muscle, a harm called ischemia-reperfusion injury. The team tested esketamine, a drug already used in clinics, against that injury.

Liu's group found that esketamine protected skeletal muscle in the mouse model. They linked the effect to regulation of autophagy, the cell's cleanup and recycling process. A drug already in human use is an attractive candidate, since its safety record is known. Much testing remains, but the finding hints that surgical patients could one day get muscle protection from a familiar drug.
plos-pone-0358225:
Asha Z Goodman, Winston T Stauffer, and Philippe A Gallay test a two drug bet against the worst outcomes of fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The logic pairs correction with repair: semaglutide, the metabolic drug, against weight and sugar, plus a cyclophilin inhibitor aimed at the inflammation and scarring that become self sustaining. Their mice developed the disease on a Western diet with sugar water and a liver toxin. Then each group received one drug alone, or both together.

The pairing's effects diverged by outcome, as the design half expected. Semaglutide clearly cut body weight and shrank the liver tumor burden, the cancer endpoint that matters most. Scar tissue, measured by collagen staining, did not differ significantly between the treatment groups. The authors report the split honestly: metabolic victory, fibrosis stalemate. Advanced liver disease may need the scar targeted earlier, harder, or by other means than these.
plos-pone-0358325:
Yeliz Yilmaz Bozok and three colleagues compared two AI chatbots answering breast cancer questions, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Patients increasingly ask chatbots about their disease, so the quality of those answers matters. The team put patient-oriented questions to both ChatGPT and Gemini and scored the replies.

Bozok's head-to-head comparison tells patients and doctors which system gave safer and more accurate answers in this test. It also shows where both systems fell short, which is just as useful. Clinics fielding patient questions about AI use gain grounded advice here. The wider lesson is that chatbot answers on cancer should be checked, and studies like this show how to check them.
plos-pone-0358425:
Rebaka Pradhan and Onn Shehory review what computing research has done about labor trafficking online, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Traffickers now recruit and coordinate through digital platforms, while traces of offline exploitation also sit in online records. The authors separate those two settings and ask which machine learning and analytics methods have been tried in each, and where the gaps lie.

Following standard scoping review practice, they searched six databases plus extra sources and screened more than two thousand records down to twenty-one articles worth mapping. Work clusters around online recruitment fraud, illicit massage businesses, supply chains, and high risk industries such as fishing. Case studies, readable classifiers, and topic modeling appear often. Their closing agenda points future researchers toward the neglected settings and data types.
plos-pone-0359425: Cao and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on reading feelings from behavior signals. Their method joins two ideas: injecting extra hub nodes into a graph as behavior unfolds, and fusing the streams with graph attention. The task is multimodal sentiment analysis, judging mood from several signal types at once. Systems that read mood well could support mental health tools and more responsive machines.
plos-pone-0359525:
Zena Abdul-Ameer Mahdi and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It investigates plant chemicals from Rhizophora mucronata, a mangrove tree. The question is whether these phytochemicals can block proteins linked to lung cancer, acting as inhibitors that slow the disease's machinery.

The approach is computational, using multiscale and in silico analyses, meaning computer simulations at several levels rather than wet-lab tests. Screening mangrove compounds on a computer is a cheap first pass for drug hunting. If any candidate looks strong, laboratory teams can test it in cells. Natural product researchers are the readers for this early-stage evidence.
plos-pone-0359625: López-González and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spotting risky drinking in Guaviare, Colombia. They adapted the AUDIT, a standard alcohol screening survey, for primary care with mixed cultural groups. The team checked that the adapted questions read clearly and made sense to local users. A screening tool that fits local speech can catch alcohol harm earlier across Latin America.
pmc-13236725:
Salim and colleagues ask whether blood-thinning drugs raise bleeding risk in people with cavernous malformations in the brain. These tangled vessel clusters can bleed into the brain, so doctors often fear prescribing antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs to patients who have them. Hard evidence for that fear has been lacking, leaving hard calls in stroke and heart care.

Using a large health records platform, the team matched patients with these malformations who took blood thinners against similar patients who did not. None had bled before. Comparing later brain bleeds between matched groups gives the fairest test short of a trial, and the answer can free needed treatment.
pmc-13237925:
Huston and colleagues test whether stimulating nerves through the ear can prime the blood to clot faster. In animals, vagus nerve stimulation reduces bleeding after injury. The signal runs through immune cells in the spleen, which raise calcium inside platelets, readying them to activate the moment tissue is torn and clots are needed.

Healthy volunteers received ear-based vagus stimulation, alone or combined with trigeminal nerve stimulation. The team then measured platelet function and standard clotting tests. A safe, wearable way to prime clotting could matter in surgery and trauma, where minutes of bleeding decide outcomes. First, though, the effect must be shown in people, as here.
pmc-13238925:
Handke and colleagues ask whether obesity helps or harms patients treated for advanced urological cancers. Extra weight is reshaping outcomes across oncology in surprising ways. Their study covers metastatic bladder, kidney, and prostate cancers, the three big cancers of the urinary and male reproductive systems, in patients given systemic drug therapy at one high-volume centre.

Looking back over cases treated from 2017 to 2025, the team compares survival between patients with and without obesity. Cancer doctors know this as the obesity paradox question: heavier patients sometimes live longer on modern drugs. A centre-level answer helps clinicians counsel patients honestly instead of assuming weight only ever works against them.
pmc-13242125:
Schöneberg's team in Frankfurt sequenced every type specimen of a Bolivian frog whose home was logged before it was named. Oreobates chiquitanus survives at three sites in the Chiquitano Dry Forest, all near active logging. A base genome came from one paratype; side genomes covered all types. The museum stores became a genetic time capsule.

History rebuilt from genes shows the population rebounding from a dip some three hundred thousand years ago. Gene variety suggests a still-healthy gene pool. Every known population sits beside logging sites all the same. The genomes now anchor a starting line for tracking future genetic erosion.
pmc-13242325:
Hyera's team at the Western Cape bathed fat cells in gold specks to block lipid storage. The work stayed in cell dishes. Citrate-capped particles of fourteen nanometres were made by simple chemistry. Mature mouse fat cells received rising doses. Staining, survival assays, and gene activity arrays tracked the response.

The particles spared cell survival while cutting cell lipid build-up dose by dose. 35 genes shifted, clustered around fat formation and lipid handling. Networks centered on PPAR signaling and fat-cell hub genes. Hyera pitches the gold particles as an obesity play awaiting animal tests.
pmc-13246525:
Smith, Jin, Miller, and co-authors built reference samples for testing milk for bird flu, in this 2026 Food and Environmental Virology paper. With highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 turning up in dairy cattle, laboratories need to detect the virus in milk, and proficiency exercises check whether labs get the right answers. That requires spiked milk samples whose virus levels are known precisely and stay uniform.

The team used digital PCR to count viral genomes in their stock and samples exactly, then confirmed the standard USDA detection assay read them consistently. Replicate samples barely varied, no milk-matrix interference appeared, and levels stayed stable over time. Such well-characterized samples, they argue, make nationwide lab evaluations trustworthy.
pmc-13246925:
Pelzer, Werthmann, and Svaldi piloted mirror exposure therapy for teenagers with anorexia nervosa in this 2026 Eating and Weight Disorders study. Distorted body image drives the illness, and guided sessions viewing oneself in a mirror reduce that distortion in adults, but evidence in adolescents was thin. Twenty-four female inpatients were randomized to twelve mirror sessions over four weeks or to usual treatment alone.

Mirror exposure added no measurable benefit on overall body image or eating-disorder symptoms; both groups improved during inpatient care anyway. Exploratory analyses hinted the mirror group reduced body-checking and avoidance behaviors, and eye tracking confirmed patients fixated on body parts they disliked, though that bias did not shift. The authors say larger trials must find which patients benefit and when.
pmc-13248325:
Ramadanov and colleagues built a prediction model for blood transfusion around hip replacement surgery, reported in 2026. Transfusions after this operation link to worse outcomes and higher costs, yet clinics lacked a tool built for this procedure. The team drew on a registry from one certified German arthroplasty center covering 2016 to 2023.

Of six hundred forty-eight patients, about one in six needed a transfusion. Low starting hemoglobin, longer operating time, greater blood loss, and lower body weight each raised the risk, while male sex lowered it. The model sorted patients accurately, and the authors ask for testing at other hospitals before routine use.
pmc-13248825:
Silveira and a Brazilian team built an antibacterial wound dressing, reported in Small Science in 2026. Infection is the most common reason skin wounds stall, so the team made zinc oxide nanoparticles using moringa leaf extract as fuel. They spun those particles into a membrane of two biodegradable plastics using an electric field method called electrospinning.

The best membrane, holding five percent nanoparticles, soaked up more than three times its weight in fluid and stayed friendly to skin cells in culture. It also held back two common wound bacteria, Staphylococcus aureus and E. coli. The authors propose the dressing for infected and slow-healing wounds, pending further testing.
pmc-13249725:
Valentine, Zhang, and Liu measured how attention treats shapes, in a 2026 perception study. When people attend to a simple feature like color, nearby feature values get a boost that fades with distance, a pattern called similarity gain. The team asked whether the same holds for shape, using a circular shape space where forms morph gradually into one another.

Volunteers watched two target shapes and ignored overlapping distractors, reporting brightness changes in the targets only. Accuracy peaked when the two targets matched and fell steadily as their shapes diverged, across two experiments with different shape ranges. The authors read this as shape-similarity gain: attention boosts look-alike shapes, suggesting the brain keeps an inner similarity map for objects.
pmc-13250225:
Iwu-Jaja and colleagues map research on fighting drug-resistant infections across the World Health Organization's African region. Their 2026 BMJ Public Health scoping review sorts interventions against the five goals of the global action plan on antimicrobial resistance. The team searched four databases, plus grey sources, in late 2025.

Forty-nine studies qualified, clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria. Most tested stewardship programs or awareness training in large hospitals and showed better prescribing or knowledge, but few tracked long-term change.
