The ABC of Relativity, published in 1925, is Russell's popular account of Einstein's special and general relativity. Einstein had remade physics, and the public needed a guide who could write clearly. Russell, a philosopher of mathematics, took the task.

He explains why events called simultaneous may not be, how gravity becomes geometry, and what the famous tests showed, using trains, lifts, and clocks instead of equations. The book avoids false simplicity: Russell admits where the ideas strain common sense and says why they must be accepted anyway. It became the standard lay introduction of its era and still serves readers well.
santayana-dialogues-limbo-1925:
Dialogues in Limbo, published in 1925, sets Santayana's arguments among the dead, in the Platonic manner. In limbo, shades of Alcibiades, Democritus, Dionysius, and a modern stranger debate philosophy, religion, and the modern world without the heat of the living.

Santayana speaks largely through the Stranger, testing his views on nature against ancient thought and modern faith. The dialogue form lets doubts be voiced that a treatise would suppress. Death gives the speakers leisure and honesty in equal measure. The book is playful, serene, and quietly radical, a favorite among his readers for its ease of manner.
scott-hermetica-vol-2-1925:
Volume two of Walter Scott's Hermetica appeared in 1925 as pure commentary. Scott works through the Corpus Hermeticum tract by tract in these notes. The first volume's texts and translations are assumed open beside it.

He explains dark passages, traces sources, and wrestles with damaged Greek. Competing readings get weighed with patience and learning. Readers who want to grasp what the Hermetic sermons actually say need this guide. Scott can be exacting, and his rearrangements of texts drew later criticism. Even so, the commentary's depth rewards patience. It remains a serious companion to the Hermetica.
shahnama-warner-vol-9-1925:
Volume 9 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1925, completing the first complete English version of the Persian national epic. Firdausi finished the Book of Kings around 1010, after some thirty years of work. The Warners' own labor ran to nine volumes over twenty years.

Final chapters close the Sasanian story and the epic itself, with indexes and notes to guide readers back through the whole. Firdausi's own words about his task and his patrons appear in the closing sections. The completed set gave English readers Persia's founding story entire for the first time. It remains a monument of translation and of the epic it carries.
shinn-game-of-life-1925:
Florence Scovel Shinn wrote The Game of Life and How to Play It in 1925. Shinn was a New York art hand turned faith guide. The book teaches the laws of wealth, health, and right life. Tales from her own work with folk fill its pages.

Words have power, Shinn holds, and what a man speaks he draws to him. Fear is the great foe, and faith the cure for all lack. Short, sharp tales show her rules at work in shops and homes. The book is one of the most read faith works of its age.
spence-atlantis-in-america-1925:
Atlantis crossed the ocean in Lewis Spence's telling of 1925. Atlantis in America makes the case that the lost land's heirs, or its kin, stood in the New World. Spence pairs Plato's old account with the ruins and myths of Mexico and its neighbors.

He reads Maya and Aztec tales, temple forms, and flood myths as echoes of an Atlantic source. The book is the key statement of the American school of Atlantis thought. Spence wrote it as the New World half of his wider Atlantis work. Readers met here a bolder, more concrete version of his claim.
spence-problem-of-atlantis-1925:
Writer Lewis Spence made a scholarly case for Atlantis in The Problem of Atlantis. Spence was a Scottish poet and occult writer of wide learning. He treated Plato's island tale as garbled history, not mere myth.

He gathers geology, myth, and reports of Atlantic lands into one brief. Cro-Magnon culture in Europe and America anchors his argument. He answers rival theories point by point in calm prose. Mainstream scholars never granted his case. The book still stands as the most reasoned fringe brief for Atlantis, useful to readers on either side.
spr-proceedings-vol35-1925:
Parts ninety three through ninety six make volume thirty five, printed in 1925. The Society for Psychical Research nears the end of the span its archive is known for. Telepathy trials take their place beside reports of sittings and cases. Mediums old and new face the society's practiced tests.

Records of sittings run long, with sitters testing claims against private facts. Apparition reports continue under the old standards of proof. Skeptics within the society publish beside the convinced. Volume thirty five keeps the journal of record true to its founding bargain. Evidence and doubt share the binding. The long debate of the era breathes in these pages.
stein-making-of-americans-1925:
The Making of Americans, published in 1925, is Stein's thousand-page novel of everyone. Begun as a history of one family, the Herslands, it swells into an attempt to describe every kind of person who has ever lived.

Stein's prose circles and repeats, working out her idea that character shows itself in the bottom nature of each person, endlessly restated. Whole chapters turn on tiny variations of a single sentence. Few readers finish it; many writers have been changed by trying. It is the long laboratory of her continuous present, the experiment behind all her later work.
stendhal-charterhouse-parma-moncrieff-19:
Fabrice del Dongo rides into Waterloo half understanding what he sees, in Stendhal's Charterhouse of Parma. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's 1925 translation, complete in two volumes, carries Balzac's praised masterpiece of court life at Parma. Balzac himself called it among the century's greatest novels, and his study of Stendhal rides along in this edition.

Prison, a great-aunt's schemes, and a forbidden love shape Fabrice's path through a petty, sparkling court. Stendhal writes fast and dry, letting politics and passion share every scene. The charterhouse of the title waits at the end as refuge, the quiet close of a life spent chasing joy.
sur-les-fonctions-du-cerveau-et-sur-cell: Sur les fonctions du cerveau, 1825. The French brain functions. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
tob-10825:
Mead edited Five Years of Theosophy in 1885, picking the best early pieces from The Theosophist, the movement's own magazine. The book shows a young creed finding its voice in print. Karma and rebirth, the astral plane, and the hidden masters said to guide the work all get long, full treatment.

The pieces teach the creed to new readers and fight its critics in the same breath. Mead later won fame as a scholar of Gnosticism, and his picks show what the first Theosophists truly taught. For those who study the group's roots, this book keeps the first five years in the words the members chose.
tob-13325:
Claud Field's translation presents al-Ghazali's Deliverance from Error, the famed teacher's own account of losing and remaking his faith. Al-Ghazali held a prestigious post in Baghdad, then suffered a crisis that left him unable to lecture. He gave up the post, left the city, and found peace as a wandering Sufi.

His narrative sorts the ways people claim knowledge, theologians, philosophers, and mystics among them, and explains why only lived experience finally cured his doubt. V1 evidence calls it Islam's most personal tale of doubt and healing. A medieval mind tells of its own crisis with a frankness modern memoirists would recognize.
tob-13725:
G. R. S. Mead, an English scholar and theosophist, completed his Thrice-Greatest Hermes in 1906 with this third volume. The set presents the writings tied to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt and Greece. Mead translated, ordered, and explained texts few English readers could reach.

Volume three gives the remaining fragments, the Kore Kosmou, and sayings preserved by later writers, with Mead's notes. Together the volumes made the Hermetica open to general readers in English. Scholars now use newer editions, but Mead's labor first carried these texts of late antique religion to a wide public.
tob-4025:
William Molyneux's early English translation presents René Descartes's Six Metaphysical Meditations, the founding text of modern philosophy in its most concentrated form. Over six days of imagined solitude, Descartes retraces his search for certainty. An evil demon, invented to make doubt total, gives way to the cogito: I think, therefore I am.

Proofs of God's existence, the mind's distinction from the body, and the route back to trusting the senses occupy the later meditations. Molyneux, an Irish philosopher and friend of Locke, carried Descartes to English readers in their own tongue. Doubt as a road to truth has rarely been walked more carefully.
tob-4125:
Herbert A. Giles presented Chuang Tzu under three titles at once: mystic, moralist, and social reformer. Giles's lively translation made the butterfly-dreamer a favorite Chinese sage for English readers. Chuang Tzu dreams he is a butterfly and wakes unsure which side of the dream is real, and the book keeps that playful uncertainty throughout.

Mystic of the Tao, Chuang Tzu dissolves fixed distinctions; moralist against convention, he mocks scholars and rulers; reformer, he imagines freedom from useless striving. Talking skulls, giant trees, and Cook Ding's effortless knife carry the lessons. Often called the most entertaining classic in Chinese literature, it earns the title by laughing while it philosophizes.
tob-4225:
The Arbatel of Magick, a slim Latin grimoire of 1575, reaches English readers in Robert Turner's translation of 1655. Unlike the dark pacts of other grimoires, the Arbatel promises wisdom through prayer and a clean life. Its seven Olympic spirits rule 196 provinces of the unseen world between them.

Aphorisms lay down the magician's conduct: honor God, harm none, keep the hours of the spirits, and hold knowledge humbly. The tone is gentle, almost pastoral, for a book of magic. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Arbatel stands as the Renaissance gentleman's magic, complete in a few dozen pages.
treaty-of-rio-1825:
Portugal and Brazil signed the Treaty of Rio de Janeiro in 1825, formally settling Brazil's break from Portuguese rule. King John of Portugal accepted Brazil as an independent empire under his son, Dom Pedro. Brazil had declared its independence three years earlier, but Lisbon's legal recognition still had to be won at the negotiating table.

The text records Portugal's recognition, the titles each ruler would keep, and the financial terms that came with the settlement. Unlike the wars that freed Spanish America, this separation was closed by agreement between father and son. Brazil became a sovereign nation with its monarchy intact and its new status accepted in Europe.
trotsky-literature-revolution-1925:
Literature and Revolution, published in English in 1925 in Rose Strunsky's translation, is Leon Trotsky's theory of art after the Russian Revolution. The exiled revolutionary, then still a leader of the Soviet state, surveys Russian literature and asks what culture the new order should want.

Trotsky defends artistic freedom against party bureaucrats, arguing that art must work by its own laws, while he judges writers by their stance toward the revolution. Futurists, formalists, and fellow travelers are weighed with wit and severity. The book is a paradox: a Marxist classic against socialist realism. Its intelligence survives its moment.
un-doc-address-to-the-united-nations-gen:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of the Republic of Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 2008. He had led the Assembly itself when the 2001 attacks shook New York. This year marked sixty years since his country's founding. A world money crisis was deepening as he spoke.

He urges a shift to low-carbon, green growth. Korea will back that path with aid and a new East Asia climate fund. Seoul will give 100 million dollars in food aid over three years. He presses North Korea to restart the shutdown of its nuclear plant under the six-party talks. His warning on the cash crisis is plain: do not turn to trade walls.

President John F. Kennedy of the United States addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1961. The Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld, had died in a plane crash days before. The Soviet Union was pressing to replace him with a three-man team. The Berlin crisis hung over the hall.

Kennedy rejects the troika plan in plain terms. One driver, he says, or the machine stalls. He lays out an American plan to end all armies save a UN peace force. Cuts would come in checked stages, with watching built in. A test ban pact sits ready for signature. He challenges Moscow to a peace race and asks that space stay free of weapons.

Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, leader of Bangladesh, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on 25 September 1974. His country had just taken its seat at the world body. Its people, 75 million strong, had won freedom in a brutal war three years before. Floods that year had pushed the young state toward famine.

He frames the fight for Bangladesh as part of a world fight for self-rule. He backs the Arabs, the Palestinians, and the freedom drives of Africa. The rich world must help build a fairer trade and money order, he argues. He notes his grant of mercy to 195 prisoners of war. Peace with Pakistan, he says, should rest on fair play.
un-ga-res-25:
Where should the United Nations plant its flag for good? Resolution 25, passed in February 1946, picks the ground: Westchester County in New York, or Fairfield County in Connecticut, close to New York City. A headquarters team must go to the area at once. It is to study the ground in full and report back, with a firm pick of the site, at the next part of the session.

The team must draw plans at five sizes, from two square miles up to forty. For each, it must price the cost of buying the land and the buildings on it. It must also ask what steps the U.S., state, and county chiefs will take to guard how the land around the site grows. In the end, the UN rose instead in Manhattan.
un-ga-res-2625:
How states must treat each other was spelled out in full in Resolution 2625, adopted by the General Assembly in 1970. Its annex holds the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. A special team had worked on the rules since 1962, meeting last in Geneva in the spring of 1970. Their report lay before the Assembly.

The rules rest on the Charter. States are equal in rights. None may use force against the land or freedom of another. Rows must be settled by peaceful means, and no state may meddle in the home affairs of another. Peoples hold the right to rule themselves. States must also work with each other in good faith. The text is still a base stone of world law.
un-ga-res-44-25:
Children hold rights of their own. The world wrote them down in the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The General Assembly adopted it in Resolution 44/25 on 20 November 1989. The pact grew from the Charter's faith in the worth of each human person. It recalls the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the two great rights pacts, which hold that all are born to the same rights and freedoms.

The pact sets out the civil, civic, trade, and social rights of each child. States that join it bind themselves in world law to guard those rights. It took force on 2 September 1990. Ratified by more states than any other rights pact in the UN shelf, it is the base text for the rights of children across the world.
un-ga-res-a-69-25:
Israel's hold on the Syrian Golan is condemned in Resolution A/69/25, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The heights have been held since the war of 1967. The text recalls the Security Council's 1981 vote, which found Israel's bid to impose its laws on the Golan void. It also states again the core rule that land may not be taken by force.

Deep concern runs through the text that Israel has not pulled out, in breach of UN votes. The building of Israeli settlements on the Golan since 1967 is called unlawful. The 1949 Geneva pact on the safety of civilians in war is held to apply to the held land in full.
un-ga-res-address-to-the-united-nations-:
Han Seung-soo, prime minister of South Korea, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 2008. He spoke days after a bank collapse in the United States shook markets across the world. Leaders at the general debate that year all faced the same spreading financial crisis.

Han set out Korea's view of the crisis and the joint response it demanded. He also spoke on climate change, aid to poorer states, and peace on the Korean peninsula. The speech shows a mid-sized power arguing that shared problems need shared rules, stated at a tense moment.

John F. Kennedy, president of the United States, addressed the United Nations General Assembly on September 25, 1961. It was his first speech to the body, given months into his term and days after the death of Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld in a plane crash. The Cold War hung over every word.

Kennedy called for an end to the arms race and a ban on nuclear tests. He proposed that weapons of war be dismantled step by step under strict checks. He also pledged support for new states winning freedom. The address remains a high point of Cold War oratory.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 25, adopted on 14 February 1946, chose the ground for the permanent headquarters of the United Nations. The Assembly settled on Westchester County in New York and Fairfield County in Connecticut, near New York City. It set the temporary headquarters in New York City itself.

A nine-state Headquarters Commission was sent to study the region closely and report to the second part of the first session. It was to price sites from two to forty square miles. It was to ask United States authorities how nearby building would be controlled. It was to leave the final choice of place and size to the Assembly, with no money promised yet.

General Assembly Resolution 2625 (XXV) was adopted on 24 October 1970. It marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of the United Nations. It approved the Declaration on Principles of International Law concerning Friendly Relations and Cooperation among States. The annexed declaration restates the Charter's core rules as seven linked principles for how states must treat each other.

The principles bar the threat or use of force against any state's land or freedom. They require disputes to be settled by peaceful means. They forbid meddling in another state's home affairs. They also demand cooperation between states. They affirm equal rights and self-rule for peoples. They affirm the equal standing of all states. They require promises made under the Charter to be kept in good faith.

Hosted under the Resolution 44/25 label, the text here is the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The General Assembly adopted it and opened it for signing through resolution 44/25 of 20 November 1989. The preamble holds that childhood deserves special care. It holds that the family is the natural setting for a child's growth. It holds that a child needs legal protection before and after birth.

The articles define a child as a person under eighteen. They set out wide rights: life and fullest growth, a name and nationality, care by parents, and a voice in matters touching the child. They guard against unfair treatment and abuse. They cover schooling, health, play, and protection in war and in the courts.

General Assembly resolution 69/25 (2014), 'The Syrian Golan,' declares that Israel has failed to comply with Security Council resolution 497 (1981). It declares that Israel's 1981 decision imposing its laws and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan is null and void. The Assembly says the continued occupation and de facto annexation block a just regional peace. It demands Israeli withdrawal from all the occupied Syrian Golan to the line of 4 June 1967. It calls for peace talks on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks to resume.
un-sc-res-1025: Number 1025 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1995. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-125: Membership business takes up Resolution 125, adopted without dissent on 5 September 1957 at the Council's 786th meeting. The Federation of Malaya had applied to join the United Nations. Having examined that application, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that the Federation of Malaya be admitted to membership. The whole decision fits in one sentence, in the standard form used for such recommendations.
un-sc-res-1325: Filed in the official record under number 1325, this Council resolution is catalogued with a 1998 date. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1425: The record catalogued as Resolution 1425, dated 2002, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1525:
Southern Lebanon's United Nations force was renewed at the start of 2004. On 30 January 2004 the Security Council extended UNIFIL until 31 July 2004. The Secretary-General had recommended the six-month term. His report noted Israel's completed withdrawal in 2000. Lebanon was working to restore its authority in the south. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and full control of its borders.

Lebanon had to keep deploying its own armed forces in the south. The Council stressed the value of those steps. It also repeated the force's founding terms from 1978. All parties had to cooperate with UNIFIL for its full deployment. The renewal followed the pattern set since the Israeli pullout.
un-sc-res-1625:
World leaders adopted United Nations Security Council Resolution 1625 at the 2005 World Summit in New York. The date was 14 September 2005. The text is not about one country. It is a declaration on how the Council should stop wars before they start, with Africa at the center of concern.

The declaration voices deep worry at the human cost and material loss caused by armed conflict. It says peace, security, and growth support one another. Stopping conflict means tackling root causes such as poverty, bad rule, and abuse of rights. It calls for closer work with the African Union and other regional bodies so disputes get fast answers.
un-sc-res-1725:
A regional protection force for Somalia was authorized in late 2006. The transitional federal institutions and the Union of Islamic Courts had signed dialogue pledges in Khartoum in June. Talks had since broken down, and the courts held Mogadishu. The Council praised Arab League and IGAD work to restart dialogue. The arms embargo of 1992 still bound all states.

The Council restated that the Transitional Federal Charter offered the only route to peace and stability in Somalia. Both sides were urged to return to peace talks without delay. The Council authorized IGAD and African Union member states to set up a protection and training mission in Somalia, IGASOM. States bordering Somalia would not send troops, as the IGAD plan set out. The arms embargo would not apply to supplies meant for the new mission. Member states were encouraged to fund it.
un-sc-res-1825: From 2008, Resolution 1825 is part of the Security Council's formal record kept in this collection via Wikisource. The members' method is consistent across the series: state the situation, cite the principles, decide the steps. This entry keeps one complete pass through that method, in the words the fifteen delegations finally agreed to publish.
un-sc-res-1925:
The Council dealt with the Democratic Republic of the Congo in Resolution 1925, adopted on 28 May 2010. The government wanted the peacekeeping force gone by 2011. Aid groups warned that a sudden exit would spark fresh conflict. The east still suffered attacks, sexual violence, and child soldier use.

The Council renames the mission MONUSCO, the stabilization mission, from 1 July 2010. Its new term runs to 30 June 2011, with up to 19,815 troops. Up to 2,000 troops may leave by 30 June 2010 where safety permits. The rest will concentrate in the east, with a reserve ready to redeploy fast. Guarding civilians stays the first duty under Chapter VII.
un-sc-res-325:
Panama invited the Security Council to meet on its soil in 1973. The charter allows the Council to sit away from headquarters. Panama proposed sessions in Panama City from 15 to 21 March. Latin American states backed the idea without dissent. On 26 January 1973 the Council accepted the invitation. The agenda would cover peace and security in Latin America. Measures to strengthen both were the theme.

Panama offered to host the meetings and supply facilities at no cost. The Council thanked its government warmly. The Secretary-General had to negotiate a conference agreement at once. The Panama sessions became famous for debate on the canal treaties. A United States veto there helped push the canal question toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-425: Within the United Nations official record, Resolution 425 is the Security Council text catalogued for 1978. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-825: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 825, catalogued here at 1993. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1025 was adopted unanimously on 30 November 1995. It is a bridge between the UNCRO operation in Croatia and the transitional administration planned for Eastern Slavonia under the Basic Agreement. The Council acts under Chapter VII. It asks the Secretary-General to report by 14 December 1995 on all aspects of setting up the transitional administration and a transitional peacekeeping force. It decides that UNCRO's mandate will end after an interim period closing on 15 January 1996. It could end sooner, once the Council decides on deployment of the new force.

Security Council resolution 125, adopted unanimously on 5 September 1957, recommends to the General Assembly that the Federation of Malaya be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Council records that it had examined Malaya's application, supported by a document filed that summer. Admission recommendations of this kind are the Council's standard screening step. The Assembly then votes a new member state into the Organization.

Women, peace, and security became a standing Council concern with this landmark text of 31 October 2000. Women and girls, it notes, bear most of the harm in modern wars, as refugees and as targets of attack. Yet they were mostly shut out of the rooms where peace was negotiated and kept.

States are urged to place more women in decision-making roles on conflict and peace at every level. The text calls for more women as envoys and peacekeepers, for training on women's rights and needs, and for firm protection of women and girls during and after wars. Peace talks, it insists, must take women's voices and needs into account.

Somalia's arms embargo is tightened on 22 July 2002. Weapons and ammunition kept flowing into the country from outside, in breach of the embargo set in 1992. In the Council's view, that flow was undercutting peace efforts and national reconciliation talks planned under regional leadership.

The embargo is clarified to ban technical advice, money, and training tied to military activity as well. A Panel of Experts of three members, based in Nairobi for six months, is set up to gather independent evidence of violations. Its findings were meant to give the embargo real effect and strengthen it, working with the Council's sanctions committee for Somalia.

South Lebanon's uneasy calm got six more months of UN watch in 2004. The force there, UNIFIL, had kept its post since 1978. Beirut wrote on 14 January 2004 to ask for a new term. The chief's report of 20 January warned of strain and flare-ups. Resolution 1525 passed with no dissent on 30 January 2004.

The mandate ran to 31 July 2004. The Council backed the chief's plan in full. It voiced strong faith in Lebanon's right to rule its own soil. Beirut was urged to stretch its grip in the south. Its army had to spread there in force. All sides had to let the UN move with ease. Breaches of the Blue Line by air, sea, and land drew blame. Mine clearing won warm praise.

Conflict prevention, above all in Africa, is the theme of Resolution 1625, adopted on 14 September 2005 at a meeting of heads of state and government. The resolution adopts an annexed declaration. It notes the high human cost of conflict and says peace, security, and development reinforce each other. Root causes named include poverty, weak governance, and the illegal trade in arms and resources.

The declaration commits the Council to watch regions at risk. It also commits it to strengthen UN prevention work. That work covers regular assessments, support for preventive diplomacy and regional mediation, and early-warning capacity in regional bodies, especially the African Union. The Secretary-General must report often on regions at risk and help at-risk countries with risk assessments and dispute management. It backs fair elections, civil-society peace work, and a ten-year capacity-building programme for the African Union, including its planned African Standby Force.

Somalia gains an African guard force in Resolution 1725, passed in December 2006. The Council told all states once more to keep the arms ban of 1992. It said it would talk with any Somali side bent on a calm, broad peace. That pledge named the Union of Islamic Courts, which held the capital at the time. Arab and regional bids to open talks won warm words.

The Council let the region's bloc and African Union states set up a guard and training force in Somalia. The grant ran for six months and drew on the Charter's hard chapter. The force would shield the interim state and train its own troops. The arms ban was eased just enough to supply it.

Nepal's mission, UNMIN, is extended on 23 July 2008, in line with the government's request. Nepal's 2006 peace agreement had ended a decade of civil war between the state and Maoist rebels. Constituent Assembly elections had been held successfully on 10 April 2008, a central step in the peace deal.

The mission's remaining tasks stay in place for a further period, above all watching the management of arms and armies from the war. The Secretary-General's plan for a phased, gradual drawdown and exit of mission staff is endorsed. All parties are called on to use the mission's expertise while it lasts, and the government is urged to finish the peace deal's remaining business, including a new constitution.

Congo's mission is renamed for a stabilization phase in Resolution 1925, adopted in 2010. MONUC had helped Congo's recovery, but armed groups persisted in the Kivus and Orientale, and the Secretary-General's April 2010 report judged it was entering a peace-consolidation phase.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC to 30 June 2010. It renames it MONUSCO, the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from 1 July 2010, authorized until 30 June 2011. MONUSCO may field up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. The forces are concentrated in the east, with a rapidly redeployable reserve. Up to 2,000 troops withdraw by 30 June 2010 where security permits. Protection of civilians under imminent threat is the first priority, using all necessary means. Future drawdowns depend on finishing operations against armed groups and building government protection capacity.

A mountain realm ringed by South Africa won its freedom in 1966. Lesotho had been a British-held land, called Basutoland. It took back its old name at freedom on 4 October. Its bid for a UN seat moved fast. Resolution 225 passed with no dissent on 14 October 1966. The vote shared a busy day. Botswana and Congo's mercenary plea were heard at the same meet.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Lesotho. The Assembly did so days hence. King Moshoeshoe II led the new state. Its fate was bound to its vast next-door state on all sides. Work and water deals with South Africa ruled its purse. This brief text marks the legal birth of one of the world's few states that sits inside one other land's bounds.

Italy, like Hungary, sought a UN seat after losing the Second World War. Its application came before the Council in May 1947. Resolution 25 was adopted on 22 May 1947. Ten members voted in favor, none against. Australia abstained. Former enemy states faced a slow road into the new organization.

The resolution refers Italy's bid to the admissions committee. That body would study the application and report back. No promise of membership was made. The step may look minor, but it mattered. It kept Italy's case moving inside the system. Italy finally joined the UN in 1955, after years of Cold War deadlock over admissions.

Panama threw open its doors to the Council in 1973. Its foreign chief wrote on 9 January with a bold ask. Host the Council for a week that March. Latin states backed the plan with one voice. A study team checked costs and needs. Resolution 325 passed on 26 January 1973. No one spoke against it.

The Council would sit in Panama City. The dates were 15 to 21 March 1973. The theme was peace and safety in Latin America, read through the Charter's lens. Panama would host and give gear and help free of charge. The chief had to strike a pact with Panama at once. Such trips were rare. The Panama week let the Council show its face far from New York glass.

Israeli forces invaded southern Lebanon in March 1978, and Lebanon protested to the Council at once. The fighting badly worsened the situation in the Middle East. Lebanon asked for a United Nations force to be sent. Resolution 425 was adopted on 19 March 1978, days after the invasion.

The Council called for strict respect for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and political independence, within its recognized borders. Israel had to stop its military action against Lebanon at once. All its forces had to leave Lebanese territory. The Council then created the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, known as UNIFIL. Its tasks were to confirm the Israeli withdrawal and restore peace and security. It would also help Lebanon's government regain authority in the south. A report on the force was due within twenty-four hours.

North Korea announced in the spring of 1993 that it would withdraw from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Its foreign minister wrote to the Council on 12 March 1993. The International Atomic Energy Agency had found North Korea in breach of its safeguards agreement. Resolution 825 was adopted on 11 May 1993.

The Council called on North Korea to reconsider the announcement. The country had to renew its commitment to the treaty. It also had to honor its non-proliferation duties in full. Its safeguards agreement with the atomic agency had to be obeyed, as the agency's board had set out. The agency's Director-General was asked to keep consulting North Korea to resolve the issues. He had to report back to the Council on progress. The text was an early step in a crisis that would run for decades.
undset-the-mistress-of-husaby-kristin-la:
Kristin Lavransdatter returns as a wife and estate holder in The Mistress of Husaby, the middle book of Undset's trilogy, in Archer's 1925 English version. Her home is the great farm of Husaby. Marriage, once her fierce goal, now brings strain and sorrow.

Her husband proves weak where she needs strength, and her sons grow wild. Old sins from her youth still weigh on her mind and faith. Undset shows married life and motherhood with rare honesty for any age. The tale deepens from romance into tragedy as Kristin's pride and guilt pull against each other.
untitled-1925: Untitled, 1925. Chemistry and modern life, in Russian. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
vita-merlini-parry-1925:
Geoffrey of Monmouth followed his famous history of Britain's kings with the Vita Merlini, a Latin poem in hexameters about Merlin. J. J. Parry translated it into English in 1925. Here the great prophet appears not at court but broken and wild in the forest.

Merlin raves, grieves for the dead, and speaks prophecy to the wind and the stars. Geoffrey mixes madness with strange wisdom, and seasons turn as the old man watches them. Parry's version made the poem widely readable in English. It remains the oddest portrait of Merlin from the Middle Ages, half seer and half wild man.
watson-behaviorism-1925:
John B. Watson published Behaviorism in 1925, the manifesto of his school of psychology. Watson argues that psychology should study only observable behavior. Thoughts, feelings, and consciousness, he claims, cannot be measured and so do not belong in science. Learning through conditioning explains habits, emotions, and personality.

Watson promises that, given a dozen healthy infants and his own world, he could train any one for any trade. The boast became famous as a symbol of environmental faith. The book grew from lectures for general readers. It shaped American psychology for decades, in labs, schools, and advertising. Later schools softened its claims, but its influence endures.
weddell-voyage-south-pole-1825:
James Weddell was a sealer who sailed far south in the years 1822 to 1824. His book of 1825 tells of the trip in the brig Jane. Weddell reached 74 degrees south, a mark no ship had passed at that time. The sea that bears his name still marks that feat.

Seal hunts, ice, and storms shape the tale, with plain talk of risk and pay. Weddell charts isles and coasts new to maps of the day. He also writes on winds, currents, and the look of the far south. The book is a key source on the seal trade.
whitehead-science-modern-world-1925:
Alfred North Whitehead published Science and the Modern World in 1925, based on his Lowell Lectures. Whitehead traces how modern science grew from the thought of the 1600s. He links Newton, poets, and philosophers in one cultural story. Science, he argues, rests on a faith in order that came from older theology.

He criticizes the split of nature into dead matter and detached mind. Romantic poets, in his view, saw nature more truly than the mechanists. The book founded much of process philosophy. It also helped start the study of science as cultural history. Whitehead writes with grace rare in technical thought.
williams-american-grain-1925:
William Carlos Williams, a New Jersey doctor and poet, wrote In the American Grain in 1925 as a counter-history of America. Against the smooth schoolbook story, he sets raw encounters between the Old World and the New.

Chapters take up Columbus, Cotton Mather, Daniel Boone, and Poe, each rendered in a prose that shifts voice to match its subject. Williams hunts for a usable past: the local, earthy contact he thought American writing needed. The book argues that America's true grain lies in its ground and its speech. It became a sourcebook for poets seeking an American idiom.
woolf-common-reader-1925:
Virginia Woolf published The Common Reader in 1925, gathering essays she had written for journals over the previous decade. The title states her creed: these pieces address the ordinary reader who reads for pleasure, not the scholar.

Essays take up Jane Austen, the modern novel, the Elizabethans, and the art of reading itself. 'Modern Fiction' argues that the novel must catch life as it falls on the mind, not as plots arrange it. Woolf's voice is light, exact, and quietly radical. The collection defined a new way of writing about books, intimate and free, and it is still a model of the essay.
woolf-mrs-dalloway-1925:
Virginia Woolf published Mrs Dalloway in 1925, after reshaping it from an earlier short story. The whole novel fits inside a single June day in London, just after the First World War. Woolf used what she called a tunnelling method, digging into her characters' pasts as they walk the city.

Clarissa Dalloway buys flowers and prepares an evening party, her mind circling old loves and choices. Across London, the shell-shocked veteran Septimus Smith sinks toward suicide under visions of his dead officer. The two never meet, yet the party scene joins their stories at the close. Woolf's flowing sentences remade the English novel. Mrs Dalloway is now her most widely read book.
yeats-a-vision-1925:
William Butler Yeats built a system of soul and history from his wife's trance writing, and A Vision states it. Printed in 1925, the book maps men and ages to the phases of the moon. Yeats was Ireland's great poet, and this was his secret engine of verse.

Twenty-eight phases sort all human types, from the fool to the saint, around a great wheel. Ages of the world turn on the same wheel, each with its faith and its wars. Yeats drew poems and plays from the scheme for the rest of his life. The book is the core text of the literary occult revival.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol25:
Volume XXV of the Journal of Discourses, from Liverpool in 1885, stands second from last in the set. Shorthand reports preserve sermons by the church's senior men, preached in a season of raids and trials over marriage law. The pulpit voice here is by turns defiant, patient, and pastoral.

Thirty years of the Journal had made it the movement's great storehouse of spoken teaching. This volume adds the words of leaders who knew the founding age at first hand. Readers who follow the set to its end meet, in Volume XXV, the old church at its most embattled.
zorzi-de-harmonia-mundi-1525:
Francesco Zorzi, a Venetian Franciscan, published De Harmonia Mundi Totius, On the Harmony of the Whole World, at Venice in 1525. He dedicated the work to Pope Clement VII. The text is in Latin. Zorzi aimed at nothing less than one system in which Plato, the Kabbalah, music, and Christian faith would sing in tune.

He builds the world on number and proportion, from the music of the spheres to the measures of the temple. Hebrew letters, Greek philosophy, and the gospel expound one another in his pages. The Inquisition later eyed the book with suspicion, which adds to its fame. Zorzi shows the Franciscan mind of the Renaissance at its most daring and most learned.
